column1: Session Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 1 - Oral 4 - Modeling Articulation Survey Talk
column4: Paper Title Bio-Informed Speech Processing, Modeling, and Generation
column6: Abstract Conventional speech technologies rely primarily on acoustic signals, without explicitly accounting for the biological mechanisms underlying human speech production and perception. This survey examines bio-informed speech processing, modeling, and generation by integrating physiological signals with modern machine learning. We investigate how multimodal articulatory dynamics can enable robust motor-control representations and silent-speech interfaces. We further explore how neural markers and individualized hearing profiles can guide perceptual optimization, enhance speech quality, and maximize intelligibility. Grounding computational models in articulatory, muscular, and neuroauditory mechanisms establishes a transformative paradigm for next-generation assistive hearing devices, speech synthesis, and personalized communication systems across diverse speakers, communication environments, clinical needs, and application scenarios.
column7: Authors

column4: ArtBoost: Synthetic Articulatory Data Augmentation for Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion
column6: Recent acoustic-to-articulatory inversion (AAI) models rely on electromagnetic articulography (EMA) data, which are costly and limited in scale. To address this limitation, we propose ArtBoost, a novel data augmentation strategy that leverages large-scale speech-mesh datasets originally developed for speech-driven 3D facial animation to improve AAI under limited EMA supervision. ArtBoost extracts pseudo articulatory trajectories from visible facial anchors and uses them for pre-training before fine-tuning on real EMA data. Experiments show consistent improvements in PCC and RMSE. Trajectory analyses confirm that the pseudo articulatory signals reflect physically meaningful visible articulatory dynamics. Additional evaluations across different AAI architectures demonstrate stable performance gains, indicating that ArtBoost can be integrated into diverse AAI models. These results suggest that speech-mesh data provide an effective and scalable source of articulatory supervision for AAI. Project page: https://cau-irislab. github.io/Interspeech26-ArtBoost/
column7: Hyung Kyu Kim(Chung-Ang University); Byungchan Hwang(Chung-Ang University); Hak Gu Kim(Chung-Ang University)

column4: STArK: Towards Synthesizing Articulatory Kinematics from Text
column6: Recent deep learning approaches in modeling articulatory kinematics have shown success in mapping speech audio to electromagnetic articulography (EMA) kinematics, but these methods are limited by the scarcity of high-quality articulatory datasets. We introduce synthesizing text to articulatory kinematics (STArK), which offers a novel approach in generating articulatory kinematics directly from text. We train STArK on the LibriTTS-R dataset with pseudo-labeled EMA features derived from a pre-trained speech-to-articulation model. STArK is the first model to demonstrate high-quality articulatory kinematics generation from text. STArK achieves comparable performance to existing multi-speaker text-to-speech models at speech synthesis, while supporting voice cloning without seeing speaker embeddings during training. STArK aims to enable the generation of scalable articulatory data from text corpora for downstream tasks.
column7: Xavier Yin(Carnegie Mellon University); Carlos Busso(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Speech Production Analysis
column6: Physics-informed neural operators (PINOs) have recently gained attention as fast numerical simulators with potential for solving inverse problems. This study proposes the first PINO-based method for speech production analysis. The model learns the governing one-dimensional wave equations directly without requiring pre-computed supervised training data. Using vocal tract shape data as input features, we compare the proposed model's predicted f0, glottal volume velocity and sound pressure at the lip for five static vowels to a conventional Runge Kutta/Finite difference approach. With errors of 0.8% for glottal volume flow and 3.2% for speech waveforms, the proposed model enables efficient GPU-parallelized simulation without iterative calculations. We conclude that PINO is a promising approach for fast analysis of speech.
column7: Kazuya Yokota(Nagaoka University of Technology); Xinmeng Luan(McGill University); Debasish Ray Mohapatra(University of British Columbia); Gary Scavone(McGill University); Sidney Fels(University of British Columbia)

column4: PyPhonPlan: Simulating phonetic planning with dynamic neural fields and task dynamics
column6: We introduce PyPhonPlan, a Python toolkit for implementing dynamical models of phonetic planning using coupled dynamic neural fields and task dynamic simulations. The toolkit provides modular components for defining planning, perception and memory fields, as well as between-field coupling, gestural inputs, and using field activation profiles to solve tract variable trajectories. We illustrate the toolkit's capabilities through an example application: simulating production/perception loops with a coupled memory field, which demonstrates the framework's ability to model interactive speech dynamics using representations that are temporally-principled, neurally-grounded, and phonetically-rich. PyPhonPlan is released as open-source software and contains executable examples to promote reproducibility, extensibility, and cumulative computational development for speech communication research.
column7: Sam Kirkham(Lancaster University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 4 - Oral 6 - Speaker Privacy and Anonymization

column4: Privacy vs. Performance: Assessing Communication Utility of Anonymized Voice Features
column6: Voice anonymization is essential for protecting user privacy, yet it may distort acoustic cues that are critical for communication assessment. In this work, we study the impact of phase vocoder time-scale modification (PV-TSM), a lightweight anonymization technique selected for operational efficiency, on acoustic and prosodic feature preservation. We integrate PV-TSM into an end-to-end speech analysis pipeline and evaluate its effects on acoustic features as well as automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance. Our results show that anonymization can largely preserve these features while effectively masking speaker identity. Further, fine-tuning the ASR model with anonymized speech mitigates recognition errors and restores downstream feature accuracy. These findings demonstrate that privacy protection and prosodic fidelity can coexist, enabling reliable communication assessment in privacy-sensitive contexts.
column7: Amanda Chan(Educational Testing Service); Chee Wee Leong(Educational Testing Service); Candy Olivia Mawalim(Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Shogo Okada(Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)

column4: DiffAnon: Diffusion-based Prosody Control for Voice Anonymization
column6: To preserve or not to preserve prosody is a central question in voice anonymization. Prosody conveys meaning and affect, yet is tightly coupled with speaker identity. Existing methods either discard prosody for privacy or lack a principled mechanism to control the utility-privacy trade-off, operating at fixed design points. We propose DiffAnon, a diffusion-based anonymization method with classifier-free guidance (CFG) that provides explicit, continuous inference-time control over prosody preservation. DiffAnon refines acoustic detail over semantic embeddings of an RVQ codec, enabling smooth interpolation between anonymization strength and prosodic fidelity within a single model. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first voice anonymization framework to provide structured, interpolatable inference-time prosody control. Experiments demonstrate structured trade-off behavior, achieving strong utility while maintaining competitive privacy across controllable operating points.
column7: Ismail Rasim Ulgen(Johns Hopkins University); Zexin Cai(Johns Hopkins University); Nicholas Andrews(Johns Hopkins University); Philipp Koehn(Johns Hopkins University); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: DP-VOXLET: Provable Speaker Anonymization for Disentangled Speech Representations
column6: Systems for speaker anonymization obfuscate the speaker of an utterance, while maintaining its original semantic contents and prosody. Recent solutions for speaker anonymization rely on learned representations that disentangle an utterance into semantic contents and speaker properties. To anonymize an utterance, these systems replace the speaker properties while leaving the semantic contents unchanged—an approach that can produce strong results on empirical measures of privacy. In this work, we introduce speaker differential privacy, a formal definition of speaker anonymization based on the framework of differential privacy, and a mechanism for speaker anonymization that provably satisfies the definition. In contrast to prior heuristic-based anonymization systems, our approach enables a provable lower bound on re-identification success rate (e.g. equal error rate) for any possible adversary. We implement our approach in a framework that is compatible with existing disentangled representations. Compared to the prior work on differential privacy for speaker anonymization, our approach achieves significantly higher utility.
column7: Ivoline Ngong(University of Vermont); Jack D'Iorio(University of Vermont); Hailey Schoppe(University of Vermont); Christopher Liberatore(Galois, Inc.); Nichole Schimanski(Galois, Inc.); Taisa Kushner(Galois, Inc.); Joseph P. Near(University of Vermont)

column4: Voice Privacy from an Attribute-based Perspective
column6: Voice privacy approaches that preserve the anonymity of speakers modify speech in an attempt to break the link with the true identity of the speaker. Current benchmarks measure speaker protection based on signal-to-signal comparisons. In this paper, we introduce an attribute-based perspective, where we measure privacy protection in terms of comparisons between sets of speaker attributes. First, we analyze privacy impact by calculating speaker uniqueness for ground truth attributes, attributes inferred on the original speech, and attributes inferred on speech protected with standard anonymization. Next, we examine a threat scenario involving only a single utterance per speaker and calculate attack error rates. Overall, we observe that inferred attributes still present a risk despite attribute inference errors. Our research points to the importance of considering both attribute-related threats and protection mechanisms in future voice privacy research.
column7: Mehtab Ur Rahman(Centre for Language Studies); Martha Larson(Centre for Language Studies; Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor-Garcia(Centre for Language Studies)

column4: Acoustic token admixture for joint speaker and content anonymization
column6: Speech recordings in regulated domains cannot be shared or reused for AI development without suppressing two independent re-identification channels: biometric speaker identity and linguistically identifying content. Existing approaches address each channel in isolation and require full re-synthesis, sacrificing the in-domain acoustic characteristics that make recordings valuable. We propose a unified acoustic token-space framework that jointly anonymizes both channels via per-frame admixture of encoder-derived and phoneme-conditioned tokens, with NER-triggered span replacement preserving surrounding prosody. On the VoicePrivacy 2024 benchmark the system achieves EER 42.54%, within one point of the challenge top submission, with WER 3.73%.
column7: Ali Golmakani(Nijta SAS); Seyed Ahmad Hosseini(Nijta SAS); Omar Manil Bendali(Nijta SAS); Emmanuel Vincent(Nijta SAS; Université de Lorraine); Brij Mohan Lal Srivastava(Nijta SAS)

column4: Privacy-Preserving End-to-End Full-Duplex Speech Dialogue Models
column6: End-to-end full-duplex speech models feed user audio through an always-on LLM backbone, yet the speaker privacy implications of their hidden representations remain unexamined. Following the VoicePrivacy 2024 protocol with a lazy-informed attacker, we show that the hidden states of SALM-Duplex and Moshi leak substantial speaker identity across probed transformer layers. Layer-wise and turn-wise analyses reveal that leakage persists across these layers, with SALM-Duplex showing stronger leakage in early layers while Moshi leaks uniformly, and that Linkability rises sharply in the first few turns. We propose two streaming anonymization setups using Stream-Voice-Anon: a waveform-level front-end (Anon-W2W) and a feature-domain replacement (Anon-W2F). Anon-W2F raises EER over 3.5× relative to the discrete encoder baseline (11.2%→41.0%), approaching the 50% chance ceiling, while Anon-W2W retains 78-93% of baseline sBERT across setups with sub-second first response latency (FRL under 0.8 s).
column7: Nikita Kuzmin(NTU; A*STAR); Tao Zhong(Huawei; CUHK); Jiajun Deng(Huawei); Yingke Zhu(Huawei); Tristan Tsoi(Huawei); Tianxiang Cao(Huawei); Simon Lui(Huawei); Kong Aik Lee(Hong Kong PolyU); Eng Siong Chng(NTU)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 5 - Oral 7 - Speech signal analysis

column4: Factorization and Latent Structure in Speech Representations
column6: Structure in speech representations facilitates controlled generation, transfer to new domains, and analysis of model behavior. This talk surveys methods for imposing and discovering structure in speech representations. We give an overview of top-down techniques for imposing structure on learned representations, including the use of factorized training objectives, model distillation, and explicit bottlenecks or interpretable control variables. We discuss the advantages and limitations of this approach and contrast them with bottom-up techniques, including probing, controlled perturbations, latent-space arithmetic, and resynthesis, for discovering and exploiting pre-existing structure in large pre-trained models. We conclude by discussing applications enabled by such structure, including controllable generation and editing, voice conversion, domain transfer, efficient speech modeling, and the separation or attribution of multiple speakers.

column4: Multilingual Word-Level Forced Alignment with Self-Supervised Representations and Learned Dynamic Programming
column6: We present a method for accurate multilingual word-level forced alignment, consisting of an alignment encoder and a learned alignment decoder. The encoder integrates two representations: one from the Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) model and another from a self-supervised phoneme boundary detector (UnSupSeg). It learns to fuse them and to estimate word-boundary probabilities over long temporal contexts. The alignment decoder is a learned dynamic programming that combines encoder outputs with segmental features over the MMS and UnSupSeg representations to infer final word boundaries. Trained iteratively on TIMIT and Buckeye, the proposed approach outperforms Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) and MMS-based alignment on both datasets. On unseen languages (Dutch, German, and Hebrew), the proposed model achieves performance consistently better than or on par with existing alignment approaches, indicating its potential to scale to 1100+ languages supported by MMS without further training.
column7: Roy Weber(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Meidan Zehavi(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Rotem Rousso(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Joseph Keshet(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology)

column4: V-Align: Visual Forced Alignment via Phoneme to Video Optimal Path Traversal
column6: Visual Forced Alignment (VFA) aims to temporally localize linguistic units within silent talking-face videos, enabling alignment when audio is noisy or unavailable. We propose V-Align, a structured framework that formulates VFA as an optimal monotonic path traversal problem over a frame-phoneme compatibility lattice. Given the lip-motion embeddings and transcript-derived phoneme representations, V-Align learns a soft traversal posterior and recovers discrete boundaries via dynamic programming. Training follows a two-stage strategy: Stage 1 encourages optimal path learning without explicit boundary supervision and already achieves competitive performance relative to fully supervised VFA baselines, while Stage 2 refines boundary precision using additional word-level supervision. Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 demonstrate state-of-the-art MAE and frame accuracy. Code and demo are available at: https://valign-interspeech.github.io/.
column7: Souvik Ghosh(IIIT Hyderabad); C. V. Jawahar(IIIT Hyderabad); Vinay Namboodiri(University of Bath)

column4: findsylls: A Language‑Agnostic Toolkit for Syllable‑Level Speech Tokenization and Embedding
column6: Syllable-level units offer compact and linguistically meaningful representations for spoken language modeling and unsupervised word discovery, but research on syllabification remains fragmented across disparate implementations, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce findsylls, a modular, language-agnostic toolkit that unifies classical syllable detectors and end-to-end syllabifiers under a common interface for syllable segmentation, embedding extraction, and multi-granular evaluation. The toolkit implements and standardizes widely used methods (e.g., Sylber, VG-HuBERT) and allows their components to be recombined, enabling controlled comparisons of representations, algorithms, and token rates. We demonstrate findsylls on English and Spanish corpora and on new hand-annotated data from Kono, an underdocumented Central Mande language, illustrating how a single framework can support reproducible syllable-level experiments across both high-resource and under-resourced settings.
column7: Héctor Javier Vázquez Martínez(University of Pennsylvania)

column4: Duration-Aware Soft Targets for Text-Independent Supervised Phone Segmentation
column6: Hard boundaries are commonly used as ground truth targets for text-independent supervised phone segmentation. However, prior works do not explicitly model the uncertainty in phone transition annotations. To address this limitation, we propose the use of soft targets in place of hard boundaries. The ambiguity of transition around boundary events is modeled using two unnormalized zero-mean half Gaussian pulses centered at each boundary indicated by the hard targets, with standard deviations proportional to neighboring segment durations. Hard labels within two standard deviations of the boundary are replaced with Gaussian function values, while the other labels remain unchanged. Using soft targets, a baseline BiGRU model achieves an R-val of 91.53% on the TIMIT test split. Experiments on out-of-domain and multilingual data show statistically significant improvements over hard targets.
column7: Raghavan Ramesh(IIT Hyderabad); Meka Nani(IIT Hyderabad); Sri Rama Murty Kodukula(IIT Hyderabad)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 7 - Oral 7 - LLM Based Speech Synthesis

column4: Decoding Order Matters in Autoregressive Speech Synthesis
column6: Autoregressive speech synthesis has traditionally followed a left-to-right order, yet generation order is a modelling choice. This paper investigates decoding order through a masked diffusion framework that enables arbitrary decoding orders at inference time. To isolate the effect of decoding order from inductive biases introduced by learned discrete encoders, we operate on scalar quantised Mel-spectrograms. Our results demonstrate that the left-to-right strategy is suboptimal for capturing complex acoustic dependencies. The reverse, right-to-left, order consistently outperforms the traditional approach, while the adaptive confidence-based strategy top1 achieves the highest Mean Opinion Score (MOS) among all model outputs. Analysis reveals that the most effective orders maintain local clusters of consecutive frames to balance long-range temporal dependencies with local coherence. These results establish decoding order as a critical parameter for improving synthesis quality.
column7: Minghui Zhao(University of Sheffield); Anton Ragni(University of Sheffield)

column4: Decoupling Search and Evaluation: Efficient Beam Decoding for Language Model-Based Text-to-Speech Synthesis
column6: Language model (LM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) systems typically rely on sampling-based decoding, which suffers from stochastic instability. While beam search offers a maximization-based alternative, it is limited in speech generation due to severe degeneration (e.g., temporal collapse) and high latency. Our analysis reveals that beam search cost is highly imbalanced between search and evaluation stages. Motivated by this, we propose Search-and-eValuatE beam decoding (SaVE-Beam), which decouples hypothesis expansion from sequence scoring. Specifically, a lightweight student model performs chunk-wise beam construction, while the teacher LM retains exact evaluation. Hard repetition constraints are introduced to prevent degenerate loops. Experiments show that SaVE-Beam achieves up to 5.1x speedup over conventional beam search without degrading speech quality, and reduces WER by up to 50% compared to sampling, enabling practical maximization-based decoding for real-time LM-based TTS.
column7: Chenlin Liu(Harbin Institute of Technology); Jie Gao(Tsinghua University); Wei Zhou(Zhejiang University); Guangyan Zhang(Zhejiang University); Minghui Fang(Tsinghua University); Jiqing Han(Harbin Institute of Technology)

column4: Eliminating Stability Hallucinations in LLM-based TTS models via Attention Guidance
column6: This paper focuses on resolving stability hallucinations (e.g., repetitive or omitted speech) in LLM-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) models by improving and leveraging the attention mechanism. First, we analyzed the alignment mechanism between text tokens and speech tokens in LLMs. We then proposed a metric termed the Optimal Alignment Score (OAS), which employs the Viterbi algorithm to evaluate text-speech alignment quality. Subsequently, OAS was integrated into the training of CosyVoice2 to assist LLMs in learning continuous, stable alignment. Additionally, the pre-trained attention value is employed to guide the training of the student CosyVoice2 via chain-of-thought (CoT), which further reduces stability hallucinations in synthesized speech. Experiments on the Seed-TTS-Eval and CV3-Eval test sets demonstrate that the proposed methods can effectively reduce the stability hallucinations of CosyVoice2 without introducing additional negative effects. The appendix is available at https://wsmzzz.github.io/llm_attn/ index.html.
column7: Shiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhihao Du(Independent Researcher); Yang Xiang(Independent Researcher); Tianyu Zhao(Independent Researcher); Han Zhao(Independent Researcher); Qian Chen(Independent Researcher); Xiangang Li(Independent Researcher); Hanjie Guo(University of Science and Technology of China); ZhenHua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: MamTra: A Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Backbone for Speech Synthesis
column6: Despite the remarkable quality of LLM-based text-to-speech systems, their reliance on autoregressive Transformers leads to quadratic computational complexity, which severely limits practical applications. Linear-time alternatives, notably Mamba, offer a potential remedy; however, they often sacrifice the global context essential for expressive synthesis. In this paper, we propose MamTra, an interleaved Mamba-Transformer framework designed to leverage the advantages of Mamba's efficiency and Transformers' modeling capability. We also introduce novel knowledge transfer strategies to distill insights from a pretrained Transformer into our hybrid architecture, thereby bypassing the prohibitive costs of training from scratch. Systematic experiments identify the optimal hybrid configuration, and demonstrate that MamTra reduces inference VRAM usage by up to 34% without compromising speech fidelity-even trained on only 2% of the original training dataset. Audio samples are available at.
column7: Tan Dat Nguyen(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Sangmin Bae(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Joon Son Chung(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Ji-Hoon Kim(Chung-Ang University)

column4: DLLM-TTS: Block Discrete Diffusion Language Model for Text-to-Speech Synthesis
column6: Current text-to-speech systems face a trade-off: autoregressive codec language models produce highly intelligible speech but require large-scale models and training data and decode tokens sequentially, while non-autoregressive approaches improve speed at the cost of linguistic accuracy. We present DLLM-TTS, a framework that formulates TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec tokens. The model decomposes sequences into blocks and applies masked diffusion within each block while processing blocks sequentially, learning both local acoustic coherence and global text-speech alignment. During inference, parallel token prediction within blocks enables efficient generation with a real-time factor (RTF) of 0.15. A 0.6B-parameter model trained on 20K hours achieves competitive performance on the Seed-TTS-eval benchmark, demonstrating that block discrete diffusion language models enable practical and data-efficient speech synthesis with parallel generation.
column7: Wasim Madha(Smallest.ai); Nityanand Mathur(Smallest.ai); Hamees Sayed(Smallest.ai); Apoorv Singh(Smallest.ai); Sameer Khurana(Smallest.ai); Akshat Mandloi(Smallest.ai); Sudarshan Kamath(Smallest.ai)

column4: Bagpiper-TTS: Natural Language Guided Universal Speech Synthesis
column6: Classical TTS systems typically rely on rigid input formats and predefined metadata slots, limiting their ability to fulfill flexible user requirements. This paper introduces Bagpiper-TTS, a universal speech synthesis system that deals with diverse natural language user requests. Given a natural language prompt, Bagpiper-TTS first reasons over the user’s intent to derive a rich caption, i.e., a comprehensive textual blueprint encompassing both transcription and nuanced metadata. Subsequently, this caption guides the synthesis of the target speech. Our model inherently supports a broad spectrum of tasks besides classical TTS applications, including multi-talker, intent-to-speech, roleplay synthesis, singing voice synthesis, and more. Experimental results demonstrate that Bagpiper-TTS achieves an 1.7% Word Error Rate (WER) on the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark and match the performance of dedicated models in both LLM-as-a-judge and human subjective evaluations across multiple application.
column7: Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Haoran Wang(Carnegie Mellon University); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Takashi Maekaku(LY Corporation); Keita Goto(LY Corporation); Jin Sakuma(LY Corporation); Yusuke Shinohara(LY Corporation); Chao-Han Huck Yang(NVIDIA Research); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 8 - Oral 2 - New Training Methods for ASR

column4: Reducing the Offline-Streaming Gap for Unified ASR Transducer with Consistency Regularization
column6: Unification of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems reduces development and maintenance costs, but training a single model to perform well in both offline and low-latency streaming settings remains challenging. We present a Unified ASR framework for Transducer (RNNT) training that supports both offline and streaming decoding within a single model, using chunk-limited attention with right context and dynamic chunked convolutions. To further close the gap between offline and streaming performance, we introduce an efficient Triton implementation of mode-consistency regularization for RNNT (MCR-RNNT), which encourages agreement across training modes. Experiments show that the proposed approach improves streaming accuracy at low latency while preserving offline performance and scaling to larger model sizes and training datasets. The proposed Unified ASR framework and the English model checkpoint are open-sourced.
column7: Andrei Andrusenko(NVIDIA, Armenia); Vladimir Bataev(NVIDIA, Armenia); Lilit Grigoryan(NVIDIA, Armenia); Nune Tadevosyan(NVIDIA, Armenia); Vitaly Lavrukhin(NVIDIA, USA); Boris Ginsburg(NVIDIA, USA)

column4: BACON: Boundary-Aware Convolution for Streaming Conformer Models
column6: We propose Boundary-Aware CONvolution (BACON), a drop-in replacement for causal convolution in streaming sequence tasks that leverage chunk-based Conformers. Streaming Conformers typically pair chunked attention with causal convolution to prevent future information leakage. We show that causal convolution is unnecessarily restrictive: within a chunk, all frames are already available, so the convolution kernel can safely look ahead up to the chunk boundary without violating the streaming constraint. BACON exploits this by splitting the depthwise convolution channels into a causal group and a boundary-aware bidirectional group, yielding a wider effective receptive field than the causal baseline while preserving parameter count. Across single-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), multi-speaker ASR, and speech-to-text translation tasks with two model architectures, BACON improves model accuracy while maintaining comparable latency.
column7: Hainan Xu(NVIDIA corporation.); Kunal Dhawan(NVIDIA corporation.); Dongji Gao(NVIDIA corporation.); Jagadeesh Balam(NVIDIA corporation.)

column4: Progressive Alignment Objectives for Aligner-Encoder based ASR
column6: Aligner-Encoders are recently proposed seq2seq end-to-end ASR models that replace decoder attention by predicting the u-th token directly from the u-th encoder position, so the encoder must learn the alignment internally without cross-attention or a transducer lattice. In practice, this alignment often forms abruptly in the upper layers, making training sensitive and brittle on long utterances. We propose InterAligner, which adds an intermediate Aligner objective so alignment can form progressively across depth, together with an intermediate CTC loss (InterCTC) to stabilize optimization. On LibriSpeech with a 17-layer Conformer, a final-only Aligner reaches 5.0/7.8 WER (test-clean/other). InterCTC improves to 3.4/6.0, and InterAligner further reduces WER to 3.1/5.6 with the largest gains on long utterances.
column7: Jaeyoung Lee(NTT, Inc.); Masato Mimura(NTT, Inc.); Takafumi Moriya(NTT, Inc.)

column4: From Bilevel to Trilevel: Joint Training for Speech Recognition
column6: This paper presents the practical optimization strategies to extend the bilevel learning into a trilevel setting for speech recognition. This method jointly trains an acoustic model according to supervised, unsupervised, and distilled learning objectives. To make trilevel training feasible in large-scale ASR models, we employ a sequential penalty-based bilevel gradient descent method that collapses the lower two levels into a bilevel subproblem and then integrates it with the upper level. This formulation allows the model to leverage the general structure from unlabeled data, the task-specific alignment from labeled speech, and the knowledge transfer from a teacher network within a single optimization loop. The experiments on LibriSpeech with a FastConformer backbone demonstrate that these strategies yield the consistent improvements over the conventional two-stage pre-training and fine-tuning pipeline, as well as over the prior bilevel optimization methods.
column7: Jen-Tzung Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yu-Chun Lin(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Xiaodong Cui(IBM T. J. Watson Research Center)

column4: LLM-as-Joiner: Decoupling Alignment from Language Modeling in Label-synchronous ASR
column6: We present LLM-as-Joiner, an LLM-based ASR architecture that decouples speech-text alignment from language modeling. A speech encoder first converts an input of T acoustic frames into U token-level speech states, one per output token, following the Aligner-Encoder framework. A pretrained LLM then predicts the transcript from these U states, with speech injected at a chosen LLM layer; only upper LLM layers are adapted via LoRA. Compared to conventional decoder-only speech-as-prefix decoding, the LLM operates on a shorter context (U rather than T + U), reducing memory and compute. On LibriSpeech and multilingual Common Voice, the proposed LLM-as-Joiner outperforms size-matched baselines, and joint training with a lightweight recognizer yields additional gains in the lightweight head, suggesting implicit transfer of linguistic knowledge from the LLM to the speech encoder.
column7: Jaeyoung Lee(NTT, Inc.; Kyoto University); Masato Mimura(NTT, Inc.); Ryo Magoshi(Kyoto University); Tatsuya Kawahara(Kyoto University)

column4: Accurate Source-Free Speech Classification via Meta-Learned Target-Centric Model Merging
column6: How can we build a speech classifier for an unseen domain when access to source-domain data is unavailable? Speech classification is widely used (e.g., voice commands, emotion recognition, etc.), but it is highly sensitive to domain shifts (e.g., languages), often causing substantial performance degradation. This issue becomes critical when source data cannot be accessed and only pretrained source models with limited target data are available. Under such constraints, typical adaptation approaches are inapplicable, and existing model merging methods easily overfit the limited target data. We propose Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ, an accurate target-centric model merging framework that combines multiple pretrained source models using limited target data. To improve generalization under scarce target labels, Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ exploits meta-learning to resolve representation misalignment and emphasize target-relevant sources. Extensive experiments show that Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ outperforms the baselines by up to 14.5 points in Macro-F1.
column7: Ka Hyun Park(Seoul National University); Junghun Kim(Seoul National University); U Kang(Seoul National University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 9 - Oral 2 - Code-Switching ASR

column4: LLM-HB: Language-Aware LLM-Guided Hotword Biasing for Code-Switching ASR
column6: Code-switching (CS) speech, characterized by language alternation within a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual communities and poses challenges to automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to rapid language transitions. We propose LLM-HB, a language-aware large language model-guided hotword biasing framework for code-switching ASR (CS-ASR). The framework incorporates a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language prediction head to better capture and differentiate multilingual representations, while hotwords are injected through LLM-based prompting. Experiments on the ASRU2019 code-switching challenge test set demonstrate that LLM-HB achieves a 20.30% relative reduction in mixed error rate (MER) over the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER under a 15-distractor hotword setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate LLM-guided biasing into code-switching ASR. We further release the extracted ASRU2019 hotword list to support future research.
column7: Yuxuan He(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; iFLYTEK Company Limited; Wuhan University); Genshun Wan(iFLYTEK Company Limited); Pengcheng Li(iFLYTEK); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); JianQing Gao(iFLYTEK); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)

column4: Improving Code-Switching ASR with Code-Mixing Guided Synthetic Speech
column6: Code-switch (CS) Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) remains challenging due to limited availability of high quality CS text-speech pairs for training. Although synthetic data augmentation via text-to-speech (TTS) has been explored, existing CS TTS approaches primarily optimise reconstruction fidelity and do not explicitly enforce language-boundary consistency, thereby limiting their effectiveness for CS ASR augmentation. This paper proposes a code-mixing guided preference-learning framework that steers synthetic speech generation toward improved code-switching fidelity using the Code Mixing Index (CMI). Experiments on the SEAME Mandarin-English conversational corpus demonstrate that the proposed method enhances the utility of synthetic data for ASR fine-tuning. Specifically, when fine-tuning Whisper Large, the proposed approach reduces Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 12.1%/17.8% to 8.9%/14.2% on the DevMAN and DevSGE sets, respectively.

Sailor(I2R ASTAR Singapore); Jeremy H. M. Wong(Google DeepMind, Singapore); Eng Siong Chng(NTU, Singapore)

column4: Reinforcement Learning for Data-Efficient Code-Switched ASR
column6: Audio-language models can be prompted for code-switched speech, but their decoding is not optimized for code-switching and often fails at language boundaries. We propose a practical reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards recipe for data-efficient adaptation of audio-language models to code-switched ASR using group relative policy optimization, combining an error rate reward with a script fidelity reward that penalizes wrong writing systems and a two-pass draft-and-refinement procedure. Using Qwen2-Audio as a reproducible testbed across 10 language pairs, training on only TTS code-switched speech, we show that RLVR with 10% of the data matches LoRA supervised fine-tuning trained on the full dataset, with the largest gains on typologically distant pairs. The error rate reward eliminates translation errors while the script fidelity reward separately reduces script contamination without degradation. These gains transfer zero-shot to a human-recorded code-switching corpus.
column7: Ziwei Ye(Independent Researcher); Peter Vickers(Spotify Canada)

column4: Direct Preference Optimization for English-Mandarin Code-Switching Speech Recognition in Audio LLMs
column6: Audio large language models (Audio LLMs) exhibit systematic failures in transcribing code-switching speech despite strong multilingual capabilities. Focusing on English-Mandarin, we identify three failure modes: language omission, translation-instead-of-transcription, and hallucination. We apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align models, constructing preference pairs in which chosen responses preserve mixed-language content while rejected responses mimic failure patterns. Training three Audio LLMs on 100K pairs (570 hours), we observe consistent behavioral shifts: models learn to preserve language composition rather than translating when prompted for transcription. This alignment yields MER reductions up to 89.6% (in-distribution) and 20.0% (out-of-distribution). Our findings suggest DPO can effectively elicit correct code-switching transcription behavior from multilingual Audio LLMs.

column4: Adding Robust Code-Switching Capabilities to High Performance Multilingual ASR
column6: Code-switching (CSW) remains challenging for large multilingual ASR systems in real-world deployment. While fine-tuning on synthetic CSW data is possible, it generally degrades strong monolingual baselines. Our goal is to preserve these capabilities while extending models to handle complex code-switching, including morphological variations across languages. We propose Bayesian factorized adaptation, which learns to efficiently integrate switching-relevant knowledge into strong pretrained models without overwriting existing capabilities. Requiring only a small amount of synthetic data, our approach reduces transcription errors by 32.87% on code-switched words while improving overall WER by 5.31%, all while maintaining monolingual performance. Our results demonstrate that effective CSW adaptation depends more on knowledge integration than data complexity.
column7: Enes Yavuz Ugan(KIT); Alexander Waibel(KIT; CMU)

column4: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
column6: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.
column7: Kazi Rafat(North South University); Afifa Imran(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Md. Ismail Hossain(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Md. Romzan Ali(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Fuad Rahman(Apurba Technologies); Sifat Momen(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Shafin Rahman(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Nabeel Mohammed(Apurba NSU R&D Lab)

column4: Expressive Speech Translation
column6: Speech to speech translation is still a challenging problem, without much consensus about model architectures, training data, evaluation methods, and so on. One frontier in this area is the preservation of the expressiveness of the input speech in the translation. Expressiveness ranges from global properties such as the speaker's voice and emotion as well as acoustic conditions, to local properties such as pauses, varying speaking rates, emphasis, and pitch for individual words. This survey will cover various aspects, such as training data, data synthesis methods, speech representation, model architectures, the use of large language models, and evaluation metrics.

column4: Personalized Keyword Spotting for User-Defined Keywords Leveraging Text-Independent Speaker Verification
column6: User-defined keyword spotting (UD-KWS) enables zero-shot wake-word detection from text, but existing systems learn speaker-invariant representations that cannot reject impostors uttering the correct keyword. We address this dual zero-shot setting—unseen keywords and unseen speakers—with ZP-KWS, a lightweight framework combining a phoneme-supervised audio encoder with a GE2E-pretrained compact speaker encoder (about 0.9M parameters). Multiplicative late fusion at inference grants each branch independent veto power, supporting modes from conventional detection to strict speaker-gated activation without retraining. On LibriPhrase, Google Speech Commands, and Qualcomm datasets, ZP-KWS reduces target-only FRR at 1% FAR by up to 60% relative to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive keyword detection, all within a 1.55M parameter budget for edge deployment.
column7: Ming-Hsiang Hu(National Taiwan Normal University); Kuan-Tang Huang(National Taiwan Normal University); Chien-Chun Wang(E.SUN Financial Holding Co., Ltd.); Hung-Shin Lee(United Link Co., Ltd.); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)

column4: wav2tok 2.0: Scalable Audio Tokenization Maintaining Explicit Pairwise Token Alignment for Efficient Audio Retrieval
column6: Learning discrete speech representations that preserve similarity across variable-length utterances is central to query-by-example spoken term detection (QbE-STD). While wav2tok introduced CTC-based sequence alignment to enforce token consistency, its tightly coupled clustering and alignment training recipe limits scalability. We propose wav2tok 2.0, a scalable alignment-aware speech tokenizer built on the BEST-STD backbone. wav2tok 2.0 employs staged training, first learning discriminative, speaker-invariant representations via contrastive learning and vector quantization, and then enforcing pairwise token consistency using a CTC alignment loss and a novel DTW-aligned framewise prediction objective with adaptive weighting. Experiments show that wav2tok 2.0 consistently outperforms BEST-STD and general-purpose tokenizers on QbE-STD while remaining efficient and scalable.
column7: Adhiraj Banerjee(Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur); Vipul Arora(Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur; KU Leuven)

column4: Rethinking Organization Entity Modeling in End-to-End Acoustic Named Entity Recognition
column6: End-to-end acoustic named entity recognition (NER) integrates speech transcription and entity detection within a unified model, avoiding error propagation in cascaded ASR-NER systems. However, organization entities remain significantly harder to detect due to multi-word spans, acronyms, and lexical variability. We present a systematic analysis of organization recognition failures in acoustic NER, revealing that conventional cross-entropy training inadequately models entity span dependencies. To address this limitation, we propose an organization-aware Whisper-based acoustic NER framework combining LLM-based targeted semantic augmentation, category-specific boundary supervision, and a structure-constrained entity learning (SCEL) objective that enforces entity span consistency during decoding. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in organization recognition while maintaining strong ASR performance, outperforming in entity-recognition for several other existing approaches.
column7: Spandan Dey(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Nidhi Mantri(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sambit Behera(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Hirak Mondal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sanjay Kurmi(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sreyasree Mandal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Atharv Joshi(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Premjeet Singh(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Gopal Agrawal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore)

column4: AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification
column6: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose ANYSIM-LITE, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate ANYSIM-LITE across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using < 1/250th of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.
column7: Sourav Ghosh(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Yash Bhatia(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Keshav Goyal(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Sahil Singh Bagri(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Mohamed Akram Ulla Shariff(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Saravana Balaji Shanmugam(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore)

column4: Personalized Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion with a Single Pre-operative Utterance
column6: Electrolaryngeal voice conversion (ELVC) enhances the mechanical speech of laryngectomees to improve naturalness and intelligibility. While personalized ELVC typically requires extensive pre-operative recordings for supervised training, this paper investigates a one-shot scenario where only one natural utterance is available for timbre preservation. We evaluate two strategies using zero-shot VC models: (1) a cascaded approach, performing ELVC followed by secondary conversion to the target timbre; and (2) a pseudo-target strategy, using a zero-shot model to generate synthetic training data for a supervised ELVC model. Results indicate that the cascaded approach outperforms the pseudo-target strategy, remarkably improving speaker similarity and quality with minimal impact on intelligibility. We also demonstrate that direct application of zero-shot models to ELVC fails due to domain mismatch, confirming the necessity of our proposed framework for one-shot personalized voice restoration.
column7: Devin Chang(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Te Hwang(Academia Sinica); Ming-Chi Yen(Academia Sinica; National Taiwan University); Shu-Wei Tsai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica)

column4: A Preclinical Study of Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion for a Novel Nasal Electrolarynx: Feature Choice and Data Augmentation
column6: Electrolaryngeal (EL) speech often exhibits reduced intelligibility and naturalness due to imperfect excitation and fixed pitch. In this preclinical study, we present the first systematic investigation of electrolaryngeal voice conversion (ELVC) for speech produced by a newly invented nasal electrolarynx (NEL), extending previous work that mainly targets cervical EL (CEL) speech. We examine the choice of features under NEL's distinctive acoustics by comparing Mel-spectrograms and WavLM features as input to a seq2seq ELVC system. To address NEL data scarcity, we propose an LLE-VC-based augmentation strategy to synthesize paired sNEL--sNL speech for VC pretraining. Experiments reveal device-dependent trends: WavLM features benefit CEL-oriented conversion and augmentation, whereas Mel-spectrogram inputs better preserve NEL-specific spectral characteristics and yield better intelligibility-related metrics and listener preferences for NEL-to-NL conversion.
column7: Qi-Yan Chen(Academia Sinica); Ming-Chi Yen(Academia Sinica; National Taiwan University); Fo-Rui Li(National Central University); Hsin-Te Hwang(Academia Sinica); Ching-Hung Lai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Shu-Wei Tsai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Ping-Cheng Yeh(National Taiwan University); Jyh-Shing Roger Jang(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica)

column4: One-to-Many Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion with Synthetic Data
column6: Restoring natural (NL) speech from electrolarynx (EL) speech is crucial for EL users who have undergone laryngectomy. While previous works have shown the effectiveness of deep learning methods for converting EL-to-NL speech with data augmentation, time-aligned conversion remains underexplored, where data scarcity is more severe due to temporal constraints. We propose a data-driven learning framework to learn from small-scale (13 minutes) EL speech data to synthesize time-aligned EL speech from NL speech of multiple speakers, for developing one-to-many EL-to-NL conversion models. Our method leverages pretrained deep learning-based any-to-many voice conversion (VC) models for finetuning on EL speech for NL-to-EL conversion, to convert the NL speech in a large-scale multi-speaker corpus to synthetic EL speech, which is used to supervise a pretrained VC model for one-to-many EL-to-NL VC. Experiments show the effectiveness of our method against baselines in intonation and intelligibility.
column7: Bowen Wu(RIKEN; ATR); Haruto Ueno(RIKEN; The University of Osaka); Carlos Toshinori Ishi(RIKEN; ATR); Chaoran Liu(RIKEN; ATR; NII)

column4: Tongue2Speech: Real-Time Speech Synthesis from Tongue Ultrasound Videos via Spatiotemporal Transformers
column6: Ultrasound-to-Speech aims to synthesize intelligible speech from tongue ultrasound video. Prior approaches rely mainly on purely convolutional or recurrent architectures. We present Tongue2Speech, a lightweight framework combining explicit 3D spatio-temporal encoding with a multi-layer Transformer to model long-range articulatory dynamics. Spectral distortion metrics (such as MSE) commonly used in prior work are weak indicators of lexical accuracy when used in isolation. Therefore, we evaluate performance using word error rate (WER). On the English TaL corpus, Tongue2Speech achieves 15.93% WER in single-speaker and 31.64% in multi-speaker settings, outperforming six strong baselines. Speaker-specific fine-tuning further improves intelligibility for unseen users. These results highlight tongue-only ultrasound as a promising pathway toward practical silent speech synthesis. Audio samples are available at: https://tongue2speech.github.io/
column7: Yash Sonkar(IIIT Hyderabad); Yasaswi Kilaru(IIIT Hyderabad); Sudheera Yelimeli(IIIT Hyderabad); Neil Shah(IIIT Hyderabad; TCS Research); Vineet Gandhi(IIIT Hyderabad)

column4: On the Role of the Tongue Region in Ultrasound-to-Acoustic Mapping
column6: Ultrasound tongue imaging is a promising modality for Silent Speech Interfaces, yet a core assumption in ultrasound-to-acoustic mapping remains untested, namely that the tongue is the primary source of acoustic information. We test this hypothesis by proposing an automatic tongue region extraction method for controlled input manipulation on a 2D-CNN baseline, and a dual encoder with cross-attention gating for mapping ultrasound frames to 80-dimensional mel-spectrograms. Based on our results, surprisingly, removing the tongue region produced no statistically significant MSE degradation, suggesting the 2D-CNN may exploit broader image cues rather than tongue-specific features. The dual encoder similarly yields no significant gain over the baseline across MSE, MCD, PESQ, and MOSnet. However, Grad-CAM maps reveal that the dual encoder focuses activations on the tongue region, unlike the baseline, representing a meaningful step towards more interpretable ultrasound-to-acoustic mapping.
column7: Ibrahim Ibrahimov(Department of TelecommBudapest University of Technology and Economics); Gábor Gosztolya(HUN-REN–SZTE Research Group on Artificial Intelligence; University of Szeged); Csaba Zainkó(Budapest University of Technology and Economics)

column4: Low-Burden Data Augmentation for Dysarthric ASR via Zero-Shot Voice Cloning
column6: Automatic speech recognition remains unreliable for dysarthric speech due to data scarcity and high inter-speaker variability. While synthetic data can address these gaps, traditional methods often require extensive speaker-specific data, reintroducing the collection bottleneck. We investigate zero-shot voice cloning as a low-burden augmentation strategy, using Higgs Audio V2 to clone speakers in the TORGO dataset. We fine-tune (FT) Whisper-medium on cloned, real, and hybrid data and evaluate on held-out real speech. Compared to the zero-shot (31.62%), Clone FT achieved a competitive 26.00% WER, nearly matching the 24.44% and 25.12% seen with Real and Hybrid FT, respectively. Notably, Clone and Hybrid FT outperform Real FT for moderate-severe speakers. Clone FT achieves the best results (11.45% relative) in cross-corpus evaluation on the SAP-1102. These results suggest that zero-shot cloning provides scalable training data that circumvents the costly data collection bottleneck.
column7: Satwinder Singh(University of Auckland); Qianli Wang(University of Auckland); Zihan Zhong(University of Auckland); Clarion Mendes(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Waleed Abdulla(University of Auckland); Seyed Reza Shahamiri(University of Auckland)

column4: One Embedding Doesn't Fit All: Rethinking Speaker Modeling Robustness Across Speaker-Centric Tasks
column6: Speaker embeddings have become a fundamental representation for a wide range of speaker-centric speech applications, including speaker verification, diarization, target speaker extraction, and personalized speech interaction. However, a speaker representation optimized for one task or acoustic condition does not necessarily generalize well to others. This survey revisits the notion of robustness in speaker modeling from a broader, task-oriented perspective. We review recent progress in learning speaker representations under variations in acoustics, speech content, duration, and domain, and discuss how speaker information is exploited differently across downstream tasks. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs between task-independent speaker representations and task-adaptive modeling. Finally, we highlight emerging challenges and opportunities toward more generalizable, transferable, and task-aware speaker modeling for future speech and multimodal systems.

column4: SDR-LLM: Speech-LLM Based End-to-End Speaker Diarization and Recognition with Sentence-Level Temporal Modeling
column6: Speaker Diarization and Recognition (SDR) is crucial for multi-speaker audio. Cascaded systems suffer from error accumulation, while many end-to-end (E2E) models fail to provide fine-grained temporal alignment. We propose a unified Speech-LLM framework that predicts speaker identities, text, and millisecond-level timestamps. Our method introduces a FIFO output sequence, integrating voiceprint IDs and temporal boundaries into autoregressive generation. Training high-accuracy E2E SDR models requires large amounts of annotated data, which is scarce. To address this, we use a two-stage approach: first, simulating speaker turns and timing with synthetic data, followed by fine-tuning with a small amount of real-world data. Experiments on AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, and OleSpeech show that our approach outperforms E2E models in transcription accuracy and achieves diarization comparable to cascaded systems. Our method balances transcription precision and temporal alignment in real-world corpus.
column7: Renjie Yu(Tsinghua University); Yixuan Zhou(Tsinghua University); Shun Lei(Tsinghua University); Xiang Li(Tsinghua University); Runchuan Ye(Tsinghua University); Yikai Huang(ModelBest Inc.); Guoyang Zeng(Tsinghua University); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University)

column4: Where Do Backdoors Live? A Component-Level Analysis of Backdoor Propagation in Speech Language Models
column6: Speech language models (SLMs) are systems of systems: independent components that unite to achieve a common goal. Despite their heterogeneous nature, SLMs are often studied end-to-end; how information flows through the pipeline remains obscure. We investigate this question through the lens of backdoor attacks. We first establish that backdoors can propagate through the SLM, leaving all tasks highly vulnerable. From this, we design a component analysis to discover the role each component takes in backdoor learning. We find that backdoor persistence or erasure is highly dependent on the targeted component. Beyond propagation, we examine how backdoors are encoded in shared multitask embeddings, showing that poisoned samples are not directly separable from benign ones, challenging a common separability assumption used in filtering defenses. Our findings emphasize the need to treat multimodal pipelines as intricate systems with unique vulnerabilities, not solely extensions of unimodal ones.
column7: Alexandrine Fortier(University of British Columbia); Thomas Thebaud(Johns Hopkins University); Jesus Villalba(Johns Hopkins University); Najim Dehak(Johns Hopkins University); Patrick Cardinal(École de technologie supérieure); Peter West(University of British Columbia)

column4: Tight Boundary Prediction in Speaker Diarization Using Causal-Anticausal Consistency
column6: Multi-talker conversational automatic speech recognition data are often used to train speaker diarization models. Because such data prioritize semantic continuity, pauses and boundary margins are included within speech segments, resulting in loose annotations. Models trained on such data tend to internalize mechanisms that reproduce this looseness, although tight speech intervals are sometimes preferable for downstream applications. In this paper, we address the novel task of enabling models to produce tight predictions using loose labels. Our method generates tighter pseudo labels using causal and anticausal models, which are inherently incapable of learning loosening behavior. We further propose a co-training scheme that iteratively tightens labels and updates both models for more progressive refinement. Experimental results show that the proposed method recovers about 70 % of the tightening effect achieved by ideal tight-label training and improves downstream performance.
column7: Shota Horiguchi(NTT, Inc.); Marc Delcroix(NTT, Inc.); Naohiro Tawara(NTT, Inc.); Takanori Ashihara(NTT, Inc.); Atsushi Ando(NTT, Inc.)

column4: Modeling Overlapped Speech with Shuffles
column6: We propose to model parallel streams of data, such as overlapped speech, using shuffles. Specifically, this paper shows how the shuffle product and partial order finite-state automata (FSAs) can be used for alignment and speaker-attributed transcription of overlapped speech. We train using the total score on these FSAs as a loss function, marginalizing over all possible serializations of overlapping sequences at subword, word, and phrase levels. To reduce graph size, we impose temporal constraints by constructing partial order FSAs. We address speaker attribution by modeling (token, speaker) tuples directly. Viterbi alignment through the shuffle product FSA directly enables one-pass alignment. We evaluate performance on synthetic LibriSpeech overlaps. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that enables single-pass alignment of multi-talker recordings. All algorithms are implemented using k2 / Icefall.
column7: Matthew Wiesner(Johns Hopkins University; LISN, CNRS); Samuele Cornell(Carnegie Mellon University); Alexander Polok(Brno University of Technology); Lucas Ondel-Yang(LISN, CNRS); Lukáš Burget(Brno University of Technology); Sanjeev Khudanpur(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: ProSarc: Prosody-Aware Sarcasm Recognition Framework via Temporal Prosodic Incongruity
column6: We present ProSarc, an audio-only framework that detects sarcasm by modelling temporal prosodic incongruity, that is, the mismatch between local prosodic dynamics and the utterance-level emotional baseline. Dual encoding paths, a Global Emotion Encoder and a Temporal Prosody Encoder (BiLSTM + multi-head attention), feed a Prosodic Incongruity Analyzer that produces a scalar incongruity score for classification. Monte Carlo dropout provides uncertainty estimates, and an attention-based mechanism localises sarcastic onset without frame-level labels. ProSarc outperforms prior audio-only methods on MUStARD++ (F1 = 75.3) and generalises to spontaneous (PodSarc, F1 = 62.9) and cross-lingual speech (MuSaG, F1 = 65.6). Ten-run validation confirms the contribution of incongruity modelling (Wilcoxon p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.51). Human evaluation shows that model uncertainty tracks perceptual ambiguity and predicted onsets align with human-annotated temporal windows.
column7: Prathamjyot Singh(Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology); Ashima Sood(Ulster University); Sahil Sharma(Ulster University); Jasmeet Singh(Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology)

column4: A Two-Stage Defence for Robust Federated Speech Emotion Recognition
column6: With machine learning and speech processing advancements, speech emotion recognition has gained popularity recently. However, speech data cannot be protected when it is uploaded and processed on servers in the internet-of-things applications of speech emotion recognition. Further, deep neural networks have proven to be vulnerable to human-indistinguishable adversarial perturbations. The adversarial attacks generated from the perturbations may result in deep neural networks wrongly predicting the emotional states. We propose a novel federated adversarial learning framework for protecting both data and deep neural networks. The proposed framework consists of i) federated learning for data privacy, and ii) adversarial training at the training stage and randomisation at the testing stage for model robustness. The experiments show our proposed framework effectively protects speech data locally and improve model robustness against a series of adversarial attacks.
column7: Yi Chang(Imperial College London); Sofiane Laridi(Leibniz University Hannover); Zhao Ren(University of Bremen); Gregory Palmer(Leibniz University Hannover); Björn W. Schuller(Imperial College London); Marco Fisichella(Leibniz University Hannover)

column4: Segregate, Refine, Integrate: Decomposing Multimodal Fusion for Sentiment Analysis
column6: Multimodal fusion must simultaneously refine modality-specific signals and model cross-modal interactions; two competing objectives typically entangled within the same operation. We propose SeRIn (Segregate, Refine, Integrate), a multimodal LM fusion scheme that enforces this separation as an architectural prior. Modality-specific representations evolve along isolated pathways, each refined against its respective encoder context, while a dedicated cross-modal pathway accumulates their joint evolution without contaminating unimodal streams. Full cross-modal interaction is deferred to a final prediction step — ablations confirm that structured interactions, not added capacity, drive the gains; gate analysis under visual corruption reveals emergent modality reweighting without explicit supervision. SeRIn achieves state-of-the-art results on CH-SIMS and CMU-MOSEI, improving all metrics on both benchmarks.
column7: Alexios Filippakopoulos(National Technical University of Athens; Synaptic Bloom); Elias Kallioras(National Technical University of Athens); Nikolaos Xiros(National Technical University of Athens; Athena Research Center); Efthymios Georgiou(National Technical University of Athens; University of Bern); Alexandros Potamianos(National Technical University of Athens; Archimedes AI; Synaptic Bloom)

column4: An Acoustic Landmark Database of the English Lexicon via Articulatory Synthesis
column6: Acoustic landmark theory treats speech as organized around the acoustic consequences of articulatory gestures that shape the vocal tract and airflow. Progress is limited by the scarcity of large, unambiguously annotated landmark datasets. We invert the problem by generating speech from landmark patterns. Using the Pink Trombone physical vocal-tract synthesizer, we produce an English lexicon for two adult configurations (male, female). With direct control of gestures, we place landmark labels algorithmically at the exact times of their physical events (e.g., oral closures/releases). The corpus contains >200,000 synthesized words, rendered for both configurations with time-aligned annotations; intelligibility is measured with STOI. We leverage it for statistics across the lexicon from an articulatory-event view, reporting landmark frequencies and dominant cue patterns, and enabling quantitative studies plus training/benchmarking of automatic landmark detectors.
column7: Mateo Cámara(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid; MIT); José Luis Blanco(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Juan Ignacio Godino-Llorente(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Jeung-Yoon Choi(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Stefanie Shattuck-Hufnagel(MIT)

column4: NewAppVoice: Tools for Visualizing and Correcting Acoustic Measures
column6: Phonetic analysis of little-studied languages, particularly those with complex segmental inventories or typologically rare features, often requires extensive manual verification of acoustic measurements. In the absence of established reference formant values, automatic extraction frequently produces systematic errors that must be visually inspected and corrected. Most large-scale scripts process datasets without interactive feedback, limiting transparency and reproducibility when manual intervention is necessary. This study presents NewAppVoice, a reproducible workflow integrating multiple formant-calculation algorithms with synchronized visualization of signals and measurements. Unlike fully automated pipelines, the software combines algorithmic processing with structured manual verification, improving reliability while ensuring transparency. The software and derived applications are freely available as open access tools supporting reproducible research on under-documented languages.
column7: Amélie Elmerich(CNRS & Sorbonne Nouvelle); Yao Dong(CNRS); Louise McKeever(CNRS & Sorbonne Nouvelle); Katia Chirkova(CNRS); Lise Crevier-Buchman(CNRS & Sorbonne Nouvelle; Université Paris Saclay); Claire Pillot-Loiseau(CNRS & Sorbonne Nouvelle); Angelique Amelot(CNRS & Sorbonne Nouvelle)
