column4: Beyond Residual Connections: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections for Robust Speaker Representation Learning
column6: Residual connections are fundamental to deep speaker recognition models, such as ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet. However, standard identity mapping limits information flow to a single path, constraining representation capacity. We introduce Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), reformulating residual paths as a multi-stream evolution where information is mixed through a doubly stochastic matrix. By employing Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations, mHC ensures energy conservation by preserving signal intensity and feature mean, which stabilizes gradients and mitigates signal degradation in complex networks. We evaluate mHC by replacing standard residual connections in backbones including ECAPA-TDNN, ResNet-34, Res2Net, and E-Res2Net. Extensive experiments on VoxCeleb1 demonstrate that mHC connections consistently enhances performance across all architectures, highlighting its effectiveness for robust speaker representation learning.
column7: Zezhong Jin(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Xiaoyu Wang(Baidu); Zhe Li(Hong Kong University); Chong-Xin Gan(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zilong Huang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Man-Wai Mak(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

column4:
Mitigating Pruning-Quantization Compound Errors for Ultra-Lightweight
ResNet34-Based Speaker Recognition
column6: While deep neural networks (DNNs) have greatly advanced speaker recognition, backbone models such as ResNet34 still suffer from computation and memory footprints, making difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices. To this end, we explored pruning and quantization techniques to compress speaker recognition model. Specifically, we propose a unified compression framework that combines channel pruning and low-bit quantization. Specifically, we propose ResRep-MB, a pruning strategy with multi-branch compactors for accurate channel importance assessment, achieving near-lossless structural compression. To mitigate the compound errors caused by pruning and INT4 quantization, we propose Progressive Pruning-Quantization Distillation (PPQD), which employs a dual-teacher mechanism. Experiments on VoxCeleb1 and CN-Celeb1 demonstrate that the compressed ResNet34 achieves a 19.2× compression ratio with only a 6.8% relative EER degradation, while maintaining robust cross-language performance.

column4: Continuous 2D Spectral—Temporal Transformer for Speaker Verification
column6: Recent speaker verification (SV) systems often employ hybrid architectures that combine spectral—temporal modeling with temporal aggregation. However, approaches such as ReDimNet perform global dependency modeling after collapsing the spectral—temporal grid into a temporal representation, which removes the explicit spectral-temporal structure. We propose Continuous 2D Spectral-Temporal Transformer (C2D-ST), which maintains the spectral—temporal representation throughout the backbone and performs global dependency modeling directly on the spectral—temporal grid, with temporal-only modeling applied only in a final stage. Experiments on VoxCeleb show that C2D-ST achieves competitive performance with strong parameter efficiency, reaching 0.507 average EER with 6.9M parameters.
column7: Seongwook Ham(Soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(Soongsil University)

column4: A Federated Learning-Based Speaker Recognition Method with Dual Classification Heads
column6: In speaker recognition tasks, acquiring data requires significant technical and financial resources for individual organizations, while also posing risks of privacy breaches. Applying federated learning architectures can address these issues, but model performance may degrade when confronting data heterogeneity challenges. In this paper, we propose a federated learning-based speaker recognition method with dual classification heads. By introducing a more knowledgeable classification head, local models can acquire more comprehensive global knowledge, thereby improving model performance. Our method achieved an average EER improvement of 46.5% over local training and 7.6% over FedAvg when trained on the VoxCeleb2 dataset. When jointly trained on the VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb datasets, the average EER improved by 68.8% over local training and 5.4% over FedAvg.
column7: Ying Meng(Xinjiang University); Zhihua Fang(Xinjiang University; AGIBOT); Liang He(Xinjiang University; Tsinghua University)

column4: Learning Global Key Knowledge for Federated Speaker Recognition via Fisher Information
column6: Speaker recognition relies on substantial data to enhance model performance, but the large-scale transmission of data by individual organizations incurs privacy and economic costs. Federated learning addresses privacy concerns by avoiding direct data transmission. However, due to inconsistent client data distributions, local models may learn redundant knowledge, leading to degraded performance. In this work, we utilise the Fisher Information Matrix to extract key dimensions from embeddings, enabling representation alignment between global and local models. By instructing local models to learn critical knowledge from the global model, we mitigate the detrimental effects of redundant knowledge, thereby enhancing overall model performance.
column7: Ying Meng(Xinjiang University); Zhihua Fang(Xinjiang University; AGIBOT); Liang He(Xinjiang University; Tsinghua University)

column4: HistoMatch: Unified Transient-Steady Assessment for Noise-Robust Semi-Supervised Speaker Verification
column6: Speaker verification systems have gained widespread applications across various domains, benefiting from advances in deep learning. However, acquiring large-scale labeled data remains challenging, making semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labeling a critical research focus. Current pseudo-labeling approaches predominantly rely on confidence thresholds-a transient metric vulnerable to distortions induced by random segmentation and noise augmentation. To overcome this limitation, we propose HistoMatch, a novel mechanism that leverages historical prediction stability as a steady-state metric. Combined with transient confidence, it forms a Dual-state History-based Stability Evaluator (DHSE) for high-quality unlabeled data selection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our semi-supervised approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three VoxCeleb1 test sets, with remarkable equal error rates (EER) of 0.91%, 1.13%, and 2.13%-closely approaching fully supervised benchmarks.
column7: Shenghan Gao(UCAS; IOA); Xueshuai Zhang(IOA); Pengyuan Zhang(UCAS; IOA); Yonghong Yan(UCAS; IOA)

column4: Self-supervised Speaker Verification with High-Confidence Pseudo-Label Selection and DINO-Style Self-Distillation Based on Pre-trained Models
column6: In this paper, we propose a self-supervised speaker verification (SS-SV) method based on pre-trained models (PTMs), which improves performance via high-confidence pseudo-label selection and DINO-style self-distillation. We select the top-K most speaker-discriminative Transformer layers from PTMs and cluster their representations separately to generate multiple pseudo-label sets. Using label alignment, we retain samples with consistent clustering as high-confidence pseudo-labeled data, while others are treated as unlabeled. We perform pseudo-supervised learning with label noise correction loss on the high-confidence set;for unlabeled data we use an EMA teacher to provide soft distillation targets and apply a consistency loss for regularization. These objectives are jointly optimized to train the SV model. Experiments on the VoxCeleb dataset show that our SS-SV method achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness.
column7: Yishuang Li(Malanshan audio & video Lab); Yi Yu(Malanshan audio & video Lab); Wanli Dong(Malanshan audio & video Lab); Weihao Gan(Malanshan audio & video Lab)

column4: Stabilizing Short Duration Speaker Verification through Neural Re-scoring with Hybrid Enrollment
column6: Short-duration speaker verification (SDSV) is crucial for personalized keyword spotting, where test utterances are typically shorter than three seconds. Limited speech duration results in unstable speaker representations and increased sensitivity to noise and phoneme variations, thereby degrading performance. To investigate this issue, we construct VoxPhrase, a large-scale SDSV corpus automatically segmented from the VoxCeleb dataset. Our analysis shows that text-dependent (TD) enrollment is constrained by duration and yields unstable speaker representations. In contrast, although text-independent (TI) enrollment introduces content mismatch, its representations become more stable as the enrollment duration increases. Accordingly, we propose a hybrid-enrollment neural re-scoring framework that combines TD and TI enrollment and performs frame-level comparison via parallel cross-attention. Experiments on VoxPhrase demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple speaker models.
column7: Zhiqi Ai(Shanghai University); Cheng Han(Shanghai University); Shiyi Mu(Shanghai University); Zhiyong Chen(Hithink RoyalFlush AI Research Institute); Yongjin Zhou(Shanghai University); Shugong Xu(Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University)

column4: VieSpeaker: A Large-Scale Vietnamese Speaker Recognition Dataset Beyond Visual Dependency
column6: Speaker recognition has advanced rapidly with large-scale training datasets, yet Vietnamese remains under-resourced, with existing corpora limited in scale and acoustic diversity. Most large-scale datasets rely on facial cues to link speech with speaker identities, restricting data collection to recordings where speakers appear on camera. We propose a face-independent dataset construction pipeline and introduce VieSpeaker, a large-scale Vietnamese speaker recognition dataset. Our approach leverages textual metadata and large language model reasoning to infer speaker identities from transcripts and contextual information. VieSpeaker contains approximately 902 hours of speech from 4,715 speakers. Experiments show that models trained on VieSpeaker achieve improved robustness and generalization compared to existing Vietnamese datasets. This work demonstrates the feasibility of face-independent dataset construction and provides a new direction for building large-scale speech resources.
column7: Viet Hoang Pham(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Tran Trung Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Bao Thu Ho(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Phuong Tuan Dat(Hanoi University of Science and Technology); Thi Thu Trang Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology)

column4: Confusion-Transport Pruning: Optimal-Transport Redundancy and CKA Geometry Distillation for Hard-Set Robust Speaker Verification
Function words: a topic independent approach to word n-gram selection for forensic speaker comparison
column6: This paper highlights an issue with likelihood ratio-based forensic speaker comparison (LR-based FSC) systems that exploit speaker idiosyncrasies in word choice. A baseline experiment using word n-gram features from speech transcripts of 104 Australian male speakers achieves a Cllr of 0.60. However, it is shown that topic dependent terms are included in the feature set, which may bias the result. In turn, this may lead to an overestimation of the strength of evidence obtainable from word n-gram based features. A simple but novel approach to circumventing this problem using function words is presented and evaluated. An explicitly defined features set of 156 function words is shown to yield a Cllr of 0.83. Subsequent evaluation of five filter based feature selection methods applied to the set demonstrates an notable improvement in performance when using the ANOVA F-ratio procedure (Cllr = 0.78). This result is coupled with a substantial reduction in dimension size to k= 50 features.
column7: Michael Carne(Australian National University)

column4: Codec-induced Mismatch, Speech Duration, and Speaker-dependent Effect in a DNN-based Forensic Speaker Recognition System
column6: The performance of forensic automatic speaker recognition (FASR) systems under the combined effects of codec-induced mismatch and different questioned-speech (QS) durations remains insufficiently understood, particularly at the individual speaker level. This study investigates the combined impact of representative lossy speech codecs (G.711 A-law, AMR-NB, and Opus) and QS duration on a DNN (ResNet34-MHA)-based FASR system. System-level performance was generally good across all codec conditions, especially with >30s speech. Codec effects vary, however, with low-bitrate AMR-NB causing the greatest degradation in performance and Opus having minimal impact. Crucially, individual-level analyses reveal substantial speaker-dependent variability that is obscured by system-level metrics: some speakers exhibit persistently poor or unstable performance, and speakers with poorer overall performance are more sensitive to codec-induced mismatch. These findings demonstrate that promising system-level performance does not guarantee good performance for all speakers and highlights the need for individual-level analysis when testing DNN-based FASR systems.
column7: Guangmou Deng(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Bruce Xiao Wang(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Vincent Hughes(University of York)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 5 - Poster 2 - Spatial Audio 4

column4: Addressing random spatial translations in measured microphone directional responses by maximizing finite order energy
column6: Directional responses measured on real-world devices are disturbed by unknown translations in space, which add uncertainty to spatial signal processing methods that use such data. In this paper we propose the concept of finite order centroid, which is the translation that maximizes directional response energy in finite order spatial harmonics. The centroid is calculated from the measured response as a second translation, to the effect that it cancels any random perturbation to the first. This leads to a calibrated directional response that is free from said positioning uncertainty, and has spatio-acoustical guarantees useful for downstream processing. We use several simple tasks to show the use of finite order centroids in spatial signal processing.
column7: Xue Wen(Samsung)

column4: Blind Room Impulse Response Identification via Reverberant Speech Spectrum Reconstruction
column6: This paper proposes Rec-RIR for blind room impulse response (RIR) identification. Based on the convolutive transfer function (CTF) approximation, we propose a multi-task deep neural network, which sequentially removes noise and reverberation from speech recording, and estimates the CTF filter by reverberant speech spectrum reconstruction. Subsequently, a pseudo intrusive measurement process is employed to convert the CTF filter into RIR by simulating a common intrusive RIR measurement procedure. Experimental results demonstrate that Rec-RIR achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in blind RIR identification.
column7: Pengyu Wang(Zhejiang University; Westlake University); Xiaofei Li(Westlake University; Westlake Institute for Advanced Study)

column4: Sensitivity Analysis of Generative Spatial Audio Metrics : A Study on Responsiveness, Smoothness, and Symmetry
column6: Evaluating generative spatial audio for First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) remains challenging due to a limited understanding of how metrics respond to changes in spatial parameters such as azimuth and elevation. We propose a framework to analyze metric sensitivity along continuous spatial trajectories, drawing on principles of sensitivity analysis in parametric sound synthesis. Using controlled FOA scenes with increasing scene complexity, we define three desiderata for metric behavior: Responsiveness, Smoothness, and Symmetry. We assess standard distribution-based and sample-based metrics, including Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD), intensity vectors, and acoustic maps. Our findings show that FAD using localization-specific embeddings and acoustic maps yield high Responsiveness and robust Smoothness and Symmetry across conditions, while intensity vectors degrade with increasing scene complexity. This is the first step towards investigating the sensitivity of metrics for generative spatial audio.
column7: Purnima Kamath(New York University); Adrian Roman(New York University); Koichi Saito(Sony AI); Yuki Mitsufuji(Sony AI; Sony Group Corporation; New York University); Juan Bello(New York University)

column4: FoleyImmersive: Decoupling What and Where for Video-to-First-Order Ambisonics
column6: We study immersive video-to-audio (V2A) by generating first-order ambisonics (FOA) from silent field-of-view (FoV) videos. Challenges include sparse semantics in video-FOA corpora and content-geometry entanglement: end-to-end models blur "what" and "where", while two-stage pipelines trade semantic fidelity for spatial coherence. We present FoleyImmersive and a semantics-augmented dataset, YT-AmbiSem, which augments YT-Ambigen with structured descriptions from Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Stage 1 (WHAT) uses a semantics-first diffusion model with multi-rate cross-frame attention and probabilistic time modulation to generate mono W. Stage 2 (WHERE) spatializes W to XYZ via a complex-STFT U-Net conditioned on per-frame visuals and camera direction; a lightweight directional residual mixer applies view-dependent bottleneck gating to stabilize localization with minimal content drift. We achieve state-of-the-art semantic and spatial metrics. Demo and dataset are available.
column7: Liming Liang(Peking University); Lingfeng Yang(South China University of Technology); Luo Chen(Peking University); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Yuexian Zou(Peking University)

column4: Learning Self-Supervised Spatial Representations via Soft Acoustic Contrastive Alignment
column6: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving downstream performance when annotated data is limited. However, most existing audio SSL methods process single-channel inputs and focus on learning spectral representations, which are often insufficient for spatially sensitive tasks like direction-of-arrival or reverberation estimation. In this work, we propose a self-supervised framework for binaural audio that integrates spatial priors directly into the pre-training objective. We introduce the Soft Acoustic Contrastive (SAC) loss, a geometric objective that structures the latent space by aligning embeddings based on shared acoustic properties, such as directionality and diffuseness, without requiring ground-truth labels. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms baselines across five downstream spatial parameter estimation tasks.
column7: Yotam Silverman(Tel Aviv University); Bracha Laufer-Goldshtein(Tel Aviv University)

column4: Geometrically Constrained Decentralized Independent Vector Analysis for Distributed Microphone Arrays
column6: This paper proposes a geometrically constrained decentral-ized independent vector analysis (GC-Dec-IVA) method for distributed microphone arrays. Recently proposed Dec-IVA method enables source separation by exchanging only power-related statistics to exploit cross-array information. However, this initial attempt often provides negligible improvement over applying IVA locally at each array, mainly due to the potential permutation inconsistency among arrays and the strong cross-array dependency implied by its source model. To address these limitations, we incorporate direction-of-arrival (DOA) information to derive GC-Dec-IVA, which mitigates permutation mismatch across arrays and enhances source alignment. Furthermore, a new source model is introduced to weaken cross-array dependency, improving robustness against permutation inconsistency in noisy environments. Experiments show the proposed method improves both the separation performance and cross-array permutation consistency.
column7: Changda Chen(Waseda University; Nanjing University); Yichen Yang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Wei Liu(Waseda University; Wuhan University); Bing Zhu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Shoji Makino(Waseda University); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University)

column4: Optimal Source Placement for TDoA-based Geometry Calibration of Distributed Microphone Arrays
column6: Distributed microphone arrays (DMAs) are widely used in various audio/speech processing applications. As these applications require the geometric structure of the DMA as a priori knowledge, geometry calibration of DMAs is indispensable. However, most existing methods use randomly placed calibration sources, which may lead to a relatively higher Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB). In this paper, we use a mobile robot to act as the multiple calibration sources, and optimize its positions to expect an improved self-localization accuracy. Specifically, we derive the CRLB using time-difference-of-arrival measurements with time offsets. Then, the optimal robot's positions are obtained by minimizing the CRLB while constraining the robot positions within a restricted room. Additionally, we also present a multi-stage solution for scenarios with limited computational resources or demanding runtime requirements. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed placement methods.
column7: Xu Wang(Inner Mongolia University); Qintuya Si(Inner Mongolia University); Qingyin Zhao(Inner Mongolia University); De Hu(Inner Mongolia University)

column4: G2C-NET: A Grid-to-Continuous Neural Network for Sound Source Localization in Distributed Microphone Arrays
column6: Grid-based sound source localization (SSL) has gained increasing attention in distributed microphone arrays as it reformulates the inherently nonconvex regression problem into a tractable classification task. However, the trade-off between grid resolution and computational complexity poses a fundamental challenge. To this end, we propose G2C-NET, a grid-to-continuous neural network which consists of two main modules: Global Likelihood Estimation (GLE) and Continuous Position Estimation (CPE). In the GLE module, we construct an adaptive pairwise feature aggregator to fuse the acoustic features from microphone pairs, generating the global likelihood distribution of source over grids. Then, the CPE module derives continuous source position via a weighted sum of high-confidence grids. Compared with existing grid-based SSL methods, G2C-NET achieves better performance at equivalent grid resolution. Experimental results validate its effectiveness.
column7: Zhiyuan Yue(Inner Mongolia University); De Hu(Inner Mongolia University)

column4: Fast Multichannel Nonnegative Matrix Factorization with Directivity Regularization for DOA-Informed Speech Separation
column6: This paper addresses DOA-informed multichannel speech separation under overdetermined conditions, where the number of speakers does not exceed the number of microphones. We focus on FastMNMF, a BSS method robust to unknown acoustic environments. Since FastMNMF represents real-source spatial covariance matrices in a jointly diagonalized domain, its diagonal components correspond to virtual spatial components rather than the real sources themselves. We propose directivity-regularized FastMNMF, which encourages each pseudo-separation filter to pass signals from the target speaker direction and suppress those from other speaker directions while tolerating DOA errors. The separation matrix is updated using a closed-form VCD-based rule. Experiments with simulated noisy simultaneous speech mixtures show that the proposed regularization improves separation performance.
column7: Ryosuke Ono(Kyoto University; RIKEN); Aditya Arie Nugraha(RIKEN); Yoshiaki Bando(AIST; RIKEN); Kazuyoshi Yoshii(Kyoto University; RIKEN)

column4: SpkGuideDOA: Speaker-wise Representation Guidance for Multiple Moving Speaker Localization
column6: Localizing multiple moving speakers in dynamic acoustic environments requires resolving time-varying spatial cues under severe spatial-spectral overlap. To address this challenge, we propose SpkGuideDOA, a framework that enhances a spatial cue estimator with speaker-wise representation guidance while maintaining computational efficiency. An auxiliary guidance generator extracts implicit speaker representations from multi-channel magnitudes and injects them via residual modulation at a pooled resolution. Training is driven by a localization objective with an additional loss that stabilizes the guidance branch. Joint permutation-invariant training ensures consistent speaker assignment across modules. Experiments on simulated mixtures and the LOCATA dataset demonstrate improved localization performance while maintaining computational efficiency.
column7: Yongseok Choi(Hanyang University); Davin Kim(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Quantifying the Uncertainty of Blindly Estimated Room Embeddings Using a Dispersion-Calibrated Score
column6: Room embeddings derived from reverberant speech are often unreliable: speech content and recording degradation can alter the representation even when speaker, room, and source-receiver geometry remain unchanged, degrading downstream task performance. We propose a framework that learns room embeddings robust to speech-content variation and a representation-level uncertainty score from reverberant speech without downstream-task supervision. The embedding is anchored to a structured room impulse response (RIR) latent space and trained using a multi-view data structure with KullbackLeibler (KL)-based alignment; a multi-positive contrastive term further refines robustness. A lightweight uncertainty head is calibrated using the dispersion of corruption-induced embeddings and optimized with a rank-based objective. Across waveform- and spectrogram-level corruptions, the score is consistent with representation dispersion and enables effective selective prediction while requiring only a single utterance at inference.
column7: Yang Xiang(University of Surrey); Philipp Götz(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen); Emanuël A. P. Habets(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen); Andreas Walther(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits IIS); Wenwu Wang(University of Surrey); Philip J. B. Jackson(University of Surrey)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 6 - Poster 6 - Multi-Channel Processing and Specialized Acquisition (UAV, Radar, Hearables)

column4: CAPS: A Cascaded Reconstruction Model to Power Saving in Hearables Using Sub-Nyquist Sampling with Bandwidth Extension
column6: Hearables are wearable computers worn on the ear. Bone conduction microphones are used with air conduction microphones in hearables for multimodal speech enhancement in noisy conditions. Despite this potential, current models largely fail to explore how jointly reducing sampling bit resolution and sampling frequency in analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) of hearables impacts both power usage and audio quality. Furthermore, current frameworks cannot do sub-Nyquist sampling in hearables because they lack a method to reconstruct wideband signals from narrowband components. We therefore propose CAPS, which (i) intentionally employs sub-Nyquist sampling and low bit resolution in ADCs, achieving a 3.3x reduction in power consumption in hearables, and (ii) supports streaming operation on mobile platforms with an inference time of 1.36ms and a memory footprint of 11.04MB. CAPS ensures robust speech intelligibility in real-world settings, bridging the gap between efficiency and power savings.
column7: Tarikul Islam(George Mason University); Sajid F. Dipto(George Mason University); Luke B. Baja-Ricketts(George Mason University); David C. Vergano(George Mason University); Anomadarshi Barua(George Mason University)

column4: An Investigation on Combining Geometry and Consistency Constraints into Phase Estimation for Speech Enhancement
column6: We propose a novel iterative phase estimation framework, termed the multi-source Griffin-Lim algorithm (MSGLA), for speech enhancement under additive noise. The key idea is to exploit the consistency constraint of complex short-time Fourier transform (STFT) spectrograms to resolve the sign ambiguity inherent in geometry-based phase estimation. We further introduce a geometric formulation based on the law of sines and cosines, enabling phase reconstruction using noise phase estimates. Oracle experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach under ideal conditions. Evaluations on VB-DMD and WSJ0-CHiME3 show that MSGLA variants match or slightly outperform existing methods, including direct phase estimation and DNN-based sign prediction, particularly in background noise suppression.
column7: Chun-Wei Ho(Georgia Institute of Technology); Pin-Jui Ku(Georgia Institute of Technology; NVIDIA); Hao Yen(Georgia Institute of Technology; Microsoft); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Universit`a degli Studi di Palermo); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Chin-Hui Lee(Georgia Institute of Technology)

column4: Through-Wall Radar Speech Acquisition via Cascaded Attention Fusion
column6: Speech acquisition using through-barrier radar sensing is challenging due to severe band limitation, distortion, and interference. Conventional deep learning models struggle to capture long-range temporal dependencies and recover missing high-frequency components. To address these challenges, we developed the Cascaded Attention Fusion Transformer (CAF-Former), which integrates progressive spectral expansion with a cascaded attention hierarchy. Temporal structure is modeled via multi-query self-attention that diversifies contextual representations while sharing a common basis. The resulting features are fused through a frequency-domain attention module that recalibrates spectral relations and models cross-frequency interactions. This design enables more effective high-frequency recovery and achieves consistent improvements over transformer baselines and state-of-the-art models under severe degradation.
column7: Ruotong Ding(Nanyang Technological University); Zhi-Wei Tan(Nanyang Technological University); V.G. Reju(Cochin University of Science and Technology); Andy W. H. Khong(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: Ego-Noise-Aware Spatial Filtering for Reliable UAV Audition in Extreme Low-SNR Conditions
column6: This paper presents a speech enhancement framework for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) audition systems operating under severe ego-noise. UAV ego-noise exhibits three structural properties: strong temporal correlation, frequency-varying noise composition, and amplitude stationarity, which respectively destabilize direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation, corrupt noise covariance matrix (NCM) estimation, and cause residual ego-noise to persist after beamforming. We utilize these properties to construct a drone-noise-aware speech enhancement system. We obtain reliable DoA via phase-consistency-guided time-frequency (TF) bin selection and use it to parameterize both a crossover-based hybrid NCM estimation and post-filter with a data-driven null direction and variance modulation for suppressing residual noise. Experiments demonstrate 98.12% DoA accuracy at −25dB SNR with consistent SI-SDR and speech quality improvements over baselines across anechoic and reverberant conditions.
column7: Chanhong Jeon(Sungkyunkwan University); Jeongmin Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Hyungjoo Seo(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Kyuhong Shim(Sungkyunkwan University); Taewook Kang(Sungkyunkwan University)

column4: Cross-Modal Consistency-Aware Structured Pruning for Efficient Speech Enhancement with Air- and Bone-Conduction Microphones
column6: Multimodal speech enhancement (MMSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments by leveraging complementary strengths of various signals. However, complex MMSE models and substantial computational demands pose challenges for implementation on wearable devices. This motivates model compression; however, prior approaches are often not tailored to multimodal fusion and may fail to preserve features critical for fusion under practical noise and cross-modal mismatch. To address these limitations, we introduce cross-modal consistency-aware structured pruning (CCAP). CCAP estimates channel importance using modality-wise zero masking and ranks channels by response consistency with the multimodal input to preserve modality-shared information. Experiments on a paired air/bone microphone dataset show that CCAP improves PESQ and STOI across multiple architectures over prior pruning baselines and reduces inference latency at equivalent pruning ratios, supporting embedded deployment.
column7: Yeeun Kim(POSTECH); Yonghun Song(POSTECH); Yunsik Kim(POSTECH); Yoonyoung Chung(POSTECH; Intus Co. Ltd.)

column4: DroFiT: A Lightweight Band-Fused Frequency Attention Toward Real-Time UAV Speech Enhancement
column6: This paper proposes DroFiT (Drone Frequency lightweight Transformer), a single-microphone speech enhancement network for severe drone ego-noise. A Full/Sub-band encoder-decoder compresses the noisy input at different ratios, where the sub-band path focuses on low-frequency detail and the full-band path retains global spectral context. A Pre-TCN(Temporal Convolutional Network) captures the harmonic and stationary structure of drone noise and a frequency-wise Transformer attends over the concatenated Full/Sub band tokens, allowing the Full/Sub-band features to complement each other in a shared attention space. The model is evaluated on the VoiceBank-DEMAND dataset mixed with recorded drone noise. Compared to drone-oriented baselines such as DCU-net and SMoLnet-T, DroFiT achieves enhancement performance while reducing computation by 15-26× and 9-15×, respectively. With 168k parameters, it supports incremental(frame-wise streaming) inference and is suitable for resource-constrained UAVs.
column7: Jeongmin Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Chanhong Jeon(Sungkyunkwan University); Hyungjoo Seo(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Kyuhong Shim(Sungkyunkwan University); Taewook Kang(Sungkyunkwan University)

column4: mmWave Radar Aware Dual-Conditioned GAN for Speech Reconstruction of Signals With Low SNR
column6: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar captures are band-limited and noisy, making for difficult reconstruction of intelligible full-bandwidth speech. In this work, we propose a two-stage speech reconstruction pipeline for mmWave using a Radar-Aware Dual-conditioned Generative Adversarial Network (RAD-GAN), which is capable of performing bandwidth extension on signals with low signal-to-noise ratios (-5 dB to -1 dB), captured through glass walls. We propose an mmWave-tailored Multi-Mel Discriminator (MMD) and a Residual Fusion Gate (RFG) to enhance the generator input to process multiple conditioning channels. The proposed two-stage pipeline involves pre-training the model on synthetically clipped clean speech and fine-tuning on fused mel spectrograms generated by the RFG. We empirically show that the proposed method, trained on a limited dataset, with no pre-trained modules, and no data augmentations, outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for this specific task.
column7: JASH KARANI(Birla Institute of Technology and Science); Adithya Chittem(Birla Institute of Technology and Science); Deepan Roy(Birla Institute of Technology and Science); Sandeep Joshi(Birla Institute of Technology and Science)

column4: Deep Learning Based Relative Transfer Matrix Estimation for Multiple Sources and Multiple Microphones
column6: The Relative Transfer Matrix (ReTM), recently introduced as a generalization of the relative transfer function for multiple receivers and sources, shows promising performance when applied to speech enhancement in noisy environments. Estimating the ReTM of sound sources by exploiting the covariance matrices of multichannel recordings is highly beneficial for practical applications and, to date, remains the only proposed approach. This paper investigates deep learning-based ReTM estimation. We propose three novel supervised learning frameworks using time- and short-time frequency transform domain convolutional networks, and a Long Short-Term Memory-based recurrent neural network. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed models achieve more accurate estimation of the ReTM using five objective metrics compared to the covariance-based method. We also show the effectiveness of the proposed frameworks for speech enhancement, achieving performance on par with the baseline method.
column7: Oshan A. B. Yalegama(University of Moratuwa); Wageesha N. Manamperi(University of Moratuwa; The Australian National University)

column4: Cloud-Boosted Low-Compute Multi-Channel Speech Enhancement
column6: Low-latency, low-compute speech enhancement is essential for wearable devices with real-time communication requirements, but strict computational constraints significantly limit on-device performance. Knowledge Boosting has been proposed as an effective approach to improve edge model performance by leveraging a more capable server-side model, but performance gains for speech enhancement have been limited. We propose a collaborative framework incorporating three techniques: (1) delayed server output as additional input, (2) layerwise feature boosting that transfers intermediate server representations to guide edge inference, and (3) collaborative multichannel Wiener filtering, which fuses weighted covariance matrices estimated from both server and edge models for improved beamforming. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed collaborative framework significantly outperforms the edge-only baseline with minimal additional computational overhead.
column7: Xulin Fan(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Juan Azcarreta(Meta Reality Labs Research); Ashutosh Pandey(Meta Reality Labs Research); Jesus Alvarez(Meta Reality Labs Research); Ke Tan(Meta Reality Labs Research); Jacob Donley(Meta Reality Labs Research); Ritwik Giri(Meta Reality Labs Research); Buye Xu(Meta Reality Labs Research)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 7 - Poster 1 - Speech Synthesis Evaluation and Benchmarking

column4: PolyBench: Benchmarking LLM-based TTS Systems for Chinese Polyphone Disambiguation
column6: Large Language Model-based Text-to-Speech (LLM-TTS) systems have achieved remarkable progress in speech synthesis. However, evaluating their ability to handle Chinese polyphonic characters remains unexplored. This paper introduces PolyBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating Chinese polyphone disambiguation in LLM-TTS systems. We construct three test sets covering 494 polyphonic characters and 88 polyphonic words across diverse categories. Additionally, we explore automatic pronunciation labeling using Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) and benchmark 17 open source systems. Evaluation results reveal that even the best system achieves only 82.02% pronunciation accuracy on polyphonic characters, with significant performance gaps in dialectal, colloquial, and literary categories, revealing the limitations of current TTS systems in polyphone disambiguation and the need for improvement.
column7: Chunhui Lu(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Rui Zhou(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Feifan Chen(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Liming Song(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); YoonChoon Hwang(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); Junkwang Oh(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); Gunu Jho(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics)

column4: Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS
column6: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.
column7: Sneha Ray Barman(IIT Guwahati); Neeraj Kumar Sharma(IIT Guwahati); Shakuntala Mahanta(IIT Guwahati)

column4: An Evaluation Framework for Text-to-Speech Voice Reconstruction
column6: Voice reconstruction using Text-to-Speech (TTS) offers a communication method for people with speech disorders, which aims to retain their speaker identity while improving intelligibility. Previous work generally relies on Mean Opinion Score (MOS) to evaluate naturalness and speaker similarity, but this has limited sensitivity and reliability. We propose an evaluation framework with subjective and objective components. Subjectively, we evaluate perceived intelligibility and speaker identity using Best Worst Scaling (BWS) with situational framing. Objectively, we demonstrate that standard measures fail to predict reconstruction success for highly unintelligible speakers, so we introduce a novel dual-reference distributional measure to assess the trade-off between intelligibility and speaker identity. By evaluating the output of 17 zero-shot TTS systems for 193 speakers, we show that our framework provides a reliable and task-aligned approach for assessing voice reconstruction.
column7: Ariadna Sanchez(University of Edinburgh); Christoph Minixhofer(University of Edinburgh); Korin Richmond(University of Edinburgh); Ondřej Klejch(University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(University of Edinburgh); Simon King(University of Edinburgh)

column4: Evaluating Automatic Laughter Phone Annotation for Socially-Situated Laughter Synthesis
column6: Laughter synthesis remains underdeveloped in current conversational agent technologies. Laughter appears in diverse forms reflecting individuality, emotion, and social context. To model this diversity and generating appropriate laughter, annotating laughter phones is crucial, but it involves an immense workload. This study evaluates automatic laughter phone annotation for conversational laughter synthesis. Using a newly annotated eleven-speaker dataset, we built an improved laughter phone recognizer and constructed two laughter synthesizers, a statistical parametric speech synthesis (SPSS)-based model and an audio-LLM-based model, using manual and automatic phone labels. Listening tests showed that the audio-LLM-based synthesizer achieved higher naturalness, whereas the SPSS-based synthesizer achieved higher reproducibility of the way of laughing, and that systems built with automatic labels did not match the performance of those using manual labels.
column7: Hiroki Mori(Utsunomiya University); Hiroto Ueda(Utsunomiya University)

column4: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion: A Japanese Case Study
column6: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion is essential for controllable and robust text-to-speech, and large language models (LLMs), with broad linguistic knowledge, offer a promising approach. We benchmarked over 30 LLMs on Japanese G2P, comparing them with conventional morphological analyzers on 3000 manually annotated sentences. We evaluated two prompting strategies: a parse mode, where the LLM performs morphological analysis followed by rule-based kana conversion, and a direct mode, where the LLM directly predicts kana readings. The results show that model size, version, and Japanese-specialized training are key factors, with the best LLMs achieving kana character error rate below 0.52% vs. the best conventional tool (1.03%). Parse mode outperforms direct mode for most models, as rule-based post-processing relieves the LLM of handling complex pronunciation rules. We also show that feeding LLM-predicted kana into a kana-input TTS yields better pronunciation than end-to-end TTS.
column7: Tomoki Koriyama(CyberAgent)

column4: The False Resonance: A Critical Examination of Emotion Embedding Similarity for Speech Generation Evaluation
column6: Objective metrics for emotional expressiveness are vital for speech generation, particularly in expressive synthesis and voice conversion requiring emotional prosody transfer. To quantify this, the field widely relies on emotion similarity between reference and generated samples. This approach computes cosine similarity of embeddings from encoders like emotion2vec, assuming they capture affective cues despite linguistic and speaker variations. We challenge this assumption through controlled adversarial tasks and human alignment tests. Despite high classification accuracy, these latent spaces are unsuitable for zero-shot similarity evaluation. Representational limitations cause linguistic and speaker interference to overshadow emotional features, degrading discriminative ability. Consequently, the metric misaligns with human perception. This acoustic vulnerability reveals it rewards acoustic mimicry over genuine emotional synthesis.
column7: Yun-Shao Tsai(National Taiwan University); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Tzu-Wen Hsu(Independent Researcher); Yun-Man Hsu(National Taiwan University); Chun Wei Chen(National Taiwan University); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)

column4: LLM-Based Multi-Reference Evaluation for Efficient and Robust Assessment of Phrase Break Annotations
column6: Reliable evaluation of phrase break annotations is crucial, as subtle variations in prosodic boundaries directly affect the clarity and naturalness of speech. However, existing approaches exhibit major limitations: single-reference evaluation assumes a unique gold phrasing for an utterance despite multiple valid phrasings, while human judgment, though flexible, is labor-intensive and unscalable. To address these, we propose LLM-based Multi-Reference Evaluation (LMRE) for phrase break annotations that models the one-to-many nature of prosodic phrasing and generates multiple valid phrasings from minimal demonstrations. On a Korean testbed of 1,356 annotations covering five strategies, LMRE shows stronger alignment with human judgment than single-reference evaluation in both acceptance behavior and score correlation. Our findings demonstrate that LMRE effectively achieves both scalability and multi-reference support, highlighting the potential of LLMs for evaluation in the speech domain.
column7: Younghan Park(NAVER Cloud; Yonsei University); Hoyeon Lee(NAVER Cloud); Hawon Jeong(NAVER Cloud; KAIST AI); Jong-Hwan Kim(NAVER Cloud)

column4: Investigating the Relationship between Objective AI-driven Metrics and Subjective MOS for In-the-Wild Speech
column6: Automated Mean Opinion Score (MOS) predictors are widely used for TTS evaluation but are trained on studio or denoising corpora. Compared to human MOS ratings, O-MOS correlations collapse on in-the-wild (ITW) discrete-token TTS. We conduct a controlled ablation across four systems-continuous clean TTS, discrete ITW TTS (MQTTS), an additive noise control, and ground-truth recordings-and collect 768 human naturalness ratings under a headphone-screened protocol. UT-MOSv2 correlation collapses from r=0.51 (p<0.01) on the continuous clean system to r=-0.01 (n.s.) on the discrete ITW system; other neural predictors also collapse. DNSMOS P.835 penalises an additive noise condition 0.42 points more severely than a generative-artefact condition despite listeners rating both equivalently, directly contradicting human perception. These findings challenge the validity of current objective metrics as standalone proxies for naturalness evaluation of in-the-wild generative TTS.
column7: Jasmer Sanjotra(Indian Institute of Technology Indore); Nagendra Kumar(Indian Institute of Technology Indore); Shekhar Nayak(University of Groningen)

column4: SongBench: A Fine-Grained Multi-Aspect Benchmark for Song Quality Assessment
column6: Recent advancements in Text-to-Song generation have enabled realistic musical content production, yet existing evaluation benchmarks lack the professional granularity to capture multi-dimensional aesthetic nuances. In this paper, we propose SongBench, a specialized framework for fine-grained song assessment across seven key dimensions: Vocal, Instrument, Melody, Structure, Arrangement, Mixing, and Musicality. Utilizing this framework, we construct an expert-annotated database comprising 11,717 samples from state-of-the-art models, labeled by music professionals. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that SongBench achieves high correlation with expert ratings. By revealing fine-grained performance gaps in current state-of-the-art models, SongBench serves as a diagnostic benchmark to steer the development toward more professional and musically coherent song generation. The evaluation toolkit is available at https://github.com/Tencent/ SongBench.
column7: Dapeng Wu(Tsinghua University); Shun Lei(Tsinghua University); Wei Tan(Tencent AI Lab); Guangzheng Li(Tencent AI Lab); Yunzhe Wang(Tencent AI Lab); Huaicheng Zhang(Tencent AI Lab); Lishi Zuo(Tencent AI Lab); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University)

column4: GRATS : A Natural Multi-Speed Mandarin Dataset for Speech Time-Scale Modification Benchmarking
column6: Despite extensive research on Speech Time-Scale Modification (STSM), evaluation for Mandarin remains limited due to the lack of naturally recorded, multi-speed parallel data. Existing studies rely on English corpora or artificially time-scaled references, which fail to capture rate-dependent prosodic and tonal characteristics. As a tonal language, Mandarin depends on fine-grained pitch-timing coordination, making it sensitive to time-scaling distortions. We introduce GRATS (Granular Rate Adaptation for Temporal Scaling), a naturally recorded parallel multi-speaker Mandarin dataset with 25 speakers and five speaking rates (0.5x, 0.75x, 1.0x, 1.25x, 1.5x), allowing comparison against authentic target-rate recordings. Benchmark results show trade-offs between intelligibility and perceptual quality, and degradation in temporal and pitch consistency under extreme rates, highlighting the importance of tone-aware and alignment-aware evaluation.
column7: Ghaida Fathin Aghniya(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Dyah A. M. G. Wisnu(Academia Sinica); Stefano Rini(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica)

column4: On the Effect of Segmentation Width and Cluster Size on Speech Resynthesis and Continuation in Generative Spoken Language Models
column6: Generative Spoken Language Modeling (GSLM) enables text-free speech modeling by training language models (LMs) using discrete speech representations instead of textual transcription. In this paper, we investigate the performance of GSLM on speech synthesis and continuation using discrete speech representations with varying bitrates. We segment speech representations with fixed widths and train K-means models in multiple cluster sizes, resulting in various bitrate settings. We demonstrate that intelligible and natural speech can be synthesized at lower bitrate settings than the baseline. Furthermore, speech continuation quality remains stable at lower bitrates across multiple metrics, suggesting that the conventional GSLM setting may be redundant for effective speech generation. Although LLM-based metrics show higher correlation with human subjective score than conventional metrics, it remains low, highlighting the need for more stable automatic evaluation methods.
column7: Shunsuke Kando(The University of Tokyo); Wataru Nakata(The University of Tokyo); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; The University of Tokyo); Yusuke Miyao(The University of Tokyo)

column4: ConformalMOS: Uncertainty-Aware MOS Prediction with Conformal Intervals and Ordinal Modeling
column6: Accurate prediction of human Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) is crucial for evaluating synthetic speech quality in text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC). Most MOS predictors output only point estimates and ignore uncertainty, limiting reliability in model selection and deployment. We propose ConformalMOS, a framework that augments MOS prediction with conformal prediction to produce statistically valid prediction intervals with guaranteed coverage under exchangeability, alongside point estimates. During training, MOS labels are modeled in an ordinal-aware manner by converting one-hot targets into Gaussian-smoothed distributions, preserving score ordering. This improves uncertainty calibration, particularly when softmax confidence is overconfident on out-of-distribution speech. On BVCC datasets, ConformalMOS achieves competitive accuracy (MSE = 0.08) while delivering empirically validated coverage, enhancing reliability for real-world TTS and VC deployment.
column7: Kehinde Elelu(Michigan State University); Joshua E. Siegel(Michigan State University); Mohammadali Saffary(Michigan State University); Tashfain Ahmed(Michigan State University); Simeon Babatunde(Clemson University); Ebuka Okpala(Clemson University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 8 - Poster 4 - ASR Under Real-World Constraints: Streaming, Adaptation, and Efficiency

column4: A Compact Fully-Open Cache-Aware Streaming Model for Japanese ASR
column6: We present a 123M-parameter fully-open cache-aware streaming model for Japanese ASR with a hybrid RNNT/CTC design. To our knowledge, no prior Japanese ASR system simultaneously provides full openness—open weights, data preparation details, code, and logs-together with streaming capability. On a 35K-hour pre-training corpus we show that CER-stratified data curation consistently benefits underrepresented domains but can hurt performance under multi-domain fine-tuning with higher decoder capacity. We further study progressive fine-tuning across five domains totaling 507 hours. Evaluated on five test sets, our model achieves 12.4% average CER (RNNT), outperforming the 1B OWSM-CTC v4 (13.5%) and 619M ReazonSpeech NeMo-v2 (14.1%) while being 5-8× smaller, with an RTFx of 1220 (batch) and 446 (streaming).
column7: Yinchang Yang(KCGI)

column4: Robust Streaming ASR with Decoupled Separation and Recognition
column6: Real-time speech transcription that is robust to background noise, room reverberation, and interfering speakers is critical for many real-world automatic speech recognition (ASR) applications. To address these interferences, multi-condition training (MCT) is commonly employed for training an ASR model, but it requires large-scale training data and degrades recognition performance on clean speech. In this work, we propose a decoupled framework that leverages an online speech separation frontend, and a streaming ASR backend trained only on clean speech, for robust streaming ASR. We benchmark the proposed approach on LibriSpeech, CHiME-4, and LibriCSS datasets, and demonstrate that the decoupled framework consistently outperforms the MCT-based baselines for streaming ASR. Our approach is also shown to generalize to large pre-trained speech models, offering a modular approach for robust streaming ASR that avoids task-specific re-training and MCT.
column7: Yufeng Yang(The Ohio State University); Cheng Yu(The Ohio State University); Vahid Ahmadi Kalkhorani(The Ohio State University); DeLiang Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: Margin-Aware Contrastive Regularization for Robust Streaming Keyword Spotting under Strict False-Alarm Constraints
column6: Edge keyword spotting (KWS) in continuous streaming must satisfy strict false-alarm (FA) budgets while maintaining high detection sensitivity. At stringent points (≤ 0.5 FA/h), CE-trained lightweight causal models suffer severe false rejection rate (FRR) degradation against phonetically similar imposters. We propose Margin-Aware Contrastive Regularization (MACR), an offline auxiliary objective that applies intra-class attraction only to target keywords to avoid globally clustering the heterogeneous Unknown category, and enforces margin-based repulsion emphasizing offline-mined hard negatives. On Google Speech Commands V2 under an event-level streaming protocol, MACR achieves > 40% relative FRR reduction over CE at strict points (0.5-0.2 FA/h) with minor changes in closed-set accuracy. As a training-only regularizer, MACR introduces zero additional parameters, MACs, or algorithmic latency to the deployed causal inference graph.
column7: Hanwen Zhang(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China); Guosong Zhu(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China); Zhen Qin(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)

column4: Mitigating Causality Mismatch with Causal Temporal Relation Distillation for Streaming Keyword Spotting
column6: On-device keyword spotting (KWS) requires strictly causal models for zero-lookahead streaming. Distilling from non-causal teachers introduces causality mismatch: teacher features encode future context. Point-wise regression to these absolute features creates capacity conflicts that severely hinder continuous inference. To mitigate this, we propose Causal Temporal Relation Distillation, transferring intra-sample temporal topology instead of point-wise features. Applying a lower-triangular mask to relation matrices establishes a strictly realizable historical anchor. Our offline bidirectional variant (Ours-Bi) utilizes the teacher's full topology as an auxiliary prior without altering the zero-lookahead inference graph. On Google Speech Commands V2, Ours-Bi improves causal 1D-CNN accuracy from 95.12% to 96.91%. Under a continuous-stream protocol, it halves the False Rejection Rate (8.52% to 4.15% at 1.0 FA/h), demonstrating vastly superior long-context robustness.
column7: Hanwen Zhang(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China); Guosong Zhu(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China); Zhen Qin(NDS Key Lab, Sichuan; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)

column4: Retention-Preserving Gradient Projection with Entropy-Guided Token-Level Distillation for Rehearsal-Free Continual ASR
column6: Large-scale pretrained automatic speech recognition (ASR) models such as Whisper achieve strong generalization but suffer catastrophic forgetting under sequential domain adaptation. We propose a strict rehearsal-free continual learning method that uses distillation from the previous model to define a retention direction. We refine it with entropy-guided token-level distillation, up-weighting confident teacher tokens and down-weighting uncertain ones. When supervised and distillation gradients conflict, we apply retention-preserving gradient projection to attenuate the opposing supervised component with a tunable projection coefficient. Based on Fisher information, we freeze the encoder and adapt only the decoder. Compared with Learning without Forgetting (LwF), our method achieves a 7.2% relative reduction in mean word error rate (WER) after sequential adaptation to LibriSpeech, AMI, TED-LIUM, and SPGISpeech. It reduces the average multilingual degradation on Common Voice by 51.5%.
column7: Seunghee Ma(Sogang University; LOTTE INNOVATE); Junseok Oh(Sogang University); Ji-Hwan Kim(Sogang University)

column4: Parameter-Efficient Continual Learning for Automatic Speech Recognition
column6: Speech foundation models enable strong general-purpose ASR and are attractive for downstream adaptation. However, their size and the catastrophic forgetting induced by sequential fine-tuning demand parameter-efficient and regularized training methods, motivating parameter-efficient continual learning (PECL). While PECL has been widely studied in NLP and vision, it has received less attention in ASR. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective PECL method based on recent advances in parameter-efficient fine-tuning for ASR. We partition pretrained weight matrices into head and tail subspaces according to singular values and restrict adaptation to approximate rotations within the low-energy tail subspace, preserving dominant components and reducing forgetting. For subsequent tasks, rotations are combined via weight averaging to further improve retention. Experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate reduced forgetting and superior overall performance compared to recent PECL baselines.
column7: Steven Vander Eeckt(KU Leuven); Hugo Van hamme(KU Leuven)

column4: MoDiCoL: A Modular Diagnostic Continual Learning Dataset for Robust Speech Recognition
column6: Modern Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have made remarkable progress on standard benchmarks, yet performance gaps have emerged under real-world distribution shifts, caused by recording conditions, accents, speech impairments, and noise. Existing datasets and benchmarks typically isolate these factors, which overlooks their co-occurrence in real-world applications. In this paper, we argue that model robustness can be treated as a dynamic capability that continually develops, and we introduce MoDiCoL, a Modular Diagnostic Continual Learning dataset designed for controlled analysis of linguistic content, speaker characteristics, and acoustic environments. Furthermore, we propose a real-world-inspired continual learning curriculum to simulate incremental updates and study how robustness is acquired, transferred, and forgotten. We evaluate three continual learning strategies and provide detailed insights into robustness under evolving conditions.
column7: Theresa Pekarek Rosin(University of Hamburg); Matthias Kerzel(University of Hamburg); Stefan Wermter(University of Hamburg)

column4: SCOLoRA: Similarity Conditioned Signed Orthogonal LoRA for Continual Speaker Adaptation
column6: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is expected to handle speaker and environmental variability, yet deployed systems encounter continual distribution shifts as new speakers arrive. Continual speaker adaptation personalizes one model along a speaker stream without revisiting past data, but sequential updates can cause catastrophic forgetting. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) offers a parameter efficient mechanism, and orthogonal low-rank adaptation (O-LoRA) reduces interference by separating update subspaces. However, enforcing task agnostic separation can suppress transfer among acoustically similar speakers. We introduce similarity conditioned signed orthogonal LoRA (SCOLoRA), which leverages speaker embedding similarity to dynamically balance subspace alignment and orthogonal separation via signed coefficients. Across ASR benchmarks, SCOLoRA consistently improves new speaker adaptation and reduces forgetting over LoRA-based continual learning baselines.
column7: Ye-Eun Ko(Hanyang University); Jae-Hong Lee(Hankuk University of Foreign Studies); Dong-Hyun Kim(Hanyang University); Jin-Seong Choi(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition
column6: We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation where one accent is held out during training, the proposed method yields a 12.3% relative improvement over single LoRA. These results indicate that phonetic-category-based decomposition offers a scalable and transferable alternative to accent-level adaptation.
column7: Santosh Dahal(Thapathali Campus); Anmol Guragain(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Tianchi Liu(National University of Singapore); Luis Fernando D'Haro(Universidad Politécnica de Madrid); Kiran Chandra Dahal(Thapathali Campus)

column4: First-to-Spike: An Early-Exit Framework for Rapid and Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks
column6: Spiking neural networks offer a promising path to energy-efficient AI, yet their potential for low-latency inference often remains unrealized. Existing early-exit SNNs typically rely on extrinsic, non-spiking criteria like confidence thresholds, complicating the model. We revisit this paradigm by demonstrating that SNNs possess an intrinsic early-exit capability. We introduce the First-to-Spike framework, where inference terminates immediately upon the first spike from a competitive output layer. This event-driven mechanism is further accelerated by a Winner-Take-All circuit and optimized by a novel Hybrid Temporal Training objective. Extensive evaluations on speech and neurophysiological datasets show that F2S sets a new state of the art, achieving higher accuracy with significantly reduced latency and energy consumption. Our work validates that the spike itself can serve as a robust and efficient decision signal for real-time applications. Source code is available online.
column7: Zheyuan Lin(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Sirui Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zeyang Song(National University of Singapore); Zhiqi Zhang(Tsinghua University); Siqi Cai(Harbin Institute of Technology); Haizhou Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 10 - Poster 1 - Multimodal Speech Processing and Speech LLM Systems

column4: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Speech-Aware LLMs for Timestamp Prediction
column6: Word-level timestamps are essential for many speech applications. Existing methods either degrade transcription quality when interleaving timestamps or require separate alignment models that do not integrate into speech LLMs. We propose a parameter efficient framework for speech recognition with timestamps (SRWT) within a single speech LLM. Our approach generates transcriptions in the first step and regenerates them with timestamps in the second, preserving transcription quality. We introduce modular low rank adaptation (LoRA) variants that train only on SRWT data without degrading base model capabilities, enabling isolated adaptation as speech LLMs scale to more tasks. We propose novel activated LoRA (aLoRA) for SRWT, enabling KV-cache reuse thus allowing improved performance through base model usage while preserving modularity. Experiments show a 27ms alignment error in English (35% relative improvement over the best baseline) and 21ms in multilingual data, while maintaining WER identical to the base model. Proposed methods also exhibit strong zero-shot transfer, achieving 37ms error on multilingual data when trained only on English.
column7: Vishal Sunder(IBM Research); Samuel Thomas(IBM Research); Xulin Fan(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Brian Kingsbury(IBM Research); George Saon(IBM Research); Avihu Dekel(IBM Research); Luis Lastras(IBM Research)

column4: ZEBRA: Zero-Shot Entropy-Regularized Prompt Learning for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Audio-Language Models
column6: Audio-Language Models (ALMs) achieve strong zero-shot performance by aligning audio with textual class descriptions. Although prompt learning improves accuracy on base classes through few-shot supervised adaptation, we observe a critical trade-off: it often degrades performance on novel classes, sometimes falling below zero-shot accuracy. This exposes a base-to-novel generalization gap in prompt learning for ALMs. To address this issue, we propose ZEBRA (Zero-shot Entropy-Regularized Prompt Learning for Base-to-Novel Generalization), a plug-and-play framework that fuses zero-shot logits with prompt-learning logits, and employs self-entropy regularization to reduce overfitting to base classes. Experiments across multiple audio classification datasets show that ZEBRA consistently improves novel-class performance while maintaining strong base accuracy, significantly reducing the base-to-novel gap compared to standard prompt learning. The code is available at: https://github.com/asif-hanif/zebra.
column7: Asif Hanif(Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)); Mohammad Yaqub(Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI))

column4: MultiEmoVec: Learning Generalised Multimodal Emotion Representation by Momentum Contrast and Multi-task Reconstruction
column6: Multimodal emotion recognition is limited by the difficulty of collecting and labelling large-scale emotional data, as well as the noisy and incomplete modalities commonly observed in emotional databases. To address these issues, we introduce MultiEmoVec, an unsupervised pre-training framework that learns general-purpose multimodal emotion representations via cross-modal reconstructions, contrastive learning, and adaptive loss scaling. Masked reconstruction recovers missing information across modalities, while denoising reconstruction improves robustness to noisy inputs. Cross-modal attention with a transformer encoder integrates features, and momentum contrast learns discriminative representations. After pre-training, the encoder is frozen to extract representations for lightweight classification on multiple databases. Results, including ablation and cross-database evaluations, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and generalisation ability.
column7: Junchen Liu(University of Auckland); Jesin James(Electrical, Computer and Software Engineering, University of Auckland, New Zealand); Karan Nathwani(India Institute of Technology); Michael Witbrock(Computer Science, University of Auckland, New Zealand)

column4: Unified Audio-Visual Modeling to Recognize Which Face Spoke When and What in Scenarios with On- and Off-Screen Participants
column6: We propose an audio-visual modeling method that recognizes which face spoke when and what from videos with or without visible speakers. The conventional method represents information about which face spoke when and what was spoken as a single serialized token sequence and performs autoregressive prediction. However, it assumes that all speakers are always visible in the video, whereas in real-world environments, some speakers may be occluded or outside the camera's view. To handle these cases, we introduce a dedicated token to indicate the absence of a speaker in videos. We compared the proposed method to the conventional method and the combined system that separately estimates when and what is spoken, and which face is speaking. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms both methods when off-screen speakers are included, while achieving almost the same performance as the dedicated conventional method when all speakers are on-screen.
column7: Naoki Makishima(NTT, Inc.); Suzuka Yamada(NTT, Inc.); Taiga Yamane(NTT, Inc.); Mana Ihori(NTT, Inc.); Tanaka Tomohiro(NTT, Inc.); Satoshi Suzuki(NTT, Inc.); Shota Orihashi(NTT, Inc.); Ryo Masumura(NTT, Inc.)

column4: Speech Recognition on TV Series with Video-Guided Post-ASR Correction
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) has achieved remarkable success with deep learning, driving advancements in conversational artificial intelligence, media transcription, and assistive technologies. However, ASR systems still struggle in complex environments such as TV series, where multiple speakers, overlapping speech, domain-specific terminology, and long-range contextual dependencies pose significant challenges to transcription accuracy. Existing approaches fail to explicitly leverage the rich temporal and contextual information available in the video. To address this limitation, we propose a Video-Guided Post-ASR Correction (VPC) framework that uses a Video-Large Multimodal Model (VLMM) to capture video context and refine ASR outputs. Evaluations on a TV-series benchmark show that our method consistently improves transcription accuracy in complex multimedia environments.
column7: Haoyuan Yang(The University of Texas Dallas); Yue Zhang(The University of Texas Dallas); Liqiang Jing(The University of Texas Dallas); John Hansen(The University of Texas Dallas)

column4: Closing the Speech-Text Gap with Limited Audio for Effective Domain Adaptation in LLM-Based ASR
column6: Conventional end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems rely on paired speech-text data for domain adaptation. Recent LLM-based ASR architectures connect a speech encoder to a large language model via a projection module, enabling adaptation with text-only data. However, this introduces a modality gap, as the LLM is not exposed to the noisy representations produced by the speech projector. We investigate whether small amounts of speech can mitigate this mismatch. We compare three strategies: text-only adaptation, paired speech-text adaptation, and mixed batching (MB), which combines both. Experiments in in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that even limited speech consistently improves performance. Notably, MB using only 10% of the target-domain (less than 4 hours) speech achieves word error rates comparable to, or better than, conventional ASR fine-tuning with the full dataset, indicating that small amounts of speech provide a strong modality-alignment signal.

column4: Improving Streaming Speaker Diarization for LLM Based Multi-talker Speech Understanding
column6: Previous work has shown that source separation with post-processing can help large language models (LLMs) handle multi-talker speech by serving as an external speaker diarization module. However, simple threshold-based approaches lack robustness under diverse acoustic conditions. We propose a two-stage framework comprising a source separation model followed by a statistical classifier (e.g., Gradient Boosting Decision Trees) for speaker tagging. To improve efficiency, we explore a Conformer-based architecture that significantly reduces parameter count. Additionally, to accommodate varying microphone geometries across smart glasses devices, we develop a multi-geometry model enabling a single source separation model to generalize across devices. Experiments on real-world multi-talker recordings demonstrate improvements in both accuracy and efficiency for speech recognition and translation tasks.

column4: DiscoPhon: Benchmarking the Unsupervised Discovery of Phoneme Inventories With Discrete Speech Units
column6: We introduce DiscoPhon, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating unsupervised phoneme discovery from discrete speech units. DiscoPhon covers 6 dev and 6 test languages, chosen to span a wide range of phonemic contrasts. Given only 10 hours of speech in a previously unseen language, systems must produce discrete units that are mapped to a predefined phoneme inventory, through either a many-to-one or a one-to-one assignment. The resulting sequences are evaluated for unit quality, recognition and segmentation. We provide four pretrained multilingual HuBERT and SpidR baselines, and show that phonemic information is available enough in current models for derived units to correlate well with phonemes, though with variations across languages.

column4: Tarsila-ASR: A Multi-Domain Test Suite for Benchmarking Brazilian Portuguese Speech Recognition
column6: Spontaneous speech recognition remains a key challenge for conversational AI, where disfluencies such as fillers, hesitations, and truncations are common. Although recent Transformer-based ASR systems perform well on read speech, their effectiveness under spontaneous Brazilian Portuguese conditions remains limited, partly due to the lack of diverse benchmarks. In this work, we introduce Tarsila ASR, a new benchmark with more than 70 hours of spontaneous speech aggregated from multiple public datasets to better reflect real world conversational variability. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate open source ASR models and improve strong baselines through fine tuning on diverse conversational data, achieving new state of the art (SOTA) performance. Our results highlight the importance of domain specific adaptation and provide publicly available resources to support future research on conversational ASR in Brazilian Portuguese.
