column4: Balalaika: Data-Centric, Prosody-Aware Annotation Pipeline for Russian Speech
column6: We introduce Balalaika, an open-source, data-centric pipeline for processing audio and producing prosody-aware annotations. It combines semantic VAD for context-preserving segmentation, multi-ASR ensembling with ROVER consensus decoding, while retaining word-level timestamps, followed by automatic quality and speaker-purity filtering. The text is further enriched with punctuation restoration, lexical stress and e/yo normalization, and IPA phonemes. Using Balalaika, we build a 5.1k-hour multi-source Russian corpus with rich annotations, and show consistent gains under equalized training budgets for both speech denoising and TTS; ablations confirm complementary benefits of stress and punctuation and improved synthesis with stricter MOS filtering. The dataset is publicly available at https://hf.co/collections/lab260/balalaika-dataset The full version paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13563
column7: Kirill Borodin(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics; BitmanagerAI); Nikita Vasiliev(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics); Vasiliy Kudryavtsev(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics; BitmanagerAI); Maxim Maslov(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics); Mikhail Gorodnichev(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics); Grach Mkrtchian(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics)

column4: Spashta Audio-Bench: Unified ASR and TTS Evaluation Framework across Indian Languages
column6: Evaluation of speech systems for Indian languages remains severely fragmented. Models are benchmarked on disjoint datasets with inconsistent preprocessing and metrics, making reproducibility and fair comparison nearly impossible. We address this with Spashta Audio-Bench, a modular, plug-and-play framework analogous to HuggingFace Evaluate, where any model checkpoint or dataset registers through a standardized interface without modifying the core pipeline. Evaluating ten open-source ASR and TTS models across seven corpora spanning 22 Indian languages and Indian-accented English, it reveals what single-dataset, single-metric benchmarking conceals: parameter scaling does not guarantee cross-language robustness, naturalness and intelligibility diverge in TTS, and domain sensitivity persists across all ASR architectures. Crucially, it introduces TTS-ASR degradation as an objective, reproducible intelligibility measure, jointly evaluating naturalness and intelligibility where prior benchmarks assess at most one. We release it as reusable infrastructure to promote standardized, multi-metric speech evaluation for Indian languages.
column7: Bikash Dutta(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Siddhant Gahankari(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Abhinav Kumar(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Siddarth Modugu(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Shalini Kapoor(EkStep Foundation); Mayank Vatsa(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Richa Singh(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur)

column4: Preference-ASR: A Preference-Aware Test Set for Benchmarking ASR in the Era of Speech LLMs
column6: Popular ASR test sets adopt inconsistent conventions for numbers, disfluencies, entities, and casing, while standard normalizers erase the format distinctions users care about. Current benchmarks therefore cannot measure whether a model follows user preferences for output style. We introduce Preference-ASR, a test set evaluating ASR systems on their ability to follow natural-language preference instructions across four categories: normalization, entities, disfluencies, and case. Built from seven open-source corpora via a two-stage LLM-assisted pipeline with human verification, it is evaluated with a preference-aware normalizer that selectively skips steps matching the active instruction. Benchmarking four models shows rankings shift across preference types, exposing quality differences traditional evaluation obscures. We publicly release the dataset.
column7: Nithin Rao Koluguri(NVIDIA); Sasha Meister(NVIDIA); Nikolay Karpov(NVIDIA); Piotr Żelasko(NVIDIA); Desh Raj(NVIDIA); Jagadeesh Balam(NVIDIA); Boris Ginsburg(NVIDIA)

column4: Open ASR Leaderboard: Towards Reproducible and Transparent Multilingual and Long-Form Speech Recognition Evaluation
column6: We present the Open ASR Leaderboard, a reproducible benchmarking platform with community contributions from academia and industry. It compares 85+ open-source and proprietary systems across 11 datasets, with English short- and long-form and multilingual short-form tracks. We standardize word error rate (WER) and inverse real-time factor (RTFx) evaluation for consistent accuracy-efficiency comparisons across model architectures and toolkits (e.g., ESPNet, NeMo, SpeechBrain, Transformers). We observe that Conformer-based encoders paired with large language model (LLM)-based decoders achieve the best average WER, while connectionist temporal classification (CTC) and token-and-duration transducer (TDT) decoders offer superior RTFx, making them better suited for long-form and batched processing. All code and dataset loaders are open-sourced to support transparent, extensible evaluation. We present our evaluation methodology to facilitate community-driven benchmarking in ASR and other tasks.
column7: Vaibhav Srivastav(Hugging Face Inc.; OpenAI); Steven Zheng(Hugging Face Inc.); Eric Bezzam(Hugging Face Inc.); Eustache Le Bihan(Hugging Face Inc.); Nithin Rao Koluguri(NVIDIA); Piotr Żelasko(NVIDIA); Somshubra Majumdar(NVIDIA); Adel Moumen(University of Cambridge); Sanchit Gandhi(Mistral AI)

column4: HALAS: A Human-Annotated Dataset of Hallucinations of Modern ASR Systems
column6: End-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems hallucinate on natural speech, yet existing mitigation methods are typically evaluated on non-speech or artificially corrupted audio. We introduce HALAS, the first human-annotated dataset of naturally occurring hallucinations from seven state-of-the-art ASR models on real unprocessed earnings call recordings. HALAS provides span-level labels, enabling analysis of hallucination patterns and their severity. Our analysis reveals strong cross-model vocabulary overlap and confirms that hallucinations also occur for almost correctly transcribed speech (characterized by a low Word Error Rate). The proposed benchmark with HALAS shows that the character and semantic-level metrics used as a proxy for hallucination detection reach 81% ROC-AUC, while state-of-the-art detection methods achieve an F1 score of only 53.1%. As such, HALAS establishes the first rigorous non-artificial benchmark for the detection and mitigation of ASR hallucinations.
column7: Mateusz Barański(AGH University of Krakow); Jan Jasiński(AGH University of Krakow); Julitta Bartolewska(AGH University of Krakow); Marcin Witkowski(AGH University of Krakow); Konrad Kowalczyk(AGH University of Krakow)

column4: CSER: Semantic Evaluation of LLM Auto-Repair for Code-Switching ASR
column6: Code-switching presents significant challenges for ASR systems in voice assistants. While traditional lexical metrics like WER, CER, and PIER measure transcription accuracy, they fail to capture semantic preservation or downstream intent quality in ASR-LLM pipelines. We introduce Code-Switching Semantic Error Rate (CSER), a metric designed to quantify the semantic impact of specific errors—such as language misidentification and minority-language substitution—while evaluating the efficacy of LLM-based auto-repair in recovering intent. Alongside CSER, we present an end-to-end evaluation framework and a multi-condition Vietnamese-English code-switching benchmark. Our experiments across commercial and in-house systems demonstrate that lexical and semantic metrics provide complementary insights, proving that both perspectives are essential for ensuring robust intent preservation at the pipeline level.
column7: Tien Dat Bui(Viettel Group); Duy Le-Tuan Nguyen(Viettel Group); Nhat Minh Le(Viettel Group); Van Hai Do(Thuyloi University)

column4: Supervised Post-training of Speech Foundation Models for Robust Adaptation in Speech Deepfake Detection
column6: Large speech foundation models have shown strong potential for speech deepfake detection, but direct fine-tuning is limited by a mismatch between self-supervised pre-training objectives and spoof-specific artifacts. To address this, we propose a mix-frame post-training strategy to create localized spoof-oriented perturbations and use frame-level supervision to encourage the SSL model to learn local inconsistencies that are critical for robust spoof detection. On ASVspoof5, we achieve state-of-the-art EER 4.50% for a single model without data augmentation. On ASVspoof2021 LA/DF, it further achieves only 0.16% absolute EER gap between LA and DF, indicating strong and balanced robustness across distinct distortion conditions. These results show that supervised post-training provides an effective and practical way to adapt speech foundation models for robust deepfake detection.
column7: Zihan Pan(A*STAR); Sailor Hardik(A*STAR); Jinyang Wu(A*STAR)

column4: Learning task-specific subspaces via interventional post-training of speech foundation models
column6: Speech foundation models, pre-trained on large corpora of unlabelled speech data, produce general-purpose representations which are useful across tasks. However, these representations encode information about salient speech variables in a distributed manner, while downstream speech tasks rely on only some of this variability. In this work, we propose a post-training refinement approach using interventional contrastive learning. By leveraging an interventional dataset and multi-part contrastive loss, we learn a transformation from the entangled representation space of speech foundation models into separate content and speaker subspaces. We evaluate the learnt representations on speaker verification and keyword spotting tasks, showing improved out-of-domain speaker verification performance and evidence that speaker and content information are separated across the learned subspaces.
column7: Jack Cox(University of Sheffield); Jon P Barker(University of Sheffield)

column4: Learning Multiple Utterance-Level Attribute Representations with a Unified Speech Encoder
column6: Speech foundation models trained with self-supervised learning produce generic speech representations that support a wide range of speech processing tasks. When further adapted with supervised learning, these models can achieve strong performance on specific downstream tasks. Recent post-training approaches, such as SAMU-XLSR and SONAR, align speech representations with utterance-level semantic representations, enabling effective multimodal (speech-text) and multilingual applications. While speech foundation models typically learn contextual embeddings at the acoustic frame level, these methods learn representations at the utterance level. In this work, we extend this paradigm to arbitrary utterance-level attributes and propose a unified post-training framework that enables a single speech foundation model to generate multiple types of utterance-level representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by jointly learning semantic and speaker representations and evaluating them on multilingual speech retrieval and speaker recognition tasks.
column7: Maryem Bouziane(LIA - Avignon Université); Salima Mdhaffar(LIA - Avignon Université); Yannick Estève(LIA - Avignon Université)

column4: PolyBench: A Benchmark for Compositional Reasoning in Polyphonic Audio
column6: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are increasingly capable of reasoning over audio. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of reasoning in polyphonic audio, where multiple sound events co-occur and induce compositional structure. In this work, we introduce PolyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate compositional reasoning in polyphonic audio. PolyBench comprises five evaluation subsets covering counting, classification, detection, concurrency, and duration estimation, requiring reasoning over multiple concurrent events and their relations. Evaluation of state-of-the-art LALMs reveals consistent performance degradation in polyphonic audio, indicating a fundamental bottleneck in current LALMs.
column7: Yuanjian Chen(Harbin University of Science and Technology); Yang Xiao(The University of Melbourne); Han Yin(KAIST); Xubo Liu(University of Surrey); Jinjie Huang(Harbin University of Science and Technology); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)

column4: Step-Audio-R1: Why Audio LLMs Fail at Reasoning — The Trap of Textual Surrogates
column6: Audio language models often perform worse when prompted to reason, unlike text and vision models. We attribute this failure to textual surrogate reasoning: models deliberate over transcript-like abstractions instead of acoustic evidence. We introduce Step-Audio-R1 and Modality-Grounded Reasoning Distillation (MGRD), an iterative framework that uses self-distillation and multimodal reinforcement learning to shift reasoning toward acoustic properties. Across speech, environmental-sound, and music benchmarks, Step-Audio-R1 outperforms Gemini 2.5 Pro and performs comparably to Gemini 3 Pro. Ablations show that acoustically grounded reasoning reverses the usual degradation with longer deliberation. These results demonstrate that test-time reasoning can improve audio intelligence when reasoning chains are anchored to the input modality, providing a path toward multimodal systems that reason across sensory domains.
column7: Yuxin Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.; StepFun); Daijiao Liu(UNSW; StepFun); Haoyang Zhang(NTU; StepFun); Xiangyu Zhang(UNSW; StepFun); Yuxin Li(NTU; StepFun); Fei Tian(StepFun); Yayue Deng(StepFun); Donghang Wu(NTU; StepFun); Jun Chen(StepFun); Liang Zhao(StepFun); Chengyuan Yao(StepFun); Gaolei Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Quanhai Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ.); Qiquan Zhang(UNSW); Hexin Liu(NTU); Eng Siong Chng(NTU); Xuerui Yang(StepFun); Xiangyu Zhang(StepFun); Daxin Jiang(StepFun); Gang Yu(StepFun)

column4: Improving Text-to-Audio Instruction Following via Fine-Grained Feedback from Audio-Aware Large Language Models
column6: Recent text-to-audio models generate high-quality audio, but often fail to follow instructions involving multiple sound events and temporal order. This gap arises because existing evaluation and training signals mainly emphasize global similarity or perceptual quality, with limited supervision on instruction-level correctness. We propose an instruction-level framework that uses audio-aware large language models (ALLMs) as fine-grained judges to verify target event presence and temporal relations in generated audio. After validating ALLM judgments on benchmarks and through human verification, we use their feedback to construct preference pairs for direct preference optimization. We further introduce S3Bench, a narrative benchmark for evaluating multi-event temporal instruction following. Experiments show that our method improves event completeness, temporal ordering, and joint instruction-following accuracy across existing benchmarks and S3Bench, while maintaining audio quality.
column7: Chun-Yi Kuan(National Taiwan University; Amazon); Siwon Kim(Amazon); Byeonggeun Kim(Amazon); Suyoun Kim(Amazon); Bo-Ru Lu(Amazon); Qingming Tang(Amazon); Ankur Gandhe(Amazon); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Chieh-Chi Kao(Amazon); Chao Wang(Amazon)

column4: CAAD: Contrastive Audio-Aware Distillation for Efficient Speech Language Models
column6: Speech Language Models achieve reasoning capabilities, but are often hindered by massive parameter counts and a tendency to prioritize linguistic priors over acoustic features. While contrastive decoding enhances grounding by contrasting audio-aware and text-only logits, it increases inference latency. We propose Contrastive Audio-Aware Distillation (CAAD), a framework that internalizes the teacher's contrastive reasoning into the student model's weights. To overcome the high computational training overhead in the dual-path token-by-token contrastive distillation process, we introduce a synchronized teacher-forcing strategy. Anchored by unified Pseudo-Ground Truths, this mechanism enables simultaneous full-sequence generation of the teacher's contrastive distributions, allowing student to distill the audio-aware signal efficiently. Overall, CAAD yields a ~8% relative gain over standard knowledge distillation on Dynamic-SUPERB and successfully reduces linguistic bias in MCR-BENCH.
column7: Chun Wei Chen(National Taiwan University); Tzu-Quan Lin(National Taiwan University); Ke-Han Lu(National Taiwan University); Wei-Ping Huang(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)

column4: Distilling LLM Semantic Priors into Encoder-Only Multi-Talker ASR with Talker-Count Routing
column6: Large language models (LLMs) provide strong semantic priors that can improve multi-talker automatic speech recognition (MT-ASR), but using an LLM as an autoregressive decoder is computationally expensive and remains fragile under heavy overlap. In this paper, we propose an encoder-only MT-ASR framework that adapts an LLM to multi-talker conditioning and distills its semantic guidance into the encoder during training, while retaining fast CTC-style decoding at inference. Our model employs a post-encoder separator with serialized CTC to produce talker-ordered transcripts, and leverages an adapted LLM-based SOT objective as a multi-talker-aware teacher signal to explicitly regularize mixed-speech representations. To further support variable numbers of talkers, we introduce a Talker-Count Head that predicts the talker count and dynamically selects the appropriate decoding branch. Experiments on LibriMix show that the proposed encoder-only model achieves comparable performance to LLM-based systems in the two-talker condition, while delivering significant improvements in the three-talker condition with significant small RTF.
column7: Hao Shi(SB Intuitions); Yusuke Fujita(SB Intuitions); Roman Koshkin(SB Intuitions); Mengjie Zhao(SB Intuitions); Yuan Gao(SB Intuitions); Lianbo Liu(SB Intuitions); Yui Sudo(SB Intuitions)

column4: TASU2: Controllable CTC Simulation for Alignment and Low-Resource Adaptation of Speech LLMs
column6: Speech LLM post-training increasingly relies on efficient cross-modal alignment and robust low-resource adaptation, yet collecting large-scale audio-text pairs remains costly. Text-only alignment methods such as TASU reduce this burden by simulating CTC posteriors from transcripts, but they provide limited control over uncertainty and error rate, making curriculum design largely heuristic. We propose TASU2, a controllable CTC simulation framework that simulates CTC posterior distributions under a specified WER range, producing text-derived supervision that better matches the acoustic decoding interface. This enables principled post-training curricula that smoothly vary supervision difficulty without TTS. Across multiple source-to-target adaptation settings, TASU2 improves in-domain and out-of-domain recognition over TASU, and consistently outperforms strong baselines including text-only fine-tuning and TTS-based augmentation, while mitigating source-domain performance degradation.
column7: Jing Peng(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Chenghao Wang(AISpeech); Yi Yang(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Lirong Qian(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Junjie Li(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Yu Xi(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University, China); Kai Yu(Shanghai Jiaotong University)

column4: Adapting Text LLMs to Speech via Multimodal Depth Up-Scaling
column6: Adapting pre-trained text Large Language Models (LLMs) into Speech Language Models (Speech LMs) via continual pre-training on speech data is promising, but often degrades the original text capabilities. We propose Multimodal Depth Up-scaling, an extension of an emerging strategy in continual LLM pre-training, where new transformer layers are inserted into a frozen text LLM and only the added layers are trained on speech data. Experiments with SmolLM2-360M and SmolLM2-1.7B on 48k hours of English Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) data show that depth up-scaling achieves ASR comparable to full fine-tuning while causing far less text degradation than both full fine-tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We further show that incorporating E-Branchformer, an architecture designed for speech recognition, as the inserted layers achieves ASR that matches or surpasses full fine-tuning on the larger model while reducing text degradation by over 75% with 60% fewer trainable parameters.
column7: Kazuki Yano(Tohoku University); Jun Suzuki(Tohoku University); Shinji Watanabe(Tohoku University; Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Localizing and Editing Knowledge in Large Audio-Language Models
column6: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have shown strong performance in speech understanding, making speech a natural interface for accessing factual information. Yet they are trained on static corpora and may encode incorrect facts. Existing model editing methods localize and update facts in textonly LLMs, but do not account for continuous speech representations, or where knowledge is stored across audio encoder or LLM backbone in LALMs. We construct the first audio benchmark for knowledge localization and editing in LALMs and propose a speech-driven locate-then-edit framework. First, we use speech-aware causal tracing to localize layers that support factual retrieval and then apply editing at identified sites. Experiments show that factual knowledge is jointly encoded in layers from audio encoder and language backbone, and that audio editing yield more effective updates than text editing or fine-tuning, enabling fine-grained knowledge control in speech AI systems.
column7: Sung Kyun Chung(The University of Melbourne); Jiaheng Dong(The University of Melbourne); Qiuchi Hu(The University of Melbourne); Jinuo Sun(The University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Hong Jia(University of Auckland); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)

column4: Towards Fine-Grained Temporal Perception: Post-Training Large Audio-Language Models with Audio-Side Time Prompt
column6: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) enable general audio understanding and demonstrate remarkable performance across various audio tasks. However, these models still face challenges in temporal perception (e.g., inferring event onset and offset), leading to limited utility in fine-grained scenarios. To address this issue, we propose Audio-Side Time Prompt and leverage Reinforcement Learning (RL) to develop the TimePro-RL framework for fine-grained temporal perception. Specifically, we encode timestamps as embeddings and interleave them within the audio feature sequence as temporal coordinates to prompt the model. Furthermore, we introduce RL following Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to directly optimize temporal alignment performance. Experiments demonstrate that TimePro-RL achieves significant performance gains across a range of audio temporal tasks, such as audio grounding, sound event detection, and dense audio captioning, validating its robust effectiveness.
column7: Yanfeng Shi(University of Science and Technology of China); Pengfei Cai(University of Science and Technology of China); Jun Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Qing Gu(University of Science and Technology of China); Nan Jiang(University of Science and Technology of China); Lirong Dai(University of Science and Technology of China); Ian Mcloughlin(Singapore Institute of Technology); Yan Song(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: Fast Speech Foundation Model Distillation Using Interleaved Stacking
column6: Distilling a large speech foundation model (SFM) into an efficient student model has been successfully applied to low-resource environments. Although distillation reduces inference latency, it requires an additional student model training. However, the training efficiency of SFM distillation remains underexplored. In this work, we explore training acceleration of SFM distillation to speed up model deployment. We examine the potential of stacking, in which the model depth is progressively increased through training until the target model depth is reached. While existing stacking methods improve training speed, they suffer from performance degradation. To handle this limitation, we propose interleaved stacking, a novel stacking method that consistently preserves layer position throughout the stacking process. This property is particularly critical in SFMs, in which each layer encodes distinct layer-specific knowledge. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method on SUPERB.
column7: Eungbeom Kim(IPAI); Kyogu Lee(IPAI; AIIS; Seoul National University)

column4: A light weight Continuous Speaker Verification System for Real time Monitoring
column6: Continuous verification of customer identity during telephone interactions is essential to prevent unauthorized access to personal information in medical insurance applications and banking scenarios. We propose a real-time speaker verification system that continuously monitors customer's speech and compares it with an enrolled voice-print to detect speaker changes during an active call. Upon mismatch, the system generates alerts on the agent interface to prevent disclosure of sensitive information. The proposed method uses a two stage architecture with a ReDimNet-B1 backbone and a projection network trained with triplet sampling for robust speaker embedding extraction. Cross-lingual, noise, and reverberation-based data augmentation techniques are used to improve robustness. The system operates in real time with RTF 0.05 and a low computational footprint of 318M MACs. The model achieves an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 2.08% on TidyVoice evaluation dataset, demonstrating strong robustness.
column7: Nikhil Keetha(Meeami Technologies); Hima Jyothi R(Meeami Technologies); Nivedita Chennupati(Meeami Technologies); Balaji Padmanaban(Meeami Technologies); Harish Rajamani(Meeami Technologies); Naveen Ambati(Meeami Technologies)

column4: WaveNorm: A Low-Complexity Time-Domain Neural Adaptive Gain Control for Real-Time Speech Applications
column6: We present WaveNorm AGC, a lightweight, low-latency neural Adaptive Gain Control(AGC) system for real-time speech normalization on edge devices. Operating in the time domain, it learns a content-aware, level-invariant gain mapping directly from raw waveforms. Unlike conventional rule-based AGC, it avoids fixed control parameters and hand-crafted envelope tracking, providing stable and responsive gain adjustment. WaveNorm AGC provides robust performance across a wide dynamic range upto -70 dB maintaining loudness compliance with ITU-T P.56 and P.79 standards under noisy conditions, while achieving ~6 dB noise reduction. The model is speaker-independent and highly efficient (49 M MACs, 55 KB of memory), making it suitable for real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices.
column7: Deepika Ijjada(Meeami Technologies); Charan Kumar Reddy B(Meeami Technologies); Ashwini Hanaganti(Meeami Technologies); Priyanka Devrao Jadhav(Meeami Technologies); Varsha Uppalanchi(Meeami Technologies); Nivedita Chennupati(Meeami Technologies); Karunakar Reddy Pucchakayala(Meeami Technologies); Balaji Padmanaban(Meeami Technologies); Harish Rajamani(Meeami Technologies); Naveen Ambati(Meeami Technologies)

column4: Argmax Pro: Frontier-level Real-time Speech-to-text with Speakers and Custom Vocabulary on Mobile Devices
column6: We introduce Argmax Pro, a unified real-time inference system that orchestrates three state-of-the-art billion-scale transformer models for speech-to-text with speaker diarization and custom vocabulary. The system is optimized to run efficiently on a wide range of mobile devices across iOS and Android without resource contention with other apps and with minimal impact to battery life and thermals. The goal of this system is to offer a peer alternative to cloud-based systems for feature-rich speech recognition with frontier-level accuracy. To achieve this, we built Argmax Pro on top of concurrent research in context biasing and streaming speaker diarization.

column4: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Companion for Real-Time Entity Extraction and SLU-Driven ASR Error Correction
column6: Contact-center agents handle thousands of entity-rich voice interactions per day, where a misrecognised customer name, account identifier, or domain term cascades into wrong CRM entries and additional manual rework. We demonstrate MACE (Multi-Agent Companion Environment), a closed-loop architecture in which a real-time companion - an AI overlay that runs alongside the live agent and surfaces extracted named entities as proactive suggestions for in-place confirmation - routes every UI correction back into the ASR stack as either a contextual-biasing entry B or, once recurrent, a post-ASR substitution rule R, with no acoustic retraining and no a-priori entity list. On the English ContextASR-Bench benchmark with Whisper-large-v3, the loop reduces NE-WER by 17.1% and EditRate by 18.6% over a no-biasing baseline, closing 23.6% of the gap to an oracle that is given the entity list in advance.
column7: Shiva Shankar Arumugam(Observe.ai); Ameyaditya Achar J(Observe.ai); Aashraya Sachdeva(Observe.ai)

column4: Gender differences in the phonetic realization of the checked tone in Kaihui Xiang
column6: Checked tones in Chinese languages often undergo smoothing, yet their phonetic mechanisms and sociophonetic conditioning remain understudied. This study examines the checked tone (T6) in Kaihui Xiang and tests whether gender differences indicate ongoing de-checking. Using F0, duration, and voice quality, we compare checked and unchecked tones across genders. Results show complete coda loss, but T6 remains distinct through a stable F0 contour and shorter duration. Phonation cues are also reorganized, with laryngealization shifting toward the syllable onset. Male speakers retain a conservative pattern with stronger durational truncation, while female speakers show weaker temporal cues and innovative phonatory dynamics. These patterns suggest Kaihui Xiang is in a late de-checking stage: tonal contrast is phonologized but phonetic grounding continues to shift, with gender asymmetry reflecting a gradual, socially conditioned redistribution of acoustic cues.
column7: Yi Zhang(City University of Hong Kong); Aini Li(City University of Hong Kong)

column4: Age-dependent acoustic changes of the frication noise in dental sibilants produced by typically developing Polish children between 5 and 8 years of age
column6: The paper aims to investigate which acoustic properties of Polish dental fricatives /s, z/ are related to the age and sex of typically developing child speakers between 61 and 96 months of age. We analyzed speech samples collected from 88 children assessed as producing /s, z/ with a target (dental) place of articulation. The analysis comprises a set of typical spectral features and spectral features of the frication noise, which are treated as markers of sibilant articulation patterns. Linear mixed-effect models showed a significant age-related increase of fricative formant distance and spectral energy above 6 kHz for /s/ productions and a decrease in spectral energy below 2,5 kHz for /z/. The results present an age-dependent spectrum shift that may indicate improvement in articulatory precision. The results are a preliminary step in quantifying the acoustic patterns in the sibilant articulation development in typically developing children.
column7: Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology); Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Natalia Moćko(University of Silesia); Magdalena Krycha(University of Silesia); Michal Krecichwost(Silesian University of Technology)

column4: Age-related Differences in the Perception of Vowel Length Contrast in Northern Vietnamese: The Case of Hoang Van (Bac Ninh) Variety
column6: Vowel length contrasts in Northern Vietnamese are acoustically distinguished by both duration and spectral cues. This study investigated the perception of long and short vowels in this language and possible differences between older and younger listeners. The results show that, at the group level, listeners in both age groups relied primarily on vowel duration, with F1 and F2 serving as secondary cues. At the individual level, a small subset of older listeners relied mainly on F1. Furthermore, acoustically incongruent stimuli (e.g., long-vowel duration integrated with short-vowel quality) elicited significantly longer response times than congruent stimuli, without significant age-related differences. These findings indicate that both duration and spectral cues contribute to the perception of vowel length in Northern Vietnamese, and the reliance on F1 as the primary cue by some older listeners may indicate a possible ongoing sound change.
column7: Van Dat Ta(Peking University); Baoya Chen(Peking University)

column4: Age-related Differences in Acoustic Realization of Aspirated Fricatives in Shaxi Bai
column6: Aspirated fricatives are realized through multiple interacting acoustic parameters rather than a single defining parameter. This study investigates the realization of aspirated fricatives in Shaxi Bai, focusing on three acoustic parameters: initial duration ratio, spectral center of gravity, and H1*–H2*. Acoustic data from 30 speakers across three age groups were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results show that the relative magnitude of acoustic effects varies across fricative types and age groups. Temporal and spectral measures exhibit robust acoustic differences, whereas phonatory measure shows weaker and less consistent effects. Young speakers show a different covariation pattern among acoustic parameters, consistent with an ongoing reorganization of the aspiration contrast. These findings support a multidimensional account of aspirated fricatives and demonstrate intergenerational change in the relative contribution of temporal, spectral, and phonatory dimensions.
column7: Xiaofang Zhang(University of Macau); Infat Lo(University of Macau); Yao Lu(Peking University)

column4: Listeners' gendered experiences and beliefs affect iconic pitch associations
column6: Certain intonational meanings have long been claimed to be iconic. For example, high vs. low voice pitch is physically linked to small vs. large body size, leading to affective meanings like submissiveness vs. dominance. While such associations have a physical basis, we claim they are also socially constructed, affected by language- and individual-specific ideological links, e.g. between dominance and masculinity. We present an experiment pairing a priming task and an Implicit Association Task (IAT) to probe variation in the strength of the pitch~size association. Primes were either strengthening or inhibiting and highlighted the affective link between size and submissiveness/dominance. The priming affected the strength of the pitch~size association as expected; however, the size of the effect differed by the gender of the listener and voice. These findings contribute to our understanding of how iconic meanings develop in speech and the crucial role of social experience and beliefs.
column7: Sasha Calhoun(Victoria University of Wellington); Paul Warren(Victoria University of Wellington); Sara Gilbert(Victoria University of Wellington)

column4: Age-Related Changes in Mandarin Lexical Tone Production: Acoustic Properties and Tonal Distinctiveness
column6: Despite growing interest in age-related speech changes, how aging affects the production of lexical tones remains underexplored. This study compared the acoustic properties and the tonal distinctiveness between younger and older speakers. Seventy-eight native Mandarin speakers produced 236 syllables covering all four lexical tones. The results revealed that older speakers exhibited gender-divergent F0 centralization of different tones, contour flattening, greater F0 variability, and longer duration, with these age-related effects varying across tones and genders. Both Bhattacharyya distance and support vector machine classification accuracy showed decreased tonal distinctiveness of the tone system with age. Critically, classification confusion was concentrated on bidirectional T2↔T3 misclassifications. These production patterns paralleled previously reported perceptual difficulties in older adults, supporting the auditory-motor integration model.
column7: Zhongxuan Mao(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Yan Feng(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Chenyu Li(Johns Hopkins University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 4 - Oral 7 - Audio Watermarking and Source Verification

column4: Countering Neural Audio Codec Distortions in Watermarking with Adaptive Restoration
column6: Neural audio codecs offer high compression efficiency but introduce structured and non-linear distortions that severely degrade audio watermarks. To address this, we propose an adaptive codec-aware restoration framework that reconstructs codec-distorted spectrograms prior to extraction. Our method employs a ConvNeXt-based U-Net to recover fine-grained spectrogram patterns and introduces a lightweight classifier to dynamically select specialized restoration models for each codec. Experimental results across various neural codecs demonstrate that our model improves bitwise accuracy from near-random levels to over 98% for RVQ-based codecs. Furthermore, by analyzing the impact of quantizer configurations on watermark survivability, we show that our method can effectively improve watermark robustness in modern codec environments.
column7: Sungho Park(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University)

column4: DuraMark: Duration-Embedded Watermarking in LLM-based TTS
column6: Large language model (LLM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved remarkable voice cloning capabilities, raising concerns about potential deepfake misuse. Speech watermarking mitigates this by embedding traceable information into generated speech. Mainstream watermarking methods operate at the signal level (waveform or spectrogram), rendering the watermark vulnerable to generative attacks (e.g., neural codec and vocoder). To address this, we propose DuraMark, a robust information-level watermarking framework. It utilizes syllable duration editing to achieve watermark embedding. Specifically, DuraMark integrates a duration-controllable LLM-based TTS model to edit syllable durations during synthesis, coupled with a duration extractor to extract these durations for detection. Experiments demonstrate DuraMark’s superior robustness against generative attacks, significantly outperforming signal-level baselines. Audio samples are available at https://muzw.github.io/duramark_demo/.
column7: Zhenwei Mou(University of Science and Technology of China); Weili Jiang(Ministry of Public Security); Liping Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhen-Hua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kai Gao(Ministry of Public Security); Boyu Zhao(Ministry of Public Security)

column4: AudioNoisePrints: Model-free audio watermarking using spatial correlation in flow matching TTS
column6: We present AudioNoisePrints, a training-free watermarking pipeline for flow matching and diffusion TTS models, which requires minimal extra computation during inference and does not require retraining the TTS model or reducing the generation quality. We exploited the fact that there are strong correlations between the initial Gaussian noises and the generated outputs in diffusion and flow matching models, such that a simple cosine correlation between the initial noise and the generated output can be used to perform watermaking. Moreover, we train a lightweight detector on top for more aggressive augmentations. Our method outperforms AudioSeal, a strong baseline for audio watermarking under strong augmentations. We experimented on F5TTS and other TTS and vocoder models, and concluded that they all exhibit similar spatial correlation properties, suggesting our watermarking scheme can be used for more flow-matching TTS models and even vocoders in the future.
column7: Timothy Tin-Long Tse(National Research Council Canada; University of British Columbia); Jian Zhu(University of British Columbia); Aidan Pine(National Research Council Canada); Mengzhe Geng(National Research Council Canada)

column4: VoxWatermark: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Audio Watermark Detection under Perturbations
column6: With the rapid deployment of speech generation systems in open environments, providing verifiable source attribution and copyright accountability for audio content has become critical. A gap in current research is the lack of a unified benchmark that systematically compares different watermark injection methods under realistic distribution shifts. To address this, we build VoxWatermark by applying 10 watermarking methods (4 neural and 6 traditional) with unified injection and annotation on multilingual, multi-source corpora, and introducing no-box, black-box, and white-box perturbations to simulate real recording and transmission conditions. Based on this benchmark, we propose AudioWMD as a robust baseline detector for large-scale, multi-method, cross-distribution settings. Results show that injection-method diversity and distribution shifts affect detection stability, while validating the effectiveness and scalability of AudioWMD. Dataset and code are publicly available.
column7: Farnaz Sedaghati(University of Tehran); Yuxi Wang(Nanyang Technological University); Zicheng Weng(Nanyang Technological University); Wei Rao(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: Phoneme-Aware Mamba Watermark: An Active Defense System Against Purified Speech Deepfakes
column6: With the rapid advancement of Text-to-Speech (TTS) and Voice Conversion (VC), forged speech has reached a highly realistic level, posing serious threats to voice biometrics. Traditional passive detection methods suffer from limited generalization against unseen synthesis models. In this paper, we propose a phoneme-aware active watermarking defense built on the Mamba framework. Leveraging a Dual-column Bidirectional State Space Model, the system captures long-range dependencies and covertly embeds identity bitstrings into speech. To resist diffusion-based purification attacks such as PhonePuRe, we introduce a phoneme-guided embedding mechanism that tightly couples the watermark with speech semantics, ensuring transfer to forged speech during speaker adaptation. Experiments demonstrate effective source tracing with ultra-low latency (about 1 s) and high True Positive Rate under strong purification attacks. Source code is available at https://github.com/Silence-ai423/ phoneme-aware-mamba-watermark.
column7: Yanda Shao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Mengke Zhang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zhixin Lin(Beijing Institute of Technology); Tianyi Yang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: The Hidden Cost of Pairwise Verification in Synthetic Speech Source Tracing
column6: Open-set source tracing is increasingly framed as a verification problem, motivating the use of pairwise metric-learning objectives from biometrics. We thus compare global anchoring and pairwise verification under matched backbones and a fixed data and epoch budget on MLAAD (in-domain) and STOPA (out-of-domain). In our runs, global anchoring yields lower in-domain error (8.61% EER) than pairwise variants (12-15% EER), even with rival mining and XLS-R finetuning. Because pairwise objectives optimize similarity directly, they concentrate variance into fewer embedding directions, reducing resolution among closely related generators. To test if this drives the drop, we impose a similar bottleneck to the globally supervised baseline, yet the baseline remains competitive. Together with an embedding-space analysis (k99), these results suggest that the gap is not explained by dimensionality alone, but rather by the pairwise objective's shaping of the retained directions.
column7: Anton Firc(Brno University of Technology); Zbyněk Lička(Brno University of Technology); Vojtěch Staněk(Brno University of Technology); Kamil Malinka(Brno University of Technology)

column4: Teacher-Agnostic Temporal Knowledge Distillation for Resource-Efficient Sound Event Detection
column6: Sound event detection (SED) needs frame-level detection, yet recent work has focused on high-capacity models, leaving resource-efficient SED relatively underexplored. We propose teacher-agnostic temporal knowledge distillation (TAT-KD), a knowledge distillation (KD) framework for SED that distills from any teacher architecture by using teacher logits as a common distillation space. To transfer temporal context, we introduce a conformer-based temporal context projector that models temporal dependencies during projection and a teacher-confidence-aware distillation loss that downweights ambiguous outputs via normalized confidence weights. On the domestic environment sound event detection benchmark, TAT-KD outperformed training from scratch and logit-/feature-based KD, achieving polyphonic sound detection score of 0.574 with 4.548M parameters and 3.668G multiply-accumulate operations, showing competitive performance with far fewer parameters and computations than state-of-the-art models.
column7: Gihun Son(Hanyang University); Pil Moo Byun(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: A Sensitivity Analysis of Multi-Event Audio Grounding in Audio LLMs
column6: Audio LLMs have shown a strong ability to understand audio samples, yet their reliability in complex acoustic scenes remains under-explored. Unlike prior work limited to small scale or less controlled query construction, we present a large-scale evaluation of event grounding and false alarms as auditory scene complexity increases. Using 71K AudioCapsV2 clips, we extract normalized (source, attribute) events and build two query types: present-event queries for ground-truth detection and absent-event queries to probe hallucinations, using similarity-filtered negative sampling in an audio-aligned text embedding space. We evaluate four SOTA Audio LLMs with 12 prompt variants over 500K yes/no queries per model. Across models, increasing event count consistently lowers true-positive rate and raises false-positive rate, while prompts induce a strong trade-off between the two. Our confidence analysis shows that models become more uncertain on multi-event audio, revealing room for improvement.
column7: Taehan Lee(Sogang University); Jaehan Jung(Sogang University); Hyukjun Lee(Sogang University)

column4: RAISE: Resolving Ambiguity in Audio Understanding with Imagination and Selective Extraction
column6: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are prone to perceptual hallucination under acoustic interference or fine-grained ambiguity. Robust auditory understanding demands active verification: even state-of-the-art reasoning models hallucinate when forced to decode ambiguous internal representations. We introduce RAISE (Resolving Ambiguity with Imagination and Selective Extraction), a training-free framework that equips Audio LLMs with two cognitively motivated listening strategies. Selective Extraction isolates target signals from noise; Auditory Imagination synthesizes candidate references for comparative reasoning. Instead of relying on ambiguous internal representations, the model grounds every prediction in explicit acoustic evidence. On two challenging benchmarks, MMAR and MMAU, RAISE delivers consistent gains of up to 12.4% without any parameter updates.
column7: Yueqian Lin(Duke University); Qinsi Wang(Duke University); Yudong Liu(Duke University); Hancheng Ye(Duke University); Hai Li(Duke University); Yiran Chen(Duke University)

column4: The silence of the weights: a structural pruning strategy for Attention-based audio signal architectures with second-order metrics
column6: Transformer-based models have become the state of the art across multiple domains, from natural language processing to machine listening, enabled by the attention mechanisms. However, the attention layers require a large number of parameters and high-end hardware for both training and inference. We propose a novel channel-pruning technique explicitly targeted at the attention mechanism, decoupling the pruning of each head and the four matrices in the attention block: query, key, value, and output projection matrices, employing a second-order metric to score the network's parameters. We compare our technique against head-pruning strategies and magnitude-driven scoring metrics, investigating the effects of pruning on Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) and Whisper. Our results show that even after pruning 50% of the parameters in the attention block, performance is largely preserved. The code is available on GitHub.
column7: Andrea Diecidue(Politecnico di Milano); Carlo Alberto Barbano(University of Turin); Piero Fraternali(Politecnico di Milano); Mathieu Fontaine(Institut Polytechnique de Paris); Enzo Tartaglione(Institut Polytechnique de Paris)

column4: Trajectory Variance: An Unsupervised Measure of Developmental Vocal Plasticity in Birdsong
column6: How much does a vocalization change over the course of development? We propose trajectory variance, a per-vocalization plasticity score that answers this question without type labels. A displacement model learns to predict age-conditioned shifts in autoencoder latent space; the variance of its predictions across target ages quantifies how much each vocalization would change if produced at different developmental stages. Evaluated on three zebra finches (183K-274K vocalizations, 40-101 days post-hatch), trajectory variance separates learned song syllables from innate calls (Cohen's d = 0.29-0.57, AUC = 0.58-0.67, after controlling for duration), while no nonparametric baseline achieves consistent separation. Trajectory variance also correlates with spectral flatness across all three birds (r = -0.48 to -0.75): more plastic vocalizations tend to have more tonal, structured spectra.
column7: Kanghwi Lee(ETH Zurich; University of Zurich)

column4: Beyond Uncertainty and Diversity: Temporal-Spectral Guided Active Learning for Audio
column6: Active Learning (AL) holds significant potential to reduce annotation costs for audio signal processing tasks under supervised finetuning by strategically selecting informative unlabeled samples for labeling. However, existing AL methods typically rely on general selection criteria such as uncertainty or representativeness, which fail to account for the intricate temporal-spectral structures inherent in audio signals. These structures play a critical role in determining sample informativeness, making direct application of existing AL approaches suboptimal for audio tasks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel AL framework for audio, named Temporal-Spectral Active Learning (TSAL), explicitly bridging the gap between model optimization and audio characteristics. Since temporal-spectral patterns cannot be directly extracted or explicitly defined, TSAL constructs these informative patterns by modeling the soft-loss distribution. Furthermore, it incorporates feature-gradient similarity to guide the selection of unlabeled samples that exhibit these distinctive patterns. Extensive experiments on several audio benchmarks demonstrate that TSAL consistently out-performs state-of-the-art AL methods, significantly improving sampling efficiency and effectiveness under limited annotation budgets, while highlighting the importance of temporal-spectral guidance for advancing audio AL.
column7: Hui Geng(National University of Defense Technology); Tianjiao Wan(National University of Defense Technology); Yi Su(National University of Defense Technology); Qisheng Xu(National University of Defense Technology); Hengzhu Liu(National University of Defense Technology); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 6 - Oral 6 - Multi-Channel, Beamforming and Spatial Speech Enhancement

column4: Towards Array-Invariant Speech Enhancement via Geometry-Aware Dynamic Convolution
column6: Multi-channel speech enhancement (SE) systems exhibit superior performance over single-channel methods but are constrained to fixed microphone array configurations. This restricts their real-world deployment across devices with diverse array geometries. While recent array-agnostic SE methods address variable microphone numbers and permutations, they largely fail to exploit explicit array geometry priors when available, missing a crucial cue for optimal spatial filtering. A Geometry-Aware Dynamic Convolution (Geo-DConv) framework is proposed, which explicitly leverages microphone coordinates to transform standard fixed-array SE models into robust array-invariant systems. Experiments are conducted on the recent real-recorded RealMAN multi-channel speech dataset. Results demonstrate that the proposed architecture enables two widely used fixed-array models to adapt to array-invariant settings, with consistent performance improvements across diverse array topologies.
column7: Zhenglong Liu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Wangyou Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; VUI Labs); Chenda Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; VUI Labs); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; VUI Labs)

column4: An All-neural Distributed Filtering Algorithm for Speech Extraction in Wireless Acoustic Sensor Networks
column6: Wireless acoustic sensor networks (WASNs) enable spatial diversity for speech enhancement, but centralized processing is often hindered by communication and computational constraints. While distributed adaptive node-specific signal estimation (DANSE) addresses this via distributed compressed-signal exchange, its iterative covariance-based optimization remains vulnerabe to low-SNR and non-stationary conditions. This paper proposes ANDFilter, an all-neural distributed filtering framework that replaces iterative optimization with end-to-end filter synthesis. The ANDFilter decomposes enhancement into three stages: a single-node filter module (SNFM) for local processing, a node selection module (NSM) for adaptive inter-node weighting, and a multi-node filter module (MNFM) for distributed spatial filtering. Experimental results on simulated WASNs with LibriSpeech and Freesound datasets show that ANDFilter consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of PESQ, ESTOI, and DNSMOS across all SNR ranges.
column7: Jiawei Wang(Institute of Acoustics; UCAS); Xiaoqing Hu(Institute of Acoustics; UCAS); Feiran Yang(Institute of Acoustics; UCAS); Jianfei Tong(Institute of Acoustics; UCAS); Guohua Sun(Institute of Acoustics)

column4: Spatial-Magnifier: Spatial upsampling for multichannel speech enhancement
column6: While the spatial directivity of multichannel speech enhancement algorithms improves with the number of microphones, fitting large capture arrays into real-world edge devices is typically limited by physical constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose Spatial-Magnifier, a neural network designed to generate virtual microphone (VM) signals from a limited set of real microphone (RM) measurements. Moreover, we introduce the Spatial Audio Representation Learning (SARL) framework, which leverages estimated VM signals and features to condition a downstream speech enhancement system. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing spatial upsampling baselines across various speech extraction systems, including end-to-end multichannel speech enhancement and neural beamforming. The proposed method nearly recovers the oracle performance achieved when all microphones are available.
column7: Dongheon Lee(Meta Reality Labs Research; KAIST); Ashutosh Pandey(Meta Reality Labs Research); Sanjeel Parekh(Meta Reality Labs Research); Daniel Wong(Meta Reality Labs Research); Jacob Donley(Meta Reality Labs Research); Buye Xu(Meta Reality Labs Research); Juan Azcarreta(Meta Reality Labs Research)

column4: A Dynamic Knowledge Distillation Framework for Mitigating Spatial Ambiguity in Lightweight Dual-Channel Speech Enhancement
column6: Multi-channel speech enhancement based on deep learning has achieved significant progress. While keeping low complexity, lightweight dual-channel models exploit spatial cues to outperform single-channel models on edge devices. However, their performance often degrades for closely-spaced sources due to unconstrained spatial reliance. To mitigate this, we propose a Dynamic Spatial-aware Knowledge Distillation (D-SKD) framework that enhances spatial discrimination. Specifically, D-SKD introduces a dynamic arbitration mechanism into the distillation process with a spatially invariant single-channel teacher, enabling the dual-channel model to adaptively regulate spatial reliance without explicit angular supervision. Experiments on dual-channel GTCRN and other models show that D-SKD consistently improves performance for closely-spaced sources while preserving quality elsewhere. Requiring no additional inference overhead or auxiliary inputs, it is well suited for lightweight deployment.
column7: Yifei Yang(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics); Zheng Wang(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics); Yu Sun(Samsung Electronics (China)); Wentao Hua(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics); Xiaobin Rong(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics); Kai Chen(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics); Jing Lu(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics)

column4: Joint Learning of Covariance Estimation and White Noise Gain for Robust MVDR Beamforming
column6: The minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beam former is widely used for multichannel speech enhancement due to strong noise suppression while preserving target signals. In practice, its performance is sensitive to microphone self-noise and array mismatches. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed, manually tuned WNG thresholds or diagonal loading, leading to suboptimal performance under unknown or time-varying acoustic conditions. This paper proposes a data-driven MVDR framework that adaptively estimates the WNG constraint using a deep neural network. The network jointly predicts a time-frequency noise mask for covariance estimation and a frequency-dependent WNG threshold, enabling dynamic robustness-directivity control. A differentiable robust MVDR layer is integrated into the framework, allowing end-to-end optimization. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in speech quality and intelligibility over conventional fixed-WNG MVDR methods.
column7: yongyi deng(Wuhan University); Hanchen Pei(Wuhan University); Jianbo Ma(Dolby Laboratories); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Jingdong Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jacob Benesty(University of Quebec)

column4: Neural Directional Coding: Joint Spatial Coding and Filtering with Configurable Directivity Patterns
column6: Recent neural directional filtering methods enable the synthesis of virtual microphone signals with configurable high-order directivity patterns using only a few omnidirectional microphones. In communication scenarios, spatial signal processing at the receiver is often desired, yet transmitting all microphone array data requires high bit rates. We propose neural directional coding (NDC), a neural network-based approach for joint spatial coding and filtering that compresses only spatial information. At the receiver, a virtual directional microphone signal with a configured directivity pattern can be reconstructed from the compressed spatial information and a single-channel reference signal. Experiments with a 4-channel, 16 kHz microphone array show that spatial information can be compressed to 0.25 kbps using a 1.4 M parameter model, matching or surpassing a 7.5 kbps baseline with 90.8 M parameters.
column7: Weilong Huang(AudioLabs Erlangen); Emanuël A. P. Habets(AudioLabs Erlangen)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 7 - Oral 4 - Flow Matching for Speech Synthesis

column4: Hierarchical Conditional Continuous Normalizing Flows for Creaky Voice Editing under Speaker Identity Preservation
column6: We propose a hierarchical conditional continuous normalizing flow that structurally disentangles high-level speaker attributes from low-level paralinguistic voice qualities. By introducing a controlled, stage-wise injection of conditioning information, the model constrains how different feature types influence the latent representation. This design reduces unintended interactions between attributes and limits the propagation of low-level manipulations to high-level characteristics. Using the example of manipulating the voice quality creak, we show that the hierarchical approach has significantly less impact on the high-level speaker attributes pitch and gender, leading to improved preservation of perceived speaker identity.
column7: Frederik Rautenberg(Paderborn University); Fritz Seebauer(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University); Reinhold Haeb-Umbach(Paderborn University)

column4: TC-DBI: A Plug-and-Play Trajectory Confidence-Guided Dynamic Block Inference Strategy for Speech Synthesis with Continuous Block Flow Matching
column6: Block Flow Matching combines block-level autoregression with intra-block parallelism for efficient and high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS). However, using a fixed block size during inference ignores the non-uniform modeling difficulty of speech, which can cause unstable velocity estimation in challenging regions. This motivates the need for a reliability metric that can guide dynamic adjustment of block size. We propose Trajectory Confidence (TC), a geometric measure derived from trajectory straightness during ODE integration, and introduce TC-Guided Dynamic Block Inference (TC-DBI), a plug-and-play strategy that truncates and regenerates unreliable regions to adapt block size without architectural changes. Experiments show that TC correlates strongly with generation errors, and TC-DBI improves robustness and perceptual quality while maintaining comparable efficiency. Audio samples are available at https://thuhcsi.github.io/ interspeech2026-TC-DBI/.
column7: Ren Wang(Tsinghua University); Zhiyu Cui(Ant Group); Shun Lei(Tsinghua University); Jiawei Jin(Tsinghua University); Dongfu Song(Tsinghua University); Zhiyong Wu(Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University)

column4: Bridging the Gap: A Hierarchical Framework for Cross-Modal Style Modeling in Expressive TTS
column6: Natural language prompts offer a highly flexible interface for expressive text-to-speech (TTS), yet cross-modal gaps and one-to-many mapping problem hinder reliable style control. To address this, we propose OTAFlow, a novel hierarchical cross-modal style modeling framework. First, optimal transport alignment, contrastive learning, and multi-task supervision are jointly optimized to construct a unified style space that preserves instance-level correspondence and expressive factor separability. Second, a conditional flow matching module is introduced to capture the residual modality gap, explicitly addressing the one-to-many challenge by generating diverse acoustic style embeddings from a single prompt. When plugged into a downstream TTS backbone, evaluations show that our method substantially outperforms baseline models in fine-grained style retrieval and synthesized style accuracy, effectively delivering diverse and controllable expressive speech. Audio samples can be found in our demo page.
column7: Jiale Chen(Zhejiang University); Jiaxun Li(Zhejiang University); Wei Li(Zhejiang University); Yuanpeng Wang(Zhejiang University); Yuehai Wang(Zhejiang University)

column4: RobustSpeechFlow: Learning Robust Text-to-Speech Trajectories via Augmentation-based Contrastive Flow Matching
column6: While flow-matching text-to-speech (TTS) achieves strong zero-shot speaker similarity and naturalness, it remains susceptible to content fidelity issues, particularly skip and repeat errors from imperfect alignment. We propose RobustSpeechFlow, a training strategy that improves alignment robustness by extending contrastive flow matching with length-preserving repeat and skip latent augmentations. Requiring no external aligners or preference data, our method directly penalizes realistic failure modes and readily integrates into existing pipelines. On Seed-TTS-eval, it reduces the word error rate (WER) from 1.44 to 1.38 using only 0.06B parameters. On our ZERO500 benchmark, it delivers consistent intelligibility improvements across diverse speaker and prosody conditions; at NFE=24, it reduces English character error rate (CER) from 0.48% to 0.35% and Korean CER from 0.81% to 0.57%. Audio samples: https://robustspeechflow.github.io/.

column4: Improving Flow Matching based Text-to-Speech with Dual-Model Preference Optimization and Classifier-Free Guidance
column6: Flow matching is a powerful generative model and has become a core component of modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems. In order to ensure high-quality speech synthesis, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is widely used during the training and inference stages of flow matching based TTS models. However, in zero-shot TTS, conventional training and inference paradigms typically cannot effectively integrate human feedback, resulting in a mismatch between training objectives and evaluation metrics. In this work, we propose a preference optimization method by separately modeling preferred and dispreferred information with two distinct models, which enables better utilization of preferred and dispreferred data. We further incorporate an improved CFG technique to enhance synthesis adherence to the text and reference audio. Experiments demonstrate that these optimizations significantly enhance intelligibility, speaker similarity and naturalness of synthesized speech, outperforming the baseline model.
column7: Minchuan Chen(Ping An Technology); Chenchen Wan(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Junjie Li(Ping An Technology); Peng Qi(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shaojun Wang(Ping An Technology); Jing Xiao(Ping An Technology)

column4: Enhancing Flow Matching with A Unified Guidance Framework for Efficient and Robust Speech Synthesis
column6: Flow Matching (FM) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for speech generation but remains constrained by high inference latency and timbre leakage. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a unified guidance framework that enhances generation efficiency and robustness through two complementary strategies. On the data front, we introduce Data-guidance via heterogeneous augmentation, encouraging the model to disentangle linguistic content from acoustic residue. In parallel, we propose an enhanced Model-guidance mechanism that synergizes trajectory rectification with a novel intrinsic guidance objective. This approach distills conditional knowledge into network weights and straightens inference trajectory path, thereby eliminating Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) overhead. Experiments demonstrate that our framework accelerates inference by nearly three times while effectively improving speaker similarity compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Audio samples are available here.

column4: AppTek Call-Center Dialogues: A Multi-Accent Long-Form Benchmark for English ASR
column6: Evaluating English ASR systems for conversational AI applications remains difficult, as many publicly available corpora are either pre-segmented into short segments, consist of read or prepared speech, or lack explicit dialect annotations to evaluate robustness for a diverse user base. This work presents the AppTek Call-Center Dialogues corpus, a collection of spontaneous, role-played agent-customer conversations spanning fourteen English accents covering sixteen service-oriented scenarios. The dataset was commissioned specifically for evaluation and none of the audio or text was publicly available prior to release, reducing the risk of overlap with existing large-scale pretraining corpora. We benchmark a set of open-source ASR systems under different segmentation approaches. Results show substantial variation across accents and segmentation methods, indicating that good performance on general American English benchmarks does not necessarily generalize to other accents.

column4: Segmental Attention Decoding With Long Form Acoustic Encodings
column6: We address the fundamental incompatibility of attention-based encoder-decoder (AED) models with long-form acoustic encodings. AED trained on segmented utterances learn to encode absolute positions by exploiting limited acoustic context beyond segment boundaries, but fail to generalize when decoding long-form segments where these cues vanish. The model loses ability to order acoustic encodings due to permutation invariance of keys and values in cross-attention. We propose four modifications: 1) injecting explicit absolute positional encodings into cross-attention, 2) long-form training with extended acoustic context to eliminate implicit absolute position encoding, 3) segment concatenation to cover diverse segmentations needed during training, 4) semantic segmentation to align AED-decoded segments with training segments. We show that these modifications close the accuracy gap between continuous and segmented acoustic encodings, enabling auto-regressive use of the attention decoder.
column7: Pawel Swietojanski(Apple); Xinwei Li(Apple); Mingbin Xu(Apple); Takaaki Hori(Apple); Dogan Can(Apple); Xiaodan Zhuang(Apple)

column4: M-LAMA: Multimodal Automated Scoring of Long-form Spoken English
column6: Automatic speech assessment (ASA) for real-world exams requires evaluating multi-minute spontaneous responses across acoustic delivery, linguistic quality, and task fulfillment. However, most prior work focuses on short utterances, leaving long-form comprehensive assessment underexplored. We investigate whether reliable scoring of extended speech requires structured multimodal modeling. We propose M-LAMA, a cross-modal framework integrating raw audio, ASR transcripts, and question context through dual encoders and a discourse-aware fusion decoder. A part-based audio structure and question-aware text encoding capture both how and what is spoken, while a three-stage training strategy addresses the bell-curve score distribution of high-stakes exams. Experiments on 87,226 full-length sessions show that structured multimodal alignment substantially improves scoring reliability across five criteria, suggesting that effective long-form ASA requires principled integration of acoustic, linguistic, and contextual evidence.
column7: Minh Dao-Xuan-Quang(HUST); Son Dinh-Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam); Thi-Mai-Anh Bui(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam); Phi-Le Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam)

column4: Attentive Mamba: Channel-wise Local Attention for Speech Recognition
column6: State space models (SSMs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to transformers for speech recognition, but the performance is constrained due to static local aggregation. This paper presents an attentive SSM that integrates a causal convolutional attention where the static convolution is upgraded with a channel-wise local attention. The proposed module first contextualizes queries, keys, and values via causal depth-wise convolutions before applying cross-channel attention over a temporally local window. This architecture is motivated by the inherent structure of speech spectrograms, where distinct frequency channels contain temporally coherent patterns that can benefit the channel-specific modeling prior to their integration. This design facilitates dynamic parameterization of the state transition matrices, leading to the expressive acoustic features. Experimental results confirm the merit of integrating dynamic channel-wise attention into SSM for speech recognition.
column7: Jen-Tzung Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Fan-Che Feng(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Ching-Hsien Lee(Industrial Technology Research Institute)

column4: Attention-Guided Reliability Scaling for Contrastive Decoding in Robust Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
column6: Large language model (LLM)-based audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) systems are robust under noise. Contrastive decoding (CD), originally introduced to stabilize LLM generation by contrasting a weaker model against a stronger one at inference time, adjusts predictions without additional training. In this work, we apply CD to AVSR by contrasting audio-only conditioning with full audio-visual conditioning within the same underlying model. However, using a fixed contrastive strength introduces a trade-off across noise levels: stronger intervention helps under severe noise but may over-correct reliable predictions in clean conditions. We propose reliability-aware scaling of CD for AVSR. Instead of using a fixed strength, we adaptively modulate the contrastive influence at each token based on reliability signals derived from attention dynamics and inter-model predictive divergence. Experiments on LRS3 show consistent improvements across clean and low-SNR conditions.
column7: YoungChae Kim(Hanyang University); Da-Hee Yang(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Listening with Attention: Entropy-Guided Explainability for Transformer-Based Audio Models
column6: Transformer-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) models such as Whisper are highly accurate, but their predictions remain difficult to interpret. Existing explainable AI (XAI) methods often lack faithfulness and precise temporal grounding. We propose Listening with Entropy-guided Attention for Faithful eXplainability (LEAF-X), a model-intrinsic XAI framework for transformer-based ASR. LEAF-X combines entropy-guided attention weighting, multi-layer attention rollout, and optional causal ablations to identify low-entropy, high-impact heads and layers, producing sparse token-to-frame attributions. Unlike perturbation-based explainers or raw attention maps, LEAF-X exploits the internal structure of encoder-decoder and speech-augmented decoder-only models to generate explanations that better reflect model computation. Results show that LEAF-X produces more faithful and stable attributions than strong baselines, supporting more transparent and auditable ASR.
column7: Ravi Kumar(Florida International University); Utkarsh Grover(University of South Florida); Xiaomin Lin(University of South Florida); Agoritsa Polyzou(Florida International University)
