column4: Hallucination Benchmark for Speech Foundation Models
column6: This work advances the detection of hallucinations in automatic speech recognition (ASR) by introducing SHALLOW, the first benchmark that categorizes ASR hallucinations along four dimensions of analysis: lexical, phonetic, morphological, and semantic. Standard ASR metrics, such as Word Error Rate (WER), fail to capture the distinctions necessary to separate hallucinations from phonetic inaccuracies, leaving a critical gap in model evaluation. SHALLOW addresses this limitation by providing targeted metrics within each dimension, yielding interpretable profiles of model behavior. Evaluations across diverse architectures and domains show that SHALLOW strongly correlates with WER under high recognition quality; however, this correlation degrades as WER increases, exposing fine-grained error patterns that aggregate metrics overlook. By disentangling hallucination phenomena from general recognition errors, SHALLOW enables targeted diagnosis of model weaknesses.
column7: Alkis Koudounas(Politecnico di Torino); Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Manuel Giollo(Amazon AGI); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo); Elena Baralis(Politecnico di Torino)

column4: INSPIRE: A Benchmark for Instruction-Aware Speech Retrieval
column6: Existing speech retrieval systems rely on fixed similarity matching and cannot adapt to diverse user intents. We introduce INSPIRE, the first benchmark for instruction-aware speech retrieval, in which natural-language instructions dynamically specify relevance criteria, including semantic content, speaker identity, speaking style, environmental sounds, and their combinations. We evaluate four retrieval paradigms: large audio-language models, cascaded pipelines, self-supervised speech models, and contrastive audio-language models. Our results reveal that no current method robustly handles all retrieval intents. Text-based approaches perform relatively better at semantic retrieval but struggle with paralinguistic attributes, while speech-based models are moderately better at capturing acoustic properties but falter at following instructions. These findings highlight the need for unified architectures capable of instruction-aware speech retrieval.
column7: Chen-An Li(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU AI-CoRE)

column4: StanceBench: A Benchmark for Audio LLM-Based Interpersonal Stance Evaluation from Speech
column6: Speech-to-speech dialogue models increasingly depend on prosody and interactional nuance to convey social intent, yet benchmarks for these cues remain limited. We introduce StanceBench, a benchmark for measuring interpersonal stance in conversational speech and evaluating audio-capable LLMs as automated judges. Using the Seamless Interaction corpus, StanceBench (1) specifies 9 stance dimensions via role-prompt poles, (2) standardizes single-speaker and interaction-based evaluations, and (3) reports LLM-as-a-judge robustness, bias, and stance inference. Across evaluated stances, empathy and politeness are the easiest. Warmth and assertiveness are moderately separable with positivity skew/asymmetry. Honesty is the hardest and shows high prompt order bias, consistent with needing cross-turn evidence. Attentiveness is separable but aligns weakly with humans. Interaction stances are more context-sensitive, with threshold gaps and high variance, especially conflict regulation.
column7: Yuzhe Wang(Johns Hopkins University); Thomas Thebaud(Johns Hopkins University); Jennifer Hu(Johns Hopkins University); Jesús Villalba-Lopez(Johns Hopkins University); Venkatesh Ravichandran(Amazon AGI); Georgi Tinchev(Amazon Research); Najim Dehak(Johns Hopkins University); Laureano Moro-Velázquez(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: NVV-SuperBench: Beyond Words, Beyond Quality—Benchmarking Nonverbal Vocalizations in Speech Generation
column6: Nonverbal vocalizations (NVVs), such as laughing, sighing, and sobbing, are essential for human-like speech, yet standardized evaluation rarely jointly assesses whether systems generate the intended NVVs, place them correctly, and keep them salient without harming speech. We present NVV-SuperBench, a bilingual English/Chinese benchmark for speech generation with NVVs. It provides a unified 45-type taxonomy and a multi-axis protocol beyond conventional speech quality assessment, evaluating NVV-specific controllability, placement, and perceptual salience. We benchmark 15 speech generation systems spanning prompt-based and tag-based control paradigms, using objective metrics, human listening tests, and LLM-based multi-rater evaluation. Results show that NVV controllability often decouples from speech quality, while low-SNR oral cues and long-duration affective NVVs remain bottlenecks. NVV-SuperBench highlights current gaps and supports progress toward more human-like speech generation.
column7: Liumeng Xue(Nanjing University; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Weizhen Bian(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Jiahao Pan(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Wenxuan Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Yilin Ren(University of Science and Technology Beijing); Boyi Kang(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Ziyang Ma(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University); Xinyuan Qian(University of Science and Technology Beijing); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Yike Guo(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)

column4: How Frequency Band Importance Affects Neural Network Predictions and Human Perception for Speech Quality Assessment
column6: Audio quality assessment models are often used for evaluating speech enhancement and noise suppression approaches. However, recent work has shown that network predictions do not always correlate well with human predictions. Explainability could help developers and users of these tools identify potential error and data bias, which would expedite development. In this work, we use Shapley additive explanations, partial dependence plots, and perturbation analysis to determine the influential frequency bands for three quality assessment models. We then conduct a listening study to determine if human perception is sensitive to the same factors as these networks. Our results show that both networks and humans are more sensitive to detrimental factors than beneficial ones. Further, the networks focus on a small portion of the input which corresponds to low frequency bands. Our work represents a step towards unifying explainability for both humans and networks.
column7: Ada Lamba(The Ohio State University); Donald Williamson(The Ohio State University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 1 - Poster 3 - Speech Production and Perception 2

column4: Vowel Allophony Improves Maximum-Likelihood Classification of Warlpiri Consonants
column6: Australian languages typically have a large number of place contrasts and relatively few manner contrasts. We investigated the acoustic cues that native speakers of Warlpiri, an Australian language with stops in five places of articulation, could use to distinguish them. Using a maximum-likelihood classifier, we show that acoustic cues intrinsic to consonants are not sufficient for this purpose. Adding information from consonant-extrinsic acoustic cues in adjacent vowels improved consonant classification for both CV and VC sequences. In both CVs and VCs, consonant classification benefited the most from allophony in formants at midpoints of adjacent vowels. We discuss the implications of our results and the potential of using maximum-likelihood classifiers for generating predictions based on probabilistic models of speech perception for low resource languages.
column7: Coralie Cram(UCLA); John McGahay(UCLA); Megha Sundara(UCLA)

column4: Towards Robust Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Recognition Learning Physics-Aware and Context-Rich Representations
column6: Silent Speech Recognition (SSR) decodes linguistic intent from non-acoustic biological signals, where Ultrasound Tongue Imaging (UTI) serves as a pivotal non-invasive modality. However, imaging artifacts and complex temporal dependencies make extracting robust features from UTI sequences challenging. To address these issues, we propose a framework for learning physics-aware and context-rich representations. Specifically, a temporal clustering strategy is employed to downsample sequences while preserving critical context, complemented by a physics-aware augmentation that enforces model robustness against imaging perturbations. Furthermore, temporal masking and a hybrid architecture integrating 3D convolutional networks with bidirectional recurrent layers are utilized to promote spatiotemporal representation learning. Our method significantly outperforms baselines, validating that modeling physical consistency and structural completeness is essential for advancing robust UTI-based SSR.
column7: Hongyu Wen(National University of Defense Technology); Yi Su(National University of Defense Technology); Yudong Yang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Siwen Guo(National University of Defense Technology); Qisheng Xu(National University of Defense Technology); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology)

column4: Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion of Clean Speech Using an MRI-Trained Model
column6: Articulatory acoustic inversion reconstructs vocal tract shapes from speech. Real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rt-MRI) allows simultaneous acquisition of both the acoustic speech signal and articulatory information. Besides the complexity of rt-MRI acquisition, the recorded audio is heavily corrupted by scanner noise and requires denoising to be usable. For practical use, it must be possible to invert speech recorded without MRI noise. In this study, we investigate the use of speech recorded in a clean acoustic environment as an alternative to denoised MRI speech. To this end we compare two signals from the same speaker with identical sentences which are aligned using phonetic segmentation. A model trained on denoised MRI speech is evaluated on both denoised MRI and clean speech. We also assess a model trained and tested only on clean speech. Results show that clean speech supports articulatory inversion effectively, achieving an RMSE of 1.56 mm, close to MRI-based performance.
column7: Sofiane Azzouz(Loria)

column4: UniVoice: Unifying Autoregressive ASR and Flow-Matching based TTS with Large Language Models
column6: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become dominant in both Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS), but existing frameworks treat these tasks as isolated, overlooking inherent synergies. While discrete tokenization enables joint modeling, information loss compromises accuracy and synthesis quality. To address the limitations, we propose UniVoice, a unified LLM integrating ASR and TTS via continuous representations. Beyond discrete tokens, UniVoice preserves acoustic details for robust autoregressive recognition and high-fidelity flow-matching generation. To bridge architectural divergence between understanding and generation, we introduce a dual-attention masking mechanism to dynamically switch between causal masks for ASR and bidirectional masks for TTS. Additionally, text-prefix guided speech infilling ensures superior zero-shot voice cloning. Experimental results show UniVoice achieves competitive or superior performance to state-of-the-art single-task models, marking a significant step toward end-to-end speech interaction systems. The code and model weights are available at https://github. com/gwh22/UniVoice.
column7: Wenhao Guan(Xiamen University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Zhikang Niu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Ziyue Jiang(Zhejiang University); Kaidi Wang(Xiamen University); Peijie Chen(Xiamen University); Qingyang Hong(Xiamen University); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Lin Li(Xiamen University)

column4: How do word frequency and syllable surprisal affect response time and acoustic duration in sentence formulation?
column6: Although predictability effects have been shown to affect acoustic realization (e.g., [1 - 8]) at different linguistic levels, they are mostly based on variation of predictability at a specific linguistic level. Yet linguistic levels are embedded within one another. ‘Frequency of occurrence’ is one type of predictability, which could occur at the level of word (word frequency) and syllable (syllable frequency). The current study explored such cross-level interaction on response time and acoustic vowel duration in German, in the context of the psycholinguistic model of speech production in [14]. We hypothesized an additive effect; however, our findings revealed selective interaction, depending on whether the word is mono- or di-syllabic. These results challenge the assumption of ‘discrete, staged and serial’ processing across levels in [14].
column7: Ivan Yuen(Saarland Univeristy); Bernd Möbius(Saarland University); Bistra Andreeva(Saarland University); Mitko Sabev(Saarland University)

column4: Extreme Few-Shot Phoneme Discovery for Indigenous Australian and Pacific Languages via Typological Transfer Learning
column6: Indigenous Australian and Pacific languages face extinction, and many have fewer than ten hours of transcribed speech. Conventional acoustic unit discovery often assumes over 100 hours of unlabeled audio--far beyond what is available for endangered languages. We propose an extreme few-shot phoneme discovery framework that operates on under one hour of audio, leveraging typological transfer from high-resource Austronesian languages through a Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE). We introduce Typological Anchor Selection (TAS), which selects optimal source languages based on phonetic inventory overlap. Evaluated on three endangered language datasets, our approach improves Normalized Mutual Information by 18.8% and cluster purity by 15.6% over multilingual self-supervised baselines. This provides a scalable path for rapid language documentation and revitalization.
column7: Prasanth Yadla(Independent Researcher)

column4: Lexical stress-conditioned spatiotemporal gestural coordination in L2 English
column6: This study examines the articulatory realisation of lexical stress in L2 English produced by speakers of Taiwanese Mandarin, a language without a perceptually salient lexical stress contrast. Electromagnetic articulography was used to record articulatory data, and multivariate functional principal component analysis with landmark-based temporal registration was applied to analyse the spatiotemporal coordination of articulatory gestures across a syllable. Accentedness ratings were used to contextualise inter-speaker differences in stress-condition separation in FPCA score space. Four of the six speakers showed evidence of separation between stress conditions, whereas the two speakers judged to have the strongest perceived foreign accents did not.
column7: Paul McGuire(Macquarie University; National Tsing Hua University); Michael Proctor(Macquarie University); Feng-fan Hsieh(National Tsing Hua University); Yueh-chin Chang(National Tsing Hua University)

column4: Automated Measurement of Geniohyoid Muscle Thickness During Speech Using Deep Learning and UltrasoundAutomated Measurement of Geniohyoid Muscle Thickness During Speech Using Deep Learning and Ultrasound
column6: Manual measurement of muscle morphology from ultrasound during speech is time-consuming and limits large-scale studies. We present SMMA, a fully automated framework combining deep learning segmentation with skeleton-based thickness quantification for analyzing geniohyoid (GH) muscle dynamics. Validation demonstrates near-human-level accuracy (Dice: 0.9037, MAE: 0.53 mm, r = 0.901). Application to Cantonese vowel production (N = 11) reveals systematic patterns: /a:/ shows significantly greater GH thickness (7.29 mm) than /i:/ (5.95 mm, p < 0.001, Cohen's d > 1.3), suggesting greater GH activation during the production of /a:/ than /i:/, consistent with its role in mandibular depression. Sex differences (5-8% greater in males) reflect anatomical scaling. SMMA achieves expert-validated accuracy while eliminating the need for manual annotation, enabling scalable investigations of speech motor control and objective assessment of speech/swallowing disorders.
column7: Alisher Myrgyyassov(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Bruce Xiao Wang(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yu Sun(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Shuming Huang(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zhen Song(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Min Ney Wong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yongping Zheng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

column4: Articulatory Dynamics using Physical Vocal-tract Models
column6: Visualizing and modeling the vocal tract during speech production is crucial in several speech-related areas, including phonetics and phonology, education in phonetics and speech science, and speech pathology. Once the observation and analysis are done, it becomes crucial to evaluate the “synthesized” speech outputs from the model. While speech synthesis is often performed on a computer, physical vocal-tract models provide an alternative and intuitive approach. Some physical models are static and their configurations cannot be altered. Others are dynamic, allowing us to change their configurations and easily adjust the articulatory parameters. Here, a physically dynamic model was tested to produce given words with different sets of articulatory timings. The model was able to show dynamic aspects of speech from the articulatory phonology point of view.
column7: Takayuki Arai(Sophia University)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 3 - Poster 4 - Speech Emotion Recognition and Representation 3

column4: AcoustEmo: An Utterance-Aware Acoustic Q-Former for Open-Vocabulary Emotion Reasoning
column6: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in Open-Vocabulary (OV) emotion recognition but often neglect fine-grained acoustic modeling. Existing methods typically use global audio encoders, failing to capture subtle, local temporal dynamics like micro-prosody and intonation shifts within individual utterances. To address this, we propose AcoustEmo, a time-sensitive MLLM featuring a novel Utterance-Aware Acoustic Q-Former. Our approach utilizes a timestamp-synchronized sliding window to dynamically extract segment-level audio tokens instead of coarse global representations. This enables the model to explicitly trace the temporal evolution of subtle acoustic clues and capture deep contextual dependencies in dialogues. Experiments on the Explainable Multimodal Emotion Recognition (EMER) task show that AcoustEmo effectively enhances complex emotion reasoning, outperforming baselines overall while maintaining robust contextual accuracy.
column7: Liyun Zhang(The University of Tokyo); Xuanmeng Sha(The University of Osaka); Shuqiong Wu(The University of Osaka); Fengkai Liu(The University of Osaka)

column4: Edge–Cloud Collaborative Speech Emotion Captioning via Token-Level Speculative Decoding in Audio-Language Models
column6: Speech Emotion Captioning (SEC) leverages large audio-language models to generate rich, context-aware affective descriptions from speech. However, real-world deployment remains challenging due to the substantial computational demands on resource-constrained edge devices and the privacy risks of transmitting biometric audio. While smaller audio-language models enable efficient on-device SEC, their limited capacity often weakens subtle paralinguistic modeling and fine-grained affective grounding. We propose an edge-cloud collaborative framework based on Uncertainty-Guided Speculative Decoding (UGSD). A lightweight edge model drafts captions locally, and only high-uncertainty token blocks are selectively escalated to a stronger cloud verifier for validation. Experiments on the MER2024 benchmark demonstrate substantial BLEU improvements up to 62.7%. UGSD further achieves 1.4× lower latency and 8.5× higher token throughput compared to an edge-only model. These results empirically characterize the quality-efficiency-privacy trade-off in deployable SEC systems.
column7: Xiangyuan Xue(University of Auckland); Jiajun Lu(University of Melbourne); Yan Gao(University of Cambridge); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Hong Jia(University of Auckland)

column4: Disentangling Reasoning in Large Audio-Language Models for Ambiguous Emotion Prediction
column6: Speech emotion recognition plays an important role in various applications. However, most existing approaches predict a single emotion label, oversimplifying the inherently ambiguous nature of human emotional expression. Recent large audio-language models show promise in generating richer outputs, but their reasoning ability for ambiguous emotional understanding remains limited. In this work, we reformulate ambiguous emotion recognition as a distributional reasoning problem and present the first systematic study of ambiguity-aware reasoning in LALMs. Our framework comprises two complementary components: an ambiguity-aware objective that aligns predictions with human perceptual distributions, and a structured ambiguity-aware chain-of-thought supervision that guides reasoning over emotional cues. Experiments on IEMOCAP and CREMA-D demonstrate consistent improvements across SFT, DPO, and GRPO training strategies.
column7: Xiaofeng Yu(University of Auckland); Jiaheng Dong(The University of Melbourne); Jean Honorio(The University of Melbourne; ARC OPTIMA); Abhirup Ghosh(University of Birmingham); Hong Jia(University of Auckland); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)

column4: AdaLTM: Adaptive Layer-wise Task Vector Merging for Categorical Speech Emotion Recognition with ASR Knowledge Integration
column6: Integrating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) into Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) enhances modeling by providing linguistic context. However, conventional feature fusion faces performance bottlenecks, and multi-task learning often suffers from optimization conflicts. While task vectors and model merging have addressed such conflicts in NLP and CV, their potential in speech tasks remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose an Adaptive Layer-wise Task Vector Merging (AdaLTM) framework based on WavLM-Large. Instead of joint optimization, we extract task vectors from in-domain ASR and SER models fine-tuned on emotion datasets. These vectors are integrated into a frozen base model using layer-wise learnable coefficients. This strategy enables depth-aware balancing of linguistic and paralinguistic knowledge across transformer layers without gradient interference. Experiments on the MSP-Podcast demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively mitigates conflicts between ASR and SER.
column7: Chia-Yu Lee(National Tsing Hua University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Tzu-Quan Lin(National Taiwan University); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Ya-Tse Wu(National Tsing Hua University); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)

column4: SETEAB: Multiscale approach with Squeeze-and-Excitation Temporal Enhanced Aware Block for Speech Emotion Recognition
column6: This paper proposes a novel lightweight multiscale architecture for speech emotion recognition (SER) with three key innovations. First, a depthwise convolution-based subsampling module is introduced to reduce model size and computation while preserving salient emotional cues. Second, a Squeeze-and-Excitation block is integrated to enhance channel-wise recalibration and improve representation robustness. Third, a new Temporal Enhanced Aware Block is designed to strengthen temporal dependency modeling and produce more discriminative emotion-aware features. The proposed model is explicitly designed to jointly improve compactness, recognition performance, and generalizability. Experiments on benchmark SER datasets show that our method achieves higher accuracy with reduced computational complexity, while also delivering stronger cross-corpus performance than most recent advanced networks for SER.
column7: Duy Vo(University of Science; Vietnam National University); Kiet Anh Hoang(University of Science; Vietnam National University; UNEY); Hao Do(University of Science; Vietnam National University)

column4: How Language-Independent Are Emotional Attributes? A Study on Training Data Scaling and Cross-Lingual Generalization
column6: Current state-of-the-art Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems rely on lots of training data, which is available only for a few languages such as English. For low-resource languages, using a cross-lingual model or adapting it to the target language might be an alternative to training a mono-lingual model from scratch. However, it is not clear what constitutes a 'low-resource', i.e. where model adaptation loses its edge over the mono-lingual approach. We investigate this topic by training and adapting several SER models on English and Mandarin data, focusing on the emotional attributes of arousal, valence and dominance. Our results show that, for arousal, model adaptation is beneficial even with two hours of data, while for valence 10-20 hours of adaptation material is required to match the performance of a mono-lingual model trained with 100 hours of data. This indicates that task-specific model adaptation may be an effective approach in low-resource speech emotion recognition problems.
column7: Dániel Halmai(University of Szeged); Gábor Gosztolya(University of Szeged; HUN-REN–SZTE Research Group on Artificial Intelligence)

column4: SISER: Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition with Entropy-Based Adversarial Training
column6: Speech emotion recognition (SER) faces two fundamental challenges: scarcity of labeled data and inter-speaker variability, both of which hinder generalization of emotion recognition systems. While prior adversarial approaches address speaker variability, they fall short in leveraging powerful pre-trained representations. We propose SISER (Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition), integrating wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder and ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. wav2vec 2.0 provides rich self-supervised representations that alleviate dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN enables suppression of speaker identity via a stronger adversarial signal than shallow classifiers. Evaluated on IEMOCAP, SISER achieves a UA of 60.63%, outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%), with ablation emphasizing that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor.
column7: Eunseo Choi(Korea University); Hyunku Kang(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)

column4: Robust Audio-Visual Emotion Recognition via Conditional Transformer U-Nets with Frequency-Injected Visual Stream
column6: We present a convolutional transformer (CTr)-based dual U-Net for robust audio-visual emotion recognition (AVER) in noisy and reverberation environments. Each CTr U-Net encoder learns compact, modality-specific bottleneck representations that capture contextual and temporal-spatial cues from audio and visual inputs, while a fusion-based emotion decoder predicts emotional states from the joint bottleneck features. Emotion-conditioned auxiliary decoders reconstruct intermediate features to enhance supervision and consistency. The audio stream incorporates an inverse filtering-based front-end, while the visual stream employs frequency-injected spatial-spectral modeling to better capture facial dynamics. Experiments demonstrate improved robustness and accuracy compared to existing unimodal and multimodal benchmarks.
column7: Hanwook Chung(Faurecia IRYStec)

column4: Diffusion Bridge Learning Between Overfitted and Underfitted Representations for speech emotion recognition
column6: Robust recognition of human emotions from speech remains difficult under domain and language shift because neural encoders often overfit to dataset-specific acoustic cues. This paper proposes a diffusion-based representation-space training framework that reshapes learned representations toward class-centered geometry. The model introduces class prototypes as anchors and learns stochastic sample–prototype transformations using a conditional denoising diffusion process with paired alignment, cycle consistency, and classifier-based regularization. Experiments on cross-lingual emotion recognition between English and Japanese show consistent improvements in weighted average recall. The proposed method achieves up to +6.42 percentage points in English-to-Japanese evaluation and +4.00 percentage points in Japanese-to-English evaluation, demonstrating improved robustness to cross-language domain shift.
column7: Shi-wook Lee(AIST)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 4 - Poster 7 - Spoofing and Deepfake Detection 3

column4: DAR-Boost: A Differentiable and Adaptive Raw Data Augmentation Framework for Robust Anti-Spoofing
column6: Audio deepfake detection systems face significant challenges in generalizing to unseen attacks and diverse acoustic environments. While raw waveform augmentation methods like RawBoost show promise by modeling recording noise, they rely on static parameters tailored for speech. This rigidity limits effectiveness in non-speech domains like environmental sounds. To address this, we propose DAR-Boost, an end-to-end differentiable augmentation framework. We reformulate traditional convolutive, impulsive, and stationary noise injections as fully differentiable layers governed by a lightweight auxiliary network. This network dynamically predicts optimal parameters based on the input waveform, enabling adaptive learning from the data distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that while DAR-Boost maintains comparable performance to RawBoost in the voice domain, it exhibits superior performance in the environmental sound domain, effectively broadening the framework's applicability.
column7: Yingdong Li(Sun Yat-sen University); Chengxin Chen(China Mobile Communications Corporation); Nanli Zeng(China Mobile Communications Corporation); Jianguo Hu(Sun Yat-sen University); Kun Zeng(Sun Yat-sen University)

column4: Quantizer-Aware Hierarchical Neural Codec Modeling for Speech Deepfake Detection
column6: Neural audio codecs discretize speech via residual vector quantization (RVQ), forming a coarse-to-fine hierarchy across quantizers. While codec models have been explored for representation learning, their discrete structure remains underutilized in speech deepfake detection. In particular, different quantization levels capture complementary acoustic cues, where early quantizers encode coarse structure and later quantizers refine residual details that reveal synthesis artifacts. Existing systems either rely on continuous encoder features or ignore this quantizer-level hierarchy. We propose a hierarchy-aware representation learning framework that models quantizer-level contributions through learnable global weighting, enabling structured codec representations aligned with forensic cues. Keeping the speech encoder backbone frozen and updating only 4.4% additional parameters, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 46.2% on ASVspoof 2019 and 13.9% on ASVspoof5 over strong baselines.
column7: Jinyang Wu(A*STAR); Zihan Pan(A*STAR); Qiquan Zhang(UNSW); Sailor Hardik(A*STAR); Soumik Mondal(A*STAR)

column4: VoxENES 2026: Benchmarking Generalization of Speech Spoofing Detectors Against LLM-Era TTS and Voice Conversion
column6: Modern LLM-driven text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC) systems produce synthetic speech that differs from the generators represented in many legacy spoofing benchmarks. This mismatch creates a temporal generalization gap that can overestimate detector robustness under real-world post-processing conditions. We bridge this gap by introducing Vox-ENES 2026, a bilingual (English and Spanish) benchmark of 53,628 audio samples generated using 10 contemporary speech synthesis methods and evaluated under 10 standardized post-processing conditions. Using VoxENES 2026, we benchmark eight pretrained detectors without fine-tuning and observe substantial performance degradation: the best model achieves 28.98% EER overall, while most perform near or below random chance across modern generators and perturbations. Our results highlight the reliance on brittle artifacts in current detectors and establish VoxENES 2026 as a practical testbed for developing robust audio spoofing countermeasures.
column7: Aastha Sharma(University of South Florida); Guangjing Wang(University of South Florida)

column4: Soft-Gating Score-Level Fusion for Spoofing-Aware Speaker Verification
column6: In Spoofing-Aware Speaker Verification (SASV), combining Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) and Countermeasure (CM) subsystems is a key challenge. Existing approaches mainly rely on static fusion schemes, which fail to fully reflect the complementary strengths of the two subsystems. To address this limitation, we propose a Soft Gating Score-Level Fusion method that dynamically adjusts subsystem contributions based on confidence. This trial-wise adjustment allows the subsystem with higher confidence to contribute more strongly to the final decision. The proposed method requires no additional training and can be directly applied to existing SASV pipelines. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under multiple model configurations show that the proposed method achieves up to 90% relative improvement in a-DCF compared to baselines. We further analyze the conditions under which the proposed fusion is most effective, providing practical insights for stable SASV deployment.
column7: Seongkyu Han(Soongsil University); Yowon Lee(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Thien Phuc Doan(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University)

column4: GradHarmony: A Gradient Alignment and Magnitude Normalization Strategy for Audio Deepfake Detection
column6: In audio deepfake detection, data augmentation improves model generalization by exposing them to diverse data variations. However, gradients computed from clean and augmented samples may become directionally misaligned and differ in magnitude. These discrepancies may be amplified in multi-augmentation settings, leading to unstable optimization. In this paper, we propose GradHarmony, a gradient alignment and magnitude normalization strategy for stable multi-augmentation training. GradHarmony computes gradients separately for clean data and each augmentation type, and aligns conflicting augmented gradients using the clean gradient as a reference. Then adaptively normalizes their magnitudes using exponential moving average (EMA)-based statistics to prevent dominance. Experimental results show performance improvements across a variety of models, with two state-of-the-art models achieving an average 22% reduction in equal error rate compared to the baseline on out-of-domain datasets.
column7: Inho Kim(soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(soongsil University)

column4: Towards Detecting Neural Audio Codec Synthesized Heart Sounds
column6: In this paper, we introduce Synthetic Heart Sound Detection (SHAC), a task aimed at identifying phonocardiograms (PCGs) synthesized using neural audio codecs (NACs). To facilitate research in this direction, we release CARDIOFAKE, the first benchmark dataset for SHAC containing both real and codec-synthesized PCGs. We benchmark spectral representations (MFCC, LFCC) and self-supervised learning (SSL) representations (e.g., WavLM) for the task. Furthermore, we propose GROOT, a fusion framework that integrates spectral and SSL features for leveraging their complementary behavior. Experiments show that GROOT, combining MFCC and WavLM, achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming individual representations and competitive baselines.
column7: Girish (UPES; IIIT-Delhi); Orchid Chetia Phukan(NTHU); Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar(VBSPU; IIIT-Delhi); Bhavinkumar Vinodbhai Kuwar(IIIT-Delhi); Swarup Ranjan Behera(Independent Researcher); Arun Balaji Buduru(IIIT-Delhi)

column4: Disentangling Speaker Traits for Deepfake Source Verification via Chebyshev Polynomial and Riemannian Metric Learning
column6: Speech deepfake source verification systems aims to determine whether two synthetic speech utterances originate from the same source generator, often assuming that the resulting source embeddings are independent of speaker traits. However, this assumption remains unverified. In this paper, we first investigate the impact of speaker factors on source verification. We propose a speaker-disentangled metric learning (SDML) framework incorporating two novel loss functions. The first leverages Chebyshev polynomial to mitigate gradient instability during disentanglement optimization. The second projects source and speaker embeddings into hyperbolic space, leveraging Riemannian metric distances to reduce speaker information and learn more discriminative source features. Experimental results on MLAAD benchmark, evaluated under four newly proposed protocols designed for source-speaker disentanglement scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of SDML framework. The code, evaluation protocols and demo website are available at .
column7: Xi Xuan(University of Eastern Finland); Wenxin Zhang(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Zhiyu Li(University of Science and Technology of China); Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton); Ville Hautamäki(University of Eastern Finland); Tomi Kinnunen(University of Eastern Finland)

column4: Interpretable Frequency-Band Attention with Gated SSL Fusion for Audio Deepfake Detection
column6: Synthetic and manipulated speech threatens automatic speaker verification. Self-supervised (SSL) front-ends achieve low error rates but operate as black boxes, revealing little about where in the spectrum spoofing artifacts reside. We propose BandMIL, a band-aware multiple instance learning (MIL) framework that augments SSL representations with interpretable frequency-band analysis. Overlapping windows are split into eight band-specific spectrogram images, encoded by a shared convolutional encoder combined with handcrafted per-band features, and pooled via band attention. Gated fusion adaptively integrates these cues with WavLM representations, and MIL aggregates window predictions into an utterance-level decision without truncation. On ASVspoof 2019 LA, BandMIL achieves 1.28% EER and 0.0331 min t-DCF, improving over SSL-only (1.73% EER). Per-attack analysis shows the band and SSL branches are complementary, while band attention reveals which frequencies drive each decision.
column7: Abeer Alhammad(Thaka); Abdullah Aldahlawi(Thaka)

column4: ArFake: A Robust Framework for Multi-Dialect Arabic Speech Spoofing Detection Benchmark
column6: Rapid advances in generative text-to-speech have made it increasingly difficult to distinguish bona fide from synthetic speech, especially for low-resource Arabic dialects, where data scarcity, complex morphology, and non-standard orthography hinder both synthesis and detection. We introduce ARFAKE, the first end-to-end framework for generating and detecting spoofed Arabic speech across eight dialects. The framework generates speech with four TTS models, then assesses quality and intelligibility using classifier-based measures, downstream ASR performance, and human mean opinion scores. We curate a mixed bona fide/synthetic corpus to train a spoofing detector and evaluate robustness both in-domain and under Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO) protocols, achieving 96% and 97%. Generalization to unseen dialects is examined with Leave-One-Dialect-Out (LODO) evaluation. ARFAKE establishes a benchmark and a scalable pathway toward stronger Arabic speech security across generators and dialects.
column7: Mohamed Elsetohy(MBZUAI); Alhassan Ehab(Queen's University); Ali Mekky(MBZUAI); Besher Hassan(MBZUAI); Shady Shehata(University of Waterloo)

column4: MSpoofTTS: Multi-Resolution Spoof-Guided Inference for Discrete Speech Synthesis
column6: Neural codec language models enable high-quality discrete speech synthesis, yet their inference remains vulnerable to token-level artifacts and distributional drift that degrade perceptual realism. Rather than relying on preference optimization or retraining, we propose MSpoofTTS, a training-free inference framework that improves zero-shot synthesis through multi-resolution spoof guidance. We introduce a Multi-Resolution Token-based Spoof Detection framework that evaluates codec sequences at different temporal granularities to detect locally inconsistent or unnatural patterns. We then integrate the spoof detectors into a hierarchical decoding strategy, progressively pruning low-quality candidates and re-ranking hypotheses. This discriminator-guided generation enhances robustness without modifying model parameters. Experiments validate the effectiveness of our framework for robust and high-quality codec-based speech generation. Demos are available online.
column7: Junchuan Zhao(National University of Singapore); Minh Duc Vu(National University of Singapore); Ye Wang(National University of Singapore)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 5 - Poster 9 - Source Separation 2

column4: MeCo: One-Step MeanFlow-based Corrector for Multi-Channel Speech Separation
column6: While discriminative models for multi-channel speech separation excel in reference-based metrics, they often exhibit suboptimal human listening quality. To address this, we propose a novel MeanFlow-based one-step generative corrector (MeCo). MeCo learns a conditional average velocity field to map discriminative estimates directly onto the clean speech manifold in a single step. To maximize one-step generation performance, we introduce Data-Space Optimization (DSO). DSO integrates an xᵣ-loss, which penalizes prediction errors on longer displacement intervals to serve as a generative objective for human listening quality, with an Endpoint SI-SDR loss that directly optimizes terminal signal fidelity. Experiments demonstrate that MeCo achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with minimal computational overhead, simultaneously achieving superior signal fidelity and human listening quality in both in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios.
column7: Dohwan Kim(KAIST); Jung-Woo Choi(KAIST)

column4: AV-FlowSep: Audio-Visual Target Speaker Separation via Flow Matching
column6: This work addresses the task of separating a target speaker's voice from mixtures using visual cues. While existing discriminative approaches achieve strong speech intelligibility, generative diffusion-based methods improve perceptual quality but require many iterative refinement steps. To address these limitations, we propose AV-FlowSep, an audio-visual target speaker separation based on conditional flow matching to learn direct transport paths from mixture to clean mel-spectrogram. We adopt a latent Diffusion Transformer where temporal visual cues from the target speaker are integrated via cross-attention. We demonstrate that AV-FlowSep can generate high perceptual quality with as few as a single inference step. Experiments on VoxCeleb2 and LRS2 across both speech-speech and speech-noise scenarios, show that our approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to existing baselines, with strong cross-dataset generalization and practical computational efficiency.
column7: Pattara Tipaksorn(NECTEC); Wayupuk Sommuang(Thammasat University); Kwanchiva Thangthai(NECTEC)

column4: Pseudo-Spatially Conditioned TF-Locoformer with MHCA+FiLM Fusion for Single-Channel Speech Separation
column6: Single-channel speech separation in noisy, reverberant environments is challenging as monaural mixtures lack explicit spatial cues. We propose pseudo-spatial conditioning that learns spatially sensitive embeddings from multi-channel training data while using only a single channel at inference. During training, multi-channel mixtures serve as privileged information to pretrain a single-channel encoder with a contrastive triplet objective guided by spatial-configuration differences. This encourages embeddings to reflect spatial configuration rather than speech content. The encoder is jointly fine-tuned with TF-Locoformer to extract pseudo-spatial embeddings. These embeddings condition the separator's time-frequency features via a fusion module combining multi-head cross-attention and feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). On WHAMR!, SI-SNRi increases from 17.4 to 17.7 dB (S) and from 18.6 to 18.9 dB (M), adding 1.0-1.2M parameters.
column7: Daichi Nitsu(Institute of Science Tokyo); Koichi Shinoda(Institute of Science Tokyo)

column4: Improving Audio Codec-based Speech Separation By Stacking Residual Vector Quantization Layers
column6: Speech separation models trained on raw waveforms achieve high performance but come with substantial computational costs. Neural Audio Codecs (NACs) offer an efficient alternative by operating in compressed latent spaces. However, the existing codec-based method aggregates per-layer Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) vectors into a single vector, collapsing the coarse-to-fine acoustic hierarchy. We propose RVQ-Grid to explicitly preserve this hierarchy by stacking per-layer RVQ vectors into a 3D grid and processing it using dual-axis recurrent blocks. On WSJ0-2Mix, RVQ-Grid achieves a +3.6 dB SI-SDRi improvement over the prior codec-based method. Our evaluation on the Automatic Speech Recognition task shows that RVQ-Grid achieves an 8.6% WER, demonstrating comparable performance to the SepFormer baseline under the same codec condition. During inference, RVQ-Grid achieves a 6x reduction in MACs compared to SepFormer.
column7: Nhu Minh Phuong Dinh(Institute of Science Tokyo); Roland Hartanto(Institute of Science Tokyo); Koichi Shinoda(Institute of Science Tokyo)

column4: Speaker Identity as Sole Supervision for Speech Separation
column6: Speech separation systems are typically trained with waveform- or spectrogram-level reconstruction losses requiring clean references, spatial cues such as multichannel recordings, or remixing strategies. We investigate whether speech separation can instead be trained using speaker identity as the sole supervision signal. We propose a contrastive objective aligning embeddings of separated outputs with embeddings of auxiliary utterances while repelling competing speakers using in-batch negatives. Unlike target speaker extraction, embeddings are used only to define the training objective and are not required at inference, resulting in a conventional speaker-independent separator. Experiments show that speaker-identity supervision alone can train separation systems from scratch to satisfactory performance and that fine-tuning supervised models on noisy mixtures with this objective further improves separation quality.
column7: Christoph Boeddeker(MERL); Yoshiki Masuyama(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Julius Richter(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Takahiro Edo(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Gordon Wichern(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Jonathan Le Roux(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL))

column4: SPOT-TSE: Spatial Point-Guided Target Speech Extraction
column6: Wearable devices such as smart glasses increasingly demand selective listening. Accordingly, recent works often explore region-based spatial target speech extraction (TSE). However, conventional fixed-boundary selection is sensitive to small spatial shifts near boundaries, and methods relying only on distance or azimuth become ambiguous under spatial overlap (e.g., sharing the same distance or azimuth). To address these issues, we propose SPOT-TSE, a multi-channel point-guided TSE framework where the target is specified by a continuous spatial point query in distance and azimuth. We stabilize point-based conditioning via spatial query encoding and proximity-weighted soft targets during training. To further handle overlap cases, we adopt hard-negative spatial sampling. Experiments on simulated smart glasses datasets show improved spatial selectivity and lower word error rate, while reducing computational cost compared to a recurrent baseline.
column7: Taewon Ryu(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Semi-Supervised Joint Separation and Diarization for Multichannel Noisy Speech Mixtures
column6: This paper presents joint separation and diarization for noisy speech mixtures without relying on isolated speech signals. Neural full-rank spatial covariance analysis with speaker activity (FCASA) trains a joint model using only speech mixtures and diarization annotations by incorporating statistical blind source separation. However, because this method largely depends on spatial information, it can be degraded by diffuse noise and result in residual noise in the separated signals. To overcome this limitation, we propose a semi-supervised method that uses clean speech mixtures (e.g., meeting recordings) together with environmental noise recordings. Our method trains noise suppression in a supervised manner while preserving unsupervised separation of speech sources. Both objectives are derived from a unified generative model of multichannel mixtures. Experimental results show that our method improves separation performance over neural FCASA in multiple metrics.
column7: Yuto Nozaki(AIST; Keio University); Kohei Saijo(AIST; Waseda University); Yoshiaki Bando(AIST); Masaki Onishi(AIST)

column4: Don't Listen to Me: A Lightweight, Low-Latency Model for Own-Voice Cancellation in Far-Field Speech Enhancement
column6: We introduce own-voice cancellation (OVC): removing a target (enrolled) speaker from a noisy multi-speaker mixture while preserving any remaining speech. Framed as the complement of target speaker extraction, OVC addresses latency-induced own-voice artifacts that arise when a far-field device streams enhanced audio back to the user, as the round-trip time easily exceeds the perceptual threshold for own-voice distortion. We condition a time-domain model with only 2 ms algorithmic latency on a short enrollment utterance and benchmark TD-SpeakerBeam alongside a lighter Mamba-MinGRU masker built from Mamba blocks with MinGRU temporal mixing. Replacing the ConvTasNet-based auxiliary network with a linear RNN encoder improves both signal-to-distortion ratio and predicted MOS while reducing compute. Results establish OVC as a practical, low-latency enhancement objective for far-field denoising.
column7: Mads Østergaard(WS Audiology); Alexander Neergaard Zahid(WS Audiology); Karl Ulbæk(WS Audiology); Andreas Bagge(WS Audiology; Technical University of Denmark); Kenny Falkær Olsen(WS Audiology; Technical University of Denmark); Rasmus Lindrup(Verth)

column1: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 6 - Poster 8 - SE Architectures, Adaptation and Audio Front-Ends

column4: Dual-Encoder Fusion with Explicit and Implicit Injection for the Interspeech 2026 Audio Encoder Capability Challenge
column6: We conduct a systematic study of dual-encoder fusion for the Interspeech 2026 Audio Encoder Capability Challenge (AECC), aiming to translate encoder complementarity into consistent gains across various audio classification and understanding tasks. Using Whisper and Dasheng as complementary encoders, we examine two injection strategies: implicit injection via parameter-efficient Dasheng adaptation before fusion, and explicit injection that decomposes representations into residual components with auxiliary regularization to isolate non-redundant information. Ablations show that explicit injection yields stronger task-wise complementarity and more per-task best results, while implicit adaptation remains competitive and robust overall. We also identify a stable backbone based on token-wise softmax-gated residual fusion with a lightweight STFT residual branch. These results provide practical design insights for modular encoder fusion in the Large Audio Language Model (LALM) framework.
column7: Yucong Zhang(Wuhan University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zhang Chen(Duke Kunshan University); Juan Liu(Wuhan University); Wei Ju(OPPO); Hongbin Suo(OPPO); Ming Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Wuhan University)

column4: Balancing Speech Reconstruction and Noise Suppression Using Dual-Asymmetric Loss
column6: AI-based speech enhancement algorithms are prevalent in speech transmission applications and consumer audio devices. These algorithms typically utilize neural networks to predict filters or masks that attenuate noise in speech signals. However, due to the often-overlapping frequency responses of speech and noise, this process can degrade speech quality or result in residual noise artifacts. In this paper, we present a novel loss function with an adjustable parameter to balance the importance of reconstructing the original speech and the effectiveness of noise suppression. We demonstrate the efficacy of this loss with a variety of state-of-the-art architectures. Experimental results demonstrate improvements over baseline models for the targeted outcome: higher speech quality or enhanced noise suppression. Furthermore, the loss function exhibits a correlation of 0.95 for speech and -0.96 for noise metrics when tested across 13 distinct parameter values.
column7: Merlin Carson(Skyworks Solutions); Suyash Dandekar(Georgia Institute of Technology)

column4: SE-AGCNet: An End-to-End Framework for Joint Speech Enhancement and Loudness Control in Meeting Scenarios
column6: Conventional audio pipelines typically treat speech enhancement (SE) and automatic gain control (AGC) as discrete modules, which often limits overall performance. For instance, applying AGC before SE may inadvertently amplify background noise, while prioritizing SE tends to over-suppress low-volume speech. To address these limitations, we propose SE-AGCNet, an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes SE and AGC. Tailored for meeting scenarios with significant volume variations, SE-AGCNet leverages the synergy between the two tasks: SE preserves quiet speech, thereby facilitating effective volume adjustment by the AGC component. Furthermore, we propose a specialized data simulation pipeline, SE-AGC-DataGen, and incorporate standardized loudness evaluation metrics: integrated loudness (LUFS), short-term loudness (St LUFS), and LRA. Experiments show that SE-AGCNet consistently achieves target loudness while improving speech quality and ASR accuracy over competitive baselines.
column7: Jinming Zhang(Zhejiang University); Wei Rao(Nanyang Technological University); Xionghu Zhong(Hunan University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: SLICE: Speech Enhancement via Layer-wise Injection of Conditioning Embeddings
column6: Real-world speech is often corrupted by multiple degradations simultaneously, including additive noise, reverberation, and nonlinear distortion. Diffusion-based enhancement methods perform well on single degradations but struggle with compound corruptions. Prior noise-aware approaches inject conditioning at the input layer only, which can degrade performance below that of an unconditioned model. To address this, we propose injecting degradation conditioning, derived from a pretrained encoder with multi-task heads for noise type, reverberation, and distortion, into the timestep embedding so that it propagates through all residual blocks without architectural changes. In controlled experiments where only the injection method varies, input-level conditioning performs worse than no encoder at all on compound degradations, while layer-wise injection achieves the best results. The method also generalizes to diverse real-world recordings.
column7: Seokhoon Moon(KAIST); Kyudan Jung(KAIST); Jaegul Choo(KAIST)

column4: Neuromorphic Speech Enhancement with Dual-Branch Spiking Neural Networks
column6: Spiking neural network (SNN)-based neuromorphic speech enhancement has emerged as a promising paradigm due to its energy efficiency, yet it still underperforms classical artificial neural network (ANN)-based approaches owing to binary activations and the lack of well-designed network architectures. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel dual-branch spiking neural network architecture equipped with a gated spiking unit (GSU), termed GSU-DBNet. Specifically, GSU-DBNet simultaneously models the speech magnitude spectrum and complex spectrum, predicting the corresponding magnitude and complex spectral masks. Meanwhile, a dual-path GSU module is adopted to exploit temporal and frequency information for enhanced spatiotemporal feature representation. Experiments on a popular benchmark dataset show that GSU-DBNet achieves a PESQ score of 3.04 with only 394K parameters, outperforming existing SNN-based methods while using only 4.5%-10.6% of the parameters of representative ANN-based models.
column7: Taiyu Meng(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Wenbin Jiang(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Haoyi Zhang(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Yuhan Zhou(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Haoyi Yin(Hangzhou Dianzi University)

column4: Parallel Time-Band Mixing with Learned Observation-Adding for Robust ASR Front-Ends
column6: Speech enhancement is often used as a front-end for robust ASR, yet recurrent temporal and cross-band modules introduce sequential dependencies that reduce parallel efficiency. In this paper, we present a sequence-parallel band-split enhancement front-end built on a Parallel Time-Band Mixer (PTBM) block that eliminates within-block recurrent unrolling. PTBM integrates intra-band temporal mixing and per-frame cross-band attention within a unified parallel architecture, enabling efficient contextual modeling across both time and frequency dimensions. The system retains the mask-plus-residual reconstruction interface and introduces learned Observation-Adding (LOA) to suppress ASR-sensitive artifacts without development-set tuning. Experiments on DNS Challenge and CHiME-4 with frozen Whisper back-ends show that the proposed front-end consistently reduces word error rate relative to recurrent band-split baselines while requiring only 0.96 M parameters and 0.58 GMAC/s for the front-end network.
column7: Xingyu Shen(Concordia University; Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology); Runze Wang(Concordia University); Wei-Ping Zhu(Concordia University); Benoit Champagne(McGill University)

column4: Dictionary-Free Discrete Key-Value Attention for Improving Speech Enhancement
column6: This paper explores novel attention mechanisms for speech enhancement tasks. Existing Harmonic Attention (HAtt) enhances the reconstructions of the voiced speech spectrum and overall speech quality by constructing a harmonic dictionary. However, HAtt often underperforms on unvoiced components, as its design is constrained by a heavy reliance on prior knowledge for modeling harmonic structures. To address this limitation, we propose a Dictionary-Free Discrete Attention (DFDA) module, which draws inspiration from finite scalar quantization to discretize both keys and values in the attention module in a data-driven manner, thereby learning latent dictionary representations without hand-crafted designs. The HAtt and proposed DFDA are adapted to the TFGridNet block as a new speech enhancement model. Results show this network significantly improves speech quality and intelligibility by effectively suppressing noise and better recovering both voiced and unvoiced spectral structures.
column7: Zihao Cui(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Jinwei Huang(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Tao Li(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Rongxiu Zhong(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Yingying Gao(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Shilei Zhang(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Chao Deng(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University); Junlan Feng(China Mobile Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.; Peking University)

column4: Time–Frequency Weighted Losses for Phoneme Reconstruction in DNN-Based Speech Enhancement
column6: Conventional training losses for speech enhancement based on the signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) treat all time-frequency (TF) regions uniformly, overlooking the fine-grained spectral cues that are relevant to specific phoneme intelligibility. We propose a TF weighting framework that modulates the SDR objective based on local speech presence, speech-to-interference ratio (SIR), and spectral flux. By integrating these factors into a differentiable objective, the framework emphasizes TF bins with high speech-noise competition while also accounting for transient cues such as consonant bursts. Experimental results show that our approach improves objective frequency-weighted enhancement metrics, as well as phoneme recognition accuracy, particularly for consonants. Spectral analysis shows better reconstruction of mid-frequency structures at less adverse SIR.
column7: Nasser-Eddine Monir(Université de Lorraine; CNRS; Inria; Loria); Paul Magron(Université de Lorraine; CNRS; Inria; Loria); Romain Serizel(Université de Lorraine; CNRS; Inria; Loria)

column4: Bridging the Distribution Gap in Real-World Far-Field Speech Enhancement via Lightweight Latent Representation Alignment
column6: Although speech enhancement models have achieved notable progress, their performance degrades in real-world far-field scenarios due to the distribution gap between simulated and real data. To address this problem, we introduce a high-quality real-world dataset. We further propose a lightweight two-stage framework that bridges the distribution gap through latent representation alignment. In the first stage, a pretrained denoising model performs initial noise and reverberation reduction. In the second stage, a distribution mapping module aligns first-stage features to the latent space learned from clean near-field speech, and the decoder reconstructs high-fidelity speech. Experiments on real-world test sets demonstrate that our method effectively suppresses noise while preserving speech structure with only 0.8 GMAC/s computational cost. It achieves 2.94 in P.835 OVRL and 3.35 in P.808, outperforming strong baselines in real-world far-field conditions.
column7: Biao Liu(CAS; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Haoyuan Xie(CAS; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Zengqiang Shang(CAS); Mou Wang(OPPO); Xin Liu(OPPO); Pengyuan Zhang(CAS; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: ARTT: Augmented Reverberant-Target Training for Unsupervised Monaural Speech Dereverberation
column6: Due to the absence of clean reference signals and spatial cues, monaural unsupervised speech dereverberation is a challenging ill-posed inverse problem. To realize it, we propose augmented reverberant-target training (ARTT), which consists of two stages. In the first stage, reverberant-target training (RTT) is proposed to first further reverberate the observed reverberant mixture signal, and then train a deep neural network (DNN) to recover the observed reverberant mixture via discriminative training. Although the target signal to fit is reverberant, we find that the resulting DNN can effectively reduce reverberation. In the second stage, an online self-distillation mechanism based on the mean-teacher algorithm is proposed to further improve dereverberation. Evaluation results demonstrate that ARTT achieves strong unsupervised dereverberation performance, significantly outperforming previous baselines.
column7: Siqi Song(Southern University of Science and Technology); Fulin Wu(Southern University of Science and Technology); Zhong-Qiu Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology)

column4: SSL-GMMVC: Interpretable Voice Conversion via Locally Linear GMM Transforms in Self-Supervised Representation Space
column6: We introduce SSL-GMMVC, an interpretable voice conversion method in self-supervised speech space. The method models paired source-target features with a Gaussian mixture model and performs conversion as a posterior-weighted sum of affine transforms. This yields locally linear transformations that adapt to heterogeneous feature-space structure while remaining analytically tractable. Through objective and subjective evaluations, we show that SSL-GMMVC improves speaker similarity with comparable intelligibility and naturalness, and that even a constrained covariance variant surpasses a deep learning baseline as the number of mixture components increases. Further analyses link component selection to phonetic structure and reveal interpretable scaling and rotation in the learned transforms. These findings highlight SSL-GMMVC as an effective, analyzable framework for voice conversion.
column7: Tomoya Tanabu(The University of Tokyo); Hiroshi Nishijima(The University of Tokyo); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)

column4: From A to B to A: Palindromic Zero-Shot Voice Conversion with Non-Parallel Data
column6: We present a voice conversion (VC) framework that utilizes K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) retrieval over WavLM representations to align non-parallel source and target speech, constructing synthetic training pairs for supervised learning. The retrieved segments serve as synthetic inputs, while real target audio provides ground-truth outputs, forming a synthetic-to-real training paradigm that naturally supports multilingual data without requiring parallel corpora or explicit alignment. To ensure consistent target-speaker identity, we incorporate a speaker loss derived from a pretrained speaker verification model. Experiments across multiple languages demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high naturalness and strong speaker similarity, outperforming competitive VC baselines, despite being trained exclusively on English data. Samples can be accessed at: https://palindromic-vc.github.io.
column7: Moshe Mandel(Independent); Shlomi E. Chazan(OriginAI)

column4: MeanVoiceFlow2: Joint Optimization of Mean Flow and Content Encoder for Fast One-Step Zero-Shot Voice Conversion
column6: Flow-matching approaches to voice conversion (VC) have gained attention owing to their high speech quality and strong speaker similarity. Among them, one-step models such as MeanVoiceFlow are particularly attractive because they enable efficient inference; however, their reliance on a computationally intensive content encoder remains a bottleneck. We therefore propose MeanVoiceFlow2, a framework that jointly optimizes a flow-based conversion module and a computationally efficient content encoder. The model is trained through conversion distillation using MeanVoiceFlow and the reconstruction of real data. We further incorporate diffusion-GAN training with sample mixing and teacher-guided conditioning augmentation to enhance realism and disentanglement. Experiments on zero-shot VC showed that MeanVoiceFlow2 achieved higher perceptual quality and approximately 9× faster inference than MeanVoiceFlow while maintaining comparable speaker similarity.
column7: Takuhiro Kaneko(NTT, Inc.); Hirokazu Kameoka(NTT, Inc.); Kou Tanaka(NTT, Inc.); Yuto Kondo(NTT, Inc.)

column4: Zero-VC: Zero-Lookahead Streaming Voice Conversion via Speaker Anonymization
column6: Streaming zero-shot voice conversion struggles to disentangle timbre from linguistic content without degrading utility or inflating latency. Current methods rely on information bottleneck (IB) or speaker perturbation. While IB filters out timbre, it discards prosody, forcing models to explicitly inject features like fundamental frequency. This often requires buffering future frames, creating algorithmic lookahead latency. On the other hand, existing perturbation methods largely overlook the crucial trade-off between timbre leakage and utility preservation. Recognizing this neglected trade-off, we find that the inherent objective of Speaker Anonymization (SA) aligns well with balancing these factors. Thus, we introduce SA as a novel perturbation mechanism to explicitly mitigate timbre leakage while retaining prosodic utility. Crucially, SA's robust representations significantly alleviate the generator's reliance on future context, enabling our strictly causal, zero-lookahead network.
column7: Yudong Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Zihao Fang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Junwen Qiu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Ruihai Jing(Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co., Ltd.); Ruixiang Hang(Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co., Ltd.); Yingda Shen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zhizheng Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute; Amphion Technology Co.,Ltd.)

column4: Improving Model Expressivity and Speaker Matching in Low-Latency Voice Conversion
column6: Real-time voice conversion systems struggle to achieve high speaker similarity in zero-shot scenarios, especially under lightweight computational constraints. This challenge stems from a lack of model expressivity and the difficulty of capturing comprehensive speaker-relevant information within the strict latency requirements. We propose a real-time voice conversion framework that addresses this limitation by adding lost prosody explicitly through an excitation signal and by fusing complementary information into the conventional global speaker embeddings. To ensure robust feature disentanglement, we furthermore employ an encoder-specific information perturbation strategy during training. Our approach maintains causal inference requirements and preserves prosodic and linguistic content while operating under low-latency constraints. Experimental evaluations demonstrate improvements in speaker-matching metrics over state-of-the-art real-time baselines.
column7: Anders R. Bargum(Aalborg University); Simon Lajboschitz(Khora & Heka VR); Stefania Serafin(Technical University of Denmark); Cumhur Erkut(Aalborg University)

column4: Universal Speech Content Factorization
column6: We propose Universal Speech Content Factorization (USCF), a simple and invertible linear method for extracting a low-rank speech representation in which speaker timbre is suppressed while phonetic content is preserved. USCF extends Speech Content Factorization, a closed-set voice conversion (VC) method, to an open-set setting by learning a universal speech-to-content mapping via least-squares optimization and deriving speaker-specific transformations from only a few seconds of target speech. We show through embedding analysis that USCF effectively removes speaker-dependent variation. As a zero-shot VC system, USCF achieves competitive intelligibility, naturalness, and speaker similarity compared to methods that require substantially more target-speaker data or additional neural training. Finally, we demonstrate that as a training-efficient timbre-disentangled speech feature, USCF features can serve as the acoustic representation for training timbre-prompted text-to-speech models. Speech samples and code are publicly available.
column7: Henry Li Xinyuan(Johns Hopkins University); Zexin Cai(Johns Hopkins University); Lin Zhang(Johns Hopkins University); Paola Garcia-Perera(Johns Hopkins University); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University); Sanjeev Khudanpur(Johns Hopkins University); Nicholas Andrews(Johns Hopkins University); Matthew Wiesner(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: CFLOW-VC: An unsupervised cycle training strategy based on normalizing flows for Voice Conversion
column6: Voice conversion (VC) aims to transfer the timbre of a target speaker while preserving the content of a source speech. A key challenge, especially in non-parallel settings, is the train-test mismatch: during training, models often learn from utterances where content and timbre are from the same speaker, hindering their ability to disentangle these factors effectively during inference. In this work, we propose CFLOW-VC, an unsupervised cycle training strategy based on normalizing flows, built upon the end-to-end VITS framework for high-fidelity waveform generation. We introduce a mel-style encoder to capture expressive style features and employ data augmentation to improve robustness in noisy environments. Experimental results demonstrate that CFLOW-VC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both objective and subjective evaluations. Audio samples are publicly available.
column7: FeiBao Song(Anhui Univeristy)

column4: WhispEar: A Bidirectional Framework for Scaling Whispered Speech Conversion via Pseudo-Parallel Whisper Generation
column6: Whispered speech lacks vocal fold vibration and fundamental frequency, resulting in degraded acoustic cues and making whisper-to-normal (W2N) conversion challenging, especially with limited parallel data. We propose WhispEar, a bidirectional framework based on unified semantic representations that capture speaking-mode-invariant information shared by whispered and normal speech. The framework contains both W2N and normal-to-whisper (N2W) models. Notably, the N2W model enables zero-shot pseudo-parallel whisper generation from abundant normal speech, allowing scalable data augmentation for W2N training. Increasing generated data consistently improves performance. We also release the largest bilingual (Chinese-English) whispered-normal parallel corpus to date. Experiments demonstrate that WhispEar outperforms strong baselines and benefits significantly from scalable pseudo-parallel data.
column7: Zihao Fang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Yingda Shen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zifan Guan(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Tongtong Song(Honor Device Co., Ltd); Zhenyi Liu(Honor Device Co., Ltd); Zhizheng Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Research Institute of Big Data; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute; Amphion Technology Co., Ltd.)

column4: Imitation Learning for Elder-Facing Speech Synthesis
column6: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis have achieved highly natural and expressive speech generation. However, these systems are designed for general adults and overlook older adults' speech comprehension needs due to age-related sensory and cognitive decline. Prior work involves older adults by collecting preference feedback to tune model parameters. However, obtaining sufficient preference data is costly and difficult, as older adults quickly become fatigued during collection. In this paper, we propose a novel imitation learning (IL) framework to learn TTS models from expert demonstrations. We further improve Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with two-stage on-policy reward learning (OPRL) to mitigate reward hacking under limited supervision from expert demonstration. Experimental results show that GRPO w/ OPRL outperforms GRPO and supervised baselines in objective and subjective metrics. Audio samples are available at https://dongru1.github.io/demo/im-efss/
column7: Dongrui Han(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Weidong Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Jiawen Kang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Mingyu Cui(Tencent Hunyuan); Helen Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xixin Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: How Linguistic Dimension Interactions Shape Meaning Preservation in Multilingual ASR
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition errors emerge from interactions across linguistic dimensions. While prior work correlated errors with external features, it remains unclear whether these patterns hold when linguistic features are measured from ASR outputs. We analysed substitution errors on the FLEURS dataset using Whisper and Seamless, computing phonetic, morphological, syntactic, and lexical similarity directly from ASR audio and transcriptions. Results revealed that semantic preservation emerges from systematic cross-dimension interactions: morphological and syntactic features operated interdependently while phonological accuracy intensified when syntax was preserved. Interaction patterns differed across architectures: Seamless showed better baseline performance, while Whisper showed heightened error sensitivity but leveraged morphological information more effectively, showing that ASR architectures integrate linguistic information through fundamentally different mechanisms.
